This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
[![News from Berkeley Lab logo](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/news-from-berkeley-lab.svg)](https://newscenter.lbl.gov)

![Researcher in blue gloves inspects a Sample Box.](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/XBD-202410-192-002_news-hero.jpg)    

# Partnering with Industry to Accelerate Quantum Computing

           

* [Article](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/all-news/?type=article)
* [Quantum](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/all-news/?topic=152608)
       

The Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley Lab) is contributing to the development of quantum computing technologies to help solve grand challenges in energy, physics, chemistry, and beyond.

A big part of this effort is serving as a go-to resource for companies at the vanguard of quantum computing R&D and preparing the quantum workforce of tomorrow. Berkeley Lab partners with industry and across the quantum research ecosystem — from [theory to application](https://www.lbl.gov/research/quantum/) — to fabricate and test quantum-based devices, develop software and algorithms, and build prototype computers and networks. These capabilities also enable Berkeley Lab to play a key role in [Quantum California](https://business.ca.gov/industries/high-tech/quantum/), a new statewide initiative to coordinate California’s leadership in quantum technology, workforce development, and economic growth. 

“Berkeley Lab’s expertise and capabilities are a vital component of the nation’s quantum ecosystem and help ensure that breakthroughs can move from experimental stages to practical applications,” said Bert de Jong, Quantum Systems Accelerator Director and Berkeley Lab scientist.

Here are several ways Berkeley Lab is already a vital part of the nation’s quantum ecosystem, supporting industry and more:

## Quantum Application Network Testbed for Novel Entanglement Technology (QUANT-NET)

[QUANT-NET](https://quantnet.lbl.gov/) is building a three-node distributed quantum computing testbed that connects Berkeley Lab with UC Berkeley, distributing quantum entanglement across 5 km of fiber. The project is [led by researchers](https://quantnet.lbl.gov/team) at Berkeley Lab and ESnet, working with co-PIs from UC Berkeley, the California Institute of Technology, and the University of Innsbruck. It is DOE’s only testbed devoted to distributed quantum computing. The QUANT-NET team collaborates with industry partners to develop and deploy their relevant components on the testbed, provides its modular software for use with other quantum networks, and shares technology advancements made on the testbed with the research community. 

The team has made significant progress toward a practical, scalable quantum network. The testbed currently offers custom-built ion-trap quantum computing nodes, with leading 3-D printed micro-traps optimized for quantum communications. The team also deployed quantum frequency conversion to telecom frequencies, and they developed an innovative modular quantum network software platform with [a two-level framework that automates quantum network operations](https://www.es.net/news-and-publications/esnet-news/2026/building-a-flexible-control-framework-for-quantum-networks/). This two-level approach recently won the [best paper award](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7368703158191099905) for the quantum networking & communications track at the IEEE Quantum Week 2025 conference.

        

### 

 ![A close-up view of an optical lens with various red, black, and metal details surrounding.](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/890x665px_Quant-Net_opticaldetail-BartNagelPhoto-5278.jpg)   

### 

 ![Four researchers in a dark lab space stand around a device with colorful wires and metallic pipes.](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/890x665px_QUANT-NETTeamCreditBartNagle.jpg)      

## Quantum Systems Accelerator (QSA)

[The Quantum Systems Accelerator (QSA)](https://quantumsystemsaccelerator.org/), led by Berkeley Lab in partnership with Sandia National Laboratories, is one of five DOE national quantum information science research centers. Established in 2020 and [renewed in 2025](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/2025/11/04/the-quantum-systems-accelerator-embarks-on-next-five-years-of-pioneering-quantum-technologies-for-science/), QSA brings together experts from leading academic institutions, industry, and national laboratories to develop quantum devices capable of tackling scientific problems beyond the reach of conventional computers, using three leading qubit technologies: trapped ions, superconducting systems, and neutral atoms.

Through these multi-sector collaborations, QSA’s scientific breakthroughs — such as reconfigurable array systems of neutral atoms — have been adopted by industry, with hardware deployed by companies like QuEra and commercial licensing of flex cable technologies. QSA has demonstrated a 256-atom quantum simulator, advancing the scalability and capabilities of quantum hardware for real-world applications. The open-source QubiC control system, also leveraged by industry collaborators like [NVIDIA’s NVQLink](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/2025/10/29/new-lab-and-nvidia-partnership-integrates-quantum-and-ai-supercomputing-for-next-generation-research/), supports scalable device benchmarking and algorithm development.

[QSA’s innovation ecosystem](https://quantumsystemsaccelerator.org/team/qsa-at-a-glance/) includes dedicated industry roundtables, and partners benefit from access to broader resources, such as world-class quantum foundries and national user facilities, open-access software, and rapid design qubit capabilities. These resources offer clear entry points for industry collaboration and have enabled successful partnerships with both established companies and startups.

    ![A researcher in a blue plaid shirt and black safety goggles stands behind a large laser experiment set up. The subject is blocked from colorful hanging wires and other apparatus.](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/1440x795px_XBD-202304-062-049.jpg)    

## National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC)

[The National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC)](https://www.nersc.gov/) enables the work of over 11,000 science researchers through high performance computing. Since 2022, NERSC’s QIS @ *Perlmutter* program, which supports projects in quantum information science with compute time and expertise, has awarded more than half a million compute hours to more than 30 QIS project teams across national labs, industry and academia. Additionally, NERSC’s [Quantum Computing Access](https://www.nersc.gov/users/user-news/apply-for-quantum-computing-access-via-qcan-program-2) program offers some users access to quantum computers at [IBM](https://www.nersc.gov/news-and-events/news/nersc-launches) and QuEra Computing for use in their research. Collaborating with companies like NVIDIA, QuEra, Xanadu, Rigetti, and others on projects in quantum simulation, error mitigation, chemistry, materials science, and condensed matter physics, NERSC is accelerating quantum simulations at supercomputing scale.

    ![The Aquila magneto-optical trap in QuEra’s facilities.](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/1440x795px_Inside_QuEra.jpg)    

## Molecular Foundry

The [Molecular Foundry](https://foundry.lbl.gov/) provides access to expertise, instrumentation, and tool development for research at the smallest scales. Since phenomena at the nanoscale touch nearly every field of science, the Foundry brings together a broad range of capabilities, all under one roof. Researchers here are working to improve fundamental understanding of quantum phenomena in materials, targeting breakthroughs in coherence and scalability in quantum computing and sensing. Industry researchers can collaborate with staff who integrate atomic-scale synthesis and design, multimodal characterization, AI accelerated theory, and device feedback to achieve these goals. Available tools include a QIS cluster tool that enables researchers to experiment with dozens of materials and methods for making qubit components in a single automated system, and a soon-to-be-delivered dilution refrigerator that will enable high-throughput analysis of qubits. 

## Advanced Light Source

The [Advanced Light Source](https://als.lbl.gov/) (ALS) produces bright beams of X-ray, ultraviolet, and infrared light for cutting-edge research. Each year, as many as 2,000 scientists from industry, academia, and national labs use the ALS to probe materials with atomic precision — work that underpins technologies from semiconductors to energy storage. ALS capabilities are advancing the quantum frontier by enabling visualization and control of quantum states in new materials, including superconductors, topological insulators, and atomically thin magnets — helping industry accelerate innovation in next-generation electronics and quantum devices.

## **Preparing Tomorrow’s Workforce**

As cutting-edge quantum research pushes the boundaries of technology, national labs are also helping to build a future workforce ready for the rapidly evolving field. At the forefront of this effort is QSA, which trains over 150 graduate students and 100 postdoctoral students annually, building a robust pipeline of quantum talent to keep American businesses and research organizations at the forefront of the field. 

Complementing QSA’s efforts at Berkeley Lab, internships and hands-on research projects at the [Advanced Quantum Testbed](https://aqt.lbl.gov/) (AQT) prepare students, postdocs, and early-career researchers for careers in fields such as quantum device design and fabrication, cryogenic engineering, and scalable quantum software. Alumni go on to lead innovation at technology companies, startups, and research institutes. Through collaborative R&D, hardware partnerships, and skilled talent, AQT [strengthens](https://aqt.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2025/06/4-CSAO-9071-AQT-Five-Year-Impact-Report_FINAL-rev-1-1.pdf) America’s leadership in transformative quantum technologies. 

Building on this strong foundation of graduate and postdoctoral training, efforts are also underway to engage students much earlier in their educational journeys. Berkeley Lab’s Academic Learning Internships and Faculty Training Office (formerly [Workforce Development & Education](https://education.lbl.gov/) and K–12 STEM Education programs), in collaboration with partners such as Sandia National Laboratories, is developing programs that introduce high school students and educators to quantum concepts well before career paths are firmly set. The aim is to spark curiosity, build foundational skills, and create pathways into future quantum careers.

One such pioneering initiative for high school students and educators is QSA’s [Quantum Computing Mathematics and Physics Summer Camp (QCaMP](https://quantumsystemsaccelerator.org/ecosystem/qcamp/)). What began as a series of short online sessions has evolved into comprehensive, in-person programs. To date, QCaMP has reached more than 300 educators as well as over 200 students nationwide. Many alumni — both students and teachers — have returned to Berkeley Lab as quantum research interns. Building on this momentum, Berkeley Lab plans to deepen partnerships with community colleges and universities in 2026, with an increased emphasis on workforce readiness.

    ![A teacher in protective glasses sets up an experiment on a table. The table displays multiple lens aparati.](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/1440x795px_XBD-202507-093-019.jpg)    

The Advanced Light Source, NERSC, and the Molecular Foundry are DOE Office of Science user facilities located at Berkeley Lab. 

###

[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory](https://www.lbl.gov/) (Berkeley Lab) is committed to groundbreaking research focused on discovery science and solutions for abundant and reliable energy supplies. The lab’s expertise spans materials, chemistry, physics, biology, earth and environmental science, mathematics, and computing. Researchers from around the world rely on the lab’s world-class scientific facilities for their own pioneering research. Founded in 1931 on the belief that the biggest problems are best addressed by teams, Berkeley Lab and its scientists have been recognized with 17 Nobel Prizes. Berkeley Lab is a multiprogram national laboratory managed by the University of California for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Science.

DOE’s Office of Science is the single largest supporter of basic research in the physical sciences in the United States, and is working to address some of the most pressing challenges of our time. For more information, please visit [energy.gov/science](http://energy.gov/science).

args.summary:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley Lab) is partnering with industry to accelerate quantum computing, serving as a key resource for quantum R&D and workforce development. The lab contributes to Quantum California, a statewide initiative, and operates several major programs:

1. **QUANT-NET**: A DOE-funded testbed for distributed quantum computing connecting Berkeley Lab with UC Berkeley via 5 km of fiber. It features custom-built ion-trap quantum computing nodes with 3D-printed micro-traps, quantum frequency conversion, and a modular software platform that won a best paper award at IEEE Quantum Week 2025.

2. **Quantum Systems Accelerator (QSA)**: Led by Berkeley Lab with Sandia National Laboratories, one of five DOE national quantum centers. Renewed in 2025, QSA develops quantum devices using trapped ions, superconducting systems, and neutral atoms. Breakthroughs include a 256-atom quantum simulator and the open-source QubiC control system used by NVIDIA. QSA trains over 150 graduate students and 100 postdoctoral students annually.

3. **NERSC**: Supports over 11,000 researchers with high-performance computing. Since 2022, the QIS @ Perlmutter program has awarded 500,000+ compute hours to 30+ QIS project teams. NERSC also offers quantum computing access via IBM and QuEra, collaborating with NVIDIA, Xanadu, Rigetti, and others.

4. **Molecular Foundry**: Provides nanoscale research tools including a QIS cluster tool for automated qubit component experimentation and a dilution refrigerator for high-throughput qubit analysis.

5. **Advanced Light Source (ALS)**: Used by ~2,000 scientists annually to probe materials with atomic precision, advancing quantum state visualization in superconductors, topological insulators, and atomically thin magnets.

The lab is also preparing tomorrow's workforce through programs like QCaMP (Quantum Computing Mathematics and Physics Summer Camp), which has reached over 300 educators and 200+ students nationwide, with plans to expand partnerships with community colleges and universities in 2026. Bert de Jong, QSA Director, stated: "Berkeley Lab's expertise and capabilities are a vital component of the nation's quantum ecosystem and help ensure that breakthroughs can move from experimental stages to practical applications."

<webpage_content>
[![Computing Sciences logo with wordmark](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/CSA-2024-Wordmark.png)](https://cs.lbl.gov)

![Close-up photo of a quantum processor unit.](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/WWD-Quantum-Information-Science-Technology-Hero-BLDS-XL-990.png)   

# Quantum Information Science and Technology

   

Berkeley Lab’s Computing Sciences Area is at the forefront of harnessing quantum information science and technology to drive discoveries that will improve our lives—from developing new materials to ensuring secure communications.

We are pioneering advancements across the quantum research ecosystem, from theory to application, by partnering with industry and academia. Together, we fabricate and test quantum-based devices, develop software and algorithms, build prototype computers and networks, and apply these innovations to achieve breakthroughs in physics and chemistry.

        

### Quantum Systems Accelerator (QSA)

 ![](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/QSA.png)  

The QSA, one of the Department of Energy’s National Quantum Information Science Research Centers, brings together national labs, industry, and universities to tackle critical challenges in quantum information science, foster research collaboration, and train the next generation of quantum scientists and engineers.

    

### Advanced Quantum Testbed (AQT)

 ![](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/2020-AQT-cryo-refrigerator-quantum-scaled-e1756332098989-890x1039.jpg)  

AQT is a collaborative laboratory that designs, fabricates, and operates superconducting quantum processors. It enables scientists to co-develop and implement quantum algorithms for solving challenging problems in optimization, materials science, and high-energy physics, utilizing open-access, intermediate-scale quantum hardware.

    

### QUANT-NET

 ![Artistic concept of a quatum network.](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Quant-Net-artistic-concept.jpg)  

QUANT-NET leverages world-leading expertise in quantum technologies, optics, materials, networks, testbed operations, and other assets from Berkeley Lab, UC Berkeley, and Caltech. It aims to build a software-controlled, application-focused quantum computing network between Berkeley Lab and UC Berkeley based on entanglement.

    

### QIS at NERSC

 ![NERSC Perlmutter](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Perlmutter-890x595.jpg)  

QIS at NERSC is a program that provides compute time on Perlmutter for projects advancing quantum information science, including quantum algorithm development, simulation, and integration with high-performance computing. The initiative supports research collaborations between academia, industry, and Berkeley Lab to accelerate breakthroughs in quantum technologies.

    

### MACH-Q

 ![Close-up view of a blue printed circuit board with electronic pathways and solder points, illuminated by glowing light effects and out-of-focus bokeh in the background.](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/iStock-1226985345-1.jpg)  

Modular and Error-Aware Software Stack for Heterogeneous Quantum Computing Ecosystems (MACH-Q) is developing a modular, readily expandable, and error-aware quantum software stack. These capabilities will enable plug-and-play deployment in emerging heterogeneous and distributed quantum computing environments, as well as integration with third-party software.

    

### Berkeley Quantum Synthesis Toolkit (BQSKit)

 ![Close-up view of a quantum computer’s superconducting processor housed within a cylindrical, gold-colored cryogenic chamber, featuring multiple stacked plates connected by intricate wiring and metallic rods.](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/AQT-4-890x544.jpg)  

BQSKit is a superoptimizing quantum compiler and research platform that integrates ideas from multiple Berkeley Lab projects into an accessible and easily extensible software suite.

    

### Superconducting Race Logic Accelerators

 ![Close-up view of a dark-colored printed circuit board with intricate gold pathways, connection points, and electronic components.](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Racelogic-1.jpg)  

Superconducting race logic accelerators are ultra-fast, energy-efficient computing devices that use superconducting electronics to advance classical computation, leveraging technologies and fabrication methods also foundational to quantum computing research.

    

### HamPerf

 ![Logo for HamPerf featuring a blue grid icon next to a circle containing a wavy line, with the word ](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/HamPerf-2.jpg)  

HamPerf is a quantum benchmarking approach that evaluates the computational utility of quantum processors by focusing on the underlying mathematical descriptions (Hamiltonians) of problems, enabling fair comparisons across different hardware and algorithms.

    

### Cryogenic Control for Quantum

 ![Logo for Cryogenic Control for Quantum, featuring a stylized snowflake and a quantum circuit diagram enclosed in a circle above the text “Cryogenic Control for Quantum” in bold blue letters.](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/CRYOGENIC-CONTROL-FOR-QUANTUM.jpg)  

Cryogenic Control for Quantum explores innovative low-temperature control solutions using superconducting technology to enable scalable, high-fidelity control of quantum systems, overcoming the limitations of current room-temperature and cryo-CMOS approaches.

  

### FABLE

 ![Logo for FABLE showing a stylized circuit board icon with interconnected lines and nodes, above the word ](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/FABLE-1.jpg)  

FABLE is a software tool that efficiently generates quantum circuits to represent large, dense matrices—enabling advanced quantum algorithms by embedding these matrices into quantum operations with minimal computational overhead.

    

### AQuA-DATA

 ![Closeup of quatum gate hardware.](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/AQT-Quantum-equipment.jpg)  

AQuA-DATA (Advanced Quantum Algorithms for Diverse Applications and Theoretical Advancements in Science), is aimed at creating new quantum algorithms with applications across various scientific fields. This work will contribute to optimizing quantum computation for diverse real-world problems, making quantum technology more accessible for practical use​.

  

### QCaMP

 ![Group of young people participating in QCamp 2024 clustered around a large display of their fellow campers who are remote.](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/CS-WWD-QCamp-BLDS-Med.jpg)  

QCaMP (Quantum, Computing, Mathematics, & Physics) is a free, hands-on summer camp hosted by Berkeley Lab that introduces high school students and teachers to the fundamentals of computing and quantum physics, offering practical experience with quantum circuits and real-world quantum computers, with programs available in the Bay Area and partner locations nationwide.

            

### Quantum Chip Hero Run

 ![](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/quantum_sim_group_shot-890x594.jpg)     

### Seven Ways Berkeley Lab is Pioneering the Quantum Future

 ![Man](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/PioneerQuantumFuture.jpg)     

### Science Power-Up: Rewriting the Rules with Quantum

 ![Portrait De-Jong-Bert](https://cs.lbl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/De-Jong-Bert-890x666.jpg)      

Last edited: December 18, 2025

### Our Organization

<webpage_content>
[![UC Berkeley](/profiles/openberkeley/themes/openberkeley_theme_base/assets/images/logo-berkeley-white-2.svg)](https://www.berkeley.edu)

# Quantum Information Science

![A quantum computer close up](https://physics.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/styles/openberkeley_image_full/public/general/quantumphysics_researchcategory_page.jpg?itok=VokkNwEv&timestamp=1701827739)

## Quantum Information Science at Berkeley

Berkeley scientists pursue a broad array of topics, including fundamental questions about the quantum world, instrumentation for quantum computations and control, and novel applications of quantum science. Recent technological breakthroughs have enabled unprecedented control over quantum systems, such as single atoms, molecules, and well-engineered materials. By harnessing those insights and opportunities, we strive to lay the foundation for the next generation of quantum technologies, including the development of quantum computing, precision metrology, and more generally, a deeper understanding of the universe.

---

## What is QIST?

Quantum Information Science and Technology (QIST) is an emerging field at the nexus of Physics, Chemistry, Engineering, and Computer Science. Quantum information combines ideas from physics and computer science to provide us with a new perspective on information and the universe itself. Probably the most exciting aspect is that QIST opens the path to solve computational and communication problems previously thought not to be tractable. On the other hand , QIST currently also transforms physics, and more generally the natural sciences, by providing a deeper understanding of quantum mechanics as well as enabling new tools such as quantum simulators and sensors. At Berkeley, we address questions on the quantum-ness of nature, such as the universe itself and its constituents, study quantum many-body physics and entanglement, develop advanced sensors to measure time and detect Dark Matter, and research how to construct quantum computers and communication devices.

---

## QIST at Berkeley falls into 5 categories:

## Quantum Computing

Fault-tolerant quantum computers promise to solve hard computational problems such as factoring of large integers or quantum chemistry calculations.

## Quantum Many-Body Physics

Using well-controlled quantum systems, we can study the properties of quantum many-body systems which are otherwise very hard to synthesize. The results of these quantum simulators can be used to benchmark quantum-many body theories.

## Quantum Sensing and Metrology

Leveraging the control of quantum systems, sensors with unprecedented accuracy and functionality can be built. Prominent examples include individual atoms for time-keeping and tests of fundamental symmetries, as well as defects in solid state materials for sensing with high spatial resolution.

## Quantum Information Theory

More generally, quantum information provides tools to better understand quantum phenomena. Thus ideas from quantum information help among other things in understanding black holes as well as measurement and emergent phenomena.

## Quantum Communication

Linking distant quantum systems allows for secure communication may also be used to improve telescopes or simply to connect quantum computers to improve their capacity.

## Our quantum efforts are centered within the following organizations:

### [NSF Challenge Institute for Quantum Computing](https://ciqc.berkeley.edu/)

CIQC addresses fundamental challenges to the development of the quantum computer by bringing together scientists with diverse background ranging from math to engineering.

### [Quantum Systems Accelerator](https://quantumsystemsaccelerator.org/)

The Quantum Systems Accelerator (QSA), led by Lawrence Berkeley National Lab, is a U.S. National Quantum Information Science Research Center funded by the Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science. The Quantum Systems Accelerator (composed of 15 partner institution universities and national laboratories) is catalyzing national leadership in quantum information science to co-design the algorithms, quantum devices, and engineering solutions needed to deliver certified quantum advantage in Department of Energy scientific applications.

### [Advanced Quantum Testbed](https://aqt.lbl.gov/)

Advanced Quantum Testbed (AQT) - The AQT is a DOE-funded advanced superconducting platform for quantum computation that fosters deep research collaborations through an open user program.

### QUANT-NET

QUANT-NET is a DOE-funded consortium of 4 research partners – Berkeley Lab, UC Berkeley, Caltech, and the University of Innsbruck – that seek to establish a three-node, distributed quantum computing network between two sites (Berkeley Lab and UC Berkeley). The grand vision of QUANT-NET is to provide the infrastructure to test and evaluate different quantum networking technologies.

### [The Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing](https://simons.berkeley.edu/homepage)

The Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing at UC Berkeley brings together the world's leading researchers in theoretical computer science with those in other fields, and hosts several workshops and intensive research programs focused on quantum information science.

This is a video transcript about an alleged discovery by Google DeepMind's Quantum AI in late 2024-2025. A hybrid quantum-classical AI system was found to be predicting future events *before* the input data existed, suggesting retrocausality (information flowing backward in time). The system was fed financial market data and other datasets (weather, seismic activity, stock markets, brain scans), and its predictions matched real future outcomes with 94% accuracy across 847 experiments. The statistical probability of this happening by chance was calculated at 1 in 10^47. Physicists proposed the "symmetrical information model" (Dr. Elena Cardona, Institute for Advanced Study) suggesting the universe has no preferred time direction. The discovery has split the scientific community between skepticism and profound unease, with implications for causality, free will, and the nature of reality. By summer 2025, at least 40 research institutions launched replication attempts, and funding for quantum AI research tripled. The video explores philosophical questions about determinism, the many-worlds interpretation, and whether the future is fixed or changeable. Military and intelligence agencies are reportedly exploring applications for "surveillance across time."
</summary>

3. Accelerate high-end talent recruitment and domestic cultivation.

URL: https://www.kitp.ucsb.edu/news/topological-quantum-computing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the KITP Newsletter (Spring 2006) describes the KITP program "Topological Phases and Quantum Computation" (Feb. 21 to May 19, 2006), which brought together approximately 80 participants from four research streams: condensed matter theorists (experts on fractional quantum Hall effect and topological phases), condensed matter experimentalists (studying fractional quantum Hall states in gallium arsenide), quantum computation theorists, and proponents of topological quantum computing. The program was organized by Chetan Nayak (Microsoft's topological quantum computing project), Sander Bais (University of Amsterdam), and John Preskill (Caltech). 

The article explains the key concepts behind topological quantum computing. Unlike conventional approaches that use qubits based on individual particles (like electron spin), topological quantum computing uses anyons—collective excitations that exist only in two-dimensional space with "fractional statistics" between bosonic and fermionic. The term "anyon" was coined in 1982 by Frank Wilczek at KITP. 

The key advantage of the topological approach is inherent error correction. Since information is stored in the topology (shape) of the system rather than local details, small perturbations don't cause errors. Computation is performed through "braiding"—moving one excitation around another—and the exact path doesn't matter, only the topological relationship. This gives an error rate of essentially zero.

Key historical developments include: Peter Shor's 1994 discovery of quantum factoring algorithms; Alexei Kitaev's 1997 landmark paper on non-abelian anyons and built-in error correction; and work by Freedman, Wang, and Larsen showing non-abelian anyons have equal computational power to standard qubits. The most promising experimental system is the 5/2 fractional quantum Hall state (discovered in 1987), with a specific computation scheme proposed in 2004 by Nayak, Freedman, and Das Sarma. The 12/5 state may be even better but more delicate. The article notes that serious experimental efforts were underway to realize topological quantum computing devices in gallium arsenide, with groups in friendly competition.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: topological quantum computation in nLab ---
URL: https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+quantum+computation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Topological Quantum Computation

## Main Topic
The nLab page on **topological quantum computation** (TQC) describes a paradigm for quantum computing that uses topological quantum field theory (TQFT) to achieve inherent protection against decoherence and noise, in contrast to conventional approaches that rely on post-hoc quantum error correction.

## Core Idea

### The Problem
Common quantum computing architectures (superconducting qubits, trapped ions, spin resonance) suffer from an intrinsic tension: quantum gates require interaction between subsystems, but coherence requires avoiding interaction. This problem plagues contemporary NISQ devices and has contributed to the "Quantum Winter."

### The Bold Solution
Topological quantum computing aims to implement quantum gates that operate **without interaction** by exploiting the quantum adiabatic theorem. The approach requires a quantum system (e.g., a crystalline quantum material) with three key properties:

1. **Ground state degeneracy**: Multiple distinct ground states even at absolute zero (the Hilbert space of ground states has dimension > 1)
2. **Energy gap**: All excitations require energy above a threshold Δ, so quanta with energy < Δ have no interaction
3. **Control parameters**: Continuously tunable parameters (strain, voltage) that maintain the above properties

### How It Works
Under adiabatic conditions, slowly varying external parameters transforms ground states into each other via Berry phases (holonomic quantum gates). These are protected from noise quanta but may still be sensitive to noise in the parameter paths themselves.

**Topological invariance** requires additional properties:
- **Parameter topology**: The parameter space has non-contractible loops (non-trivial fundamental group)
- **Local parameter independence**: Continuously deformable parameter paths yield the same transformation (flat Berry connection)

Materials with all these properties are **topologically ordered**, and the resulting processes are **topological quantum gates**, protected against both external noise and parameter path noise.

## Via Anyon Braiding

The most developed approach (originally proposed by Kitaev 2003 and Freedman et al. 2003) envisions:
- A 2D quantum material (like graphene)
- With defect points whose positions constitute the control parameters
- The configuration space of points yields braid group representations acting on ground states
- These defects are referred to as **defect anyons**

### Experimental Status
- **Abelian anyons** have been observed in fractional quantum Hall systems, though controlled movement seems out of reach
- **Non-Abelian anyons** (needed for universal quantum computation) remain theoretically expected but experimentally challenging
- Claims of Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in the 2010s "seem not to hold water"
- More recent work focuses on **quantum simulation of anyons** on ordinary quantum hardware

### Mathematical Framework
Defect anyons are expected to be described by Chern-Simons theory/Reshetikhin-Turaev theory, classified by modular tensor categories. Quantum gates are encoded by braid group elements and executed through braid representations on the space of quantum states.

### Topological Quantum Compilation
Braid-based quantum gates differ significantly from standard quantum gates. For example, a single CNOT gate requires a lengthy braid. This makes **compilation** of quantum algorithms to machine-level gates a major challenge, with formal verification likely a practical necessity.

## Key References
Foundational works include Kitaev (2003), Freedman, Kitaev, Larsen & Wang (2003), and Nayak et al. (2008). Monographs by Wang (2010), Pachos (2012), and Simon (2023) provide comprehensive treatments.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The idea of topological quantum computation is to implement quantum computation on quantum systems whose dynamics is described by topological quantum field theory (TQFT), so that the defining invariance of TQFTs under local perturbations implements protection of the quantum coherence by fundamental physical principles, instead of after the fact by quantum error correction.,Find quantum gates operating without interaction!,The chief advantage of anyonic [topological quantum] computation would be physical error correction... In contrast, the presumptive qubit-model of quantum computation, which repairs errors combinatorically, requires a fantastically low initial error rate...,The central idea of TQC is to encode qubits into states of topological phases of matter. Qubits encoded in such states are expected to be topologically protected, or robust, against the prying eyes of the environment, which are believed to be the bane of conventional quantum computation.,What is missing is the breakthrough... bypassing quantum error correction by using far-more-stable qubits, in an approach called topological quantum computing.

Google's Quantum AI team has proposed a five-stage framework to guide the development of useful quantum computing applications, as detailed in a paper published on arXiv and a companion blog post by Ryan Babbush, Director of Research, Quantum Algorithms and Applications. The framework shifts the focus from hardware milestones (like qubit counts) to application maturity and real-world utility.

The five stages are:
- **Stage I – Discovery:** New quantum algorithms in abstract mathematical settings. The researchers note a concerning decline in foundational algorithm research due to risk-averse incentives in funding.
- **Stage II – Hard Instances:** Identifying concrete problem instances where quantum computers outperform classical ones. This stage is often overlooked but critical for bridging theory to practice.
- **Stage III – Theory-to-Application Gap:** Demonstrating quantum advantage on real-world tasks. This is identified as the most significant bottleneck. Google recommends an "algorithm-first" approach (starting with known quantum primitives like simulation) rather than a "problem-first" approach.
- **Stage IV – Engineering the Advantage:** Optimizing, compiling, and estimating resources (qubits, gates) for implementation. This is described as tedious but essential, with tools like Qualtran, Q#, QREF, and Bartiq emerging to help.
- **Stage V – Deployment:** Application in real production environments. No confirmed real-world quantum advantage exists yet, but early efforts like certified random number generation hint at the path forward.

The researchers call for renewed investment in foundational research, cross-disciplinary collaboration, open-source tools, and a shift toward measuring progress by problems solved rather than qubit counts. Google suggests AI (including large language models like Gemini) could help bridge knowledge gaps by scanning for real-world problems matching known quantum speedups. Microsoft and UC Santa Barbara researchers unveiled an eight-qubit topological quantum processor, the first of its kind, on Wednesday. The chip, developed by Microsoft Station Q led by UCSB physics professor Chetan Nayak, represents a breakthrough in quantum computing by creating a "topological superconductor" — a new state of matter that hosts Majorana zero modes (MZMs). These quasiparticles, which are their own antiparticles and can retain memory of their positions over time, enable more stable and fault-tolerant quantum computing by distributing quantum information across a physical system rather than individual particles. The researchers realized MZMs by placing an indium arsenide semiconductor nanowire close to an aluminum superconductor. The eight-qubit processor serves as a proof-of-concept, accompanied by a paper in Nature and a preprint roadmap for scaling up the technology. The topological approach promises more robust error correction built at the hardware level, reducing the need for additional qubits for error correction. Key collaborators include Chris Palmstrom (materials), Susanne Stemmer (fabrication), and the work builds on Nobel Prize-winning ideas of the late Herb Kroemer.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Deloitte article (published August 11, 2025, by Scott Buchholz, Diana Kearns-Manolatos, and Natasha Buckley) explores scenario planning for quantum computing over the next five years (leading into 2030). It argues that organizations should act now on quantum strategy regardless of when commercial scalability arrives.

The article presents four plausible futures based on two key uncertainties: (1) whether the quantum talent and operating environment is undeveloped vs. developed, and (2) whether scalable quantum computing arrives sooner vs. later than expected.

**The Four Scenarios:**

1. **Surprise** – Scalable quantum arrives sooner, but talent ecosystem is undeveloped, leading to talent wars. Early movers gain advantages; laggards struggle to catch up.
2. **Quandary** – Neither talent ecosystem nor scalable quantum develops quickly. Organizations that continue experimenting gain incremental advantages and institutional knowledge.
3. **Explosion** – Both talent and scalable quantum arrive sooner. Those with prior POC experience and roadmaps are best positioned to capitalize.
4. **Leap** – Talent ecosystem develops but scalable quantum is delayed. Early investors benefit from established relationships and secondary advantages.

**Key Signals:**
- 250,000 quantum computing jobs needed by 2030; current job postings are growing slowly
- Major tech breakthroughs: Amazon's cat qubit chip, Microsoft's topoconductor, Google targeting commercial quantum within 5 years, PsiQuantum planning useful quantum computer by 2027
- Quantum patent filings growing; companies have filed over 1,100 quantum patents in the last 5 years
- 25% of surveyed US business leaders invested in quantum in 2024 (3x increase from 2023)
- Quantum venture investment reached ~$2B in 2024 vs. ~$132B for AI
- Quantum computing market estimated to grow nearly 35% annually from 2024 to 2032

**Recommended Actions:**
- Develop a quantum road map with executive sponsorship now
- Build relationships with quantum ecosystem vendors and partners
- Start small-scale proofs of concept to build understanding
- Cross-train AI scientists on quantum mechanics
- Monitor for technical milestones but don't wait for the inflection point to act
- Prepare for post-quantum cryptography risks

The article emphasizes that developing quantum infrastructure and talent takes significant time, so waiting for the breakthrough means being too late. The key quote: "Whether commercial quantum computing arrives in three to five years or 10 to 15, the time to pursue a strategic road map is now."

1. **Hysteresis experiments**: First-ever hysteresis experiments on quantum computers, published in Science Advances. Hysteresis (memory effects in magnetic systems) is difficult to simulate with classical computers but naturally occurs in coupled qubits.

2. **Magnetic memory theory**: Frank Barrows led development of a conceptual framework understanding how qubits handle memory, showing programmable analog quantum computers as testbeds for non-equilibrium dynamics.

3. **Shannon information entropy**: Research led by Elijah Pelofske used Shannon entropy to quantify classical memory retention under quantum fluctuations, helping differentiate quantum vs. classical behavior.

4. **Criticality and temperature studies**: Published in Nature Communications, the team pushed D-Wave machines to Boltzmann sampling limits and demonstrated renormalization group methods for studying phase transitions, without suffering from critical slowing down. Additional research investigated thermometry of these quantum systems.

The team's work contrasts with the view that near-term quantum hardware is not useful, showing immediate applications for non-equilibrium dynamics, hysteresis, critical phenomena, Boltzmann sampling, and materials-relevant behavior. The research was supported by the Laboratory Directed Research and Development program, with collaborations including the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory.

This appears to not work as easily as one could have hoped. Hence, we wanted to go back to basics, and find simpler, more restricted ways of learning, but which could actually work and also have certain guarantees," said Martin Larocca., "This is the Holy Grail of Bayesian learning. More than a mathematical curiosity, our result has concrete practical implications... Our result implies that the same principle can now be applied in quantum computing," said Diego Garcia-Martin, the paper's first author., "This is the quest we've had. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Deloitte article (published August 11, 2025, by Scott Buchholz, Diana Kearns-Manolatos, and Natasha Buckley) explores scenario planning for quantum computing over the next five years (leading into 2030). It argues that organizations should act now on quantum strategy regardless of when commercial scalability arrives.

The article presents four plausible futures based on two key uncertainties: (1) whether the quantum talent and operating environment is undeveloped vs. developed, and (2) whether scalable quantum computing arrives sooner vs. later than expected.

**The Four Scenarios:**

1. **Surprise** – Scalable quantum arrives sooner, but talent ecosystem is undeveloped, leading to talent wars. Early movers gain advantages; laggards struggle to catch up.
2. **Quandary** – Neither talent ecosystem nor scalable quantum develops quickly. Organizations that continue experimenting gain incremental advantages and institutional knowledge.
3. **Explosion** – Both talent and scalable quantum arrive sooner. Those with prior POC experience and roadmaps are best positioned to capitalize.
4. **Leap** – Talent ecosystem develops but scalable quantum is delayed. Early investors benefit from established relationships and secondary advantages.

**Key Signals:**
- 250,000 quantum computing jobs needed by 2030; current job postings are growing slowly
- Major tech breakthroughs: Amazon's cat qubit chip, Microsoft's topoconductor, Google targeting commercial quantum within 5 years, PsiQuantum planning useful quantum computer by 2027
- Quantum patent filings growing; companies have filed over 1,100 quantum patents in the last 5 years
- 25% of surveyed US business leaders invested in quantum in 2024 (3x increase from 2023)
- Quantum venture investment reached ~$2B in 2024 vs. ~$132B for AI
- Quantum computing market estimated to grow nearly 35% annually from 2024 to 2032

**Recommended Actions:**
- Develop a quantum road map with executive sponsorship now
- Build relationships with quantum ecosystem vendors and partners
- Start small-scale proofs of concept to build understanding
- Cross-train AI scientists on quantum mechanics
- Monitor for technical milestones but don't wait for the inflection point to act
- Prepare for post-quantum cryptography risks

The article emphasizes that developing quantum infrastructure and talent takes significant time, so waiting for the breakthrough means being too late. The key quote: "Whether commercial quantum computing arrives in three to five years or 10 to 15, the time to pursue a strategic road map is now."

Led by Cristiano Nisoli, an interdisciplinary team achieved several breakthroughs:

1. **Hysteresis experiments**: First-ever hysteresis experiments on quantum computers, published in Science Advances. Hysteresis (memory effects in magnetic systems) is difficult to simulate with classical computers but naturally occurs in coupled qubits.

2. **Magnetic memory theory**: Frank Barrows led development of a conceptual framework understanding how qubits handle memory, showing programmable analog quantum computers as testbeds for non-equilibrium dynamics.

3. **Shannon information entropy**: Research led by Elijah Pelofske used Shannon entropy to quantify classical memory retention under quantum fluctuations, helping differentiate quantum vs. classical behavior.

4. **Criticality and temperature studies**: Published in Nature Communications, the team pushed D-Wave machines to Boltzmann sampling limits and demonstrated renormalization group methods for studying phase transitions, without suffering from critical slowing down. Additional research investigated thermometry of these quantum systems.

The team's work contrasts with the view that near-term quantum hardware is not useful, showing immediate applications for non-equilibrium dynamics, hysteresis, critical phenomena, Boltzmann sampling, and materials-relevant behavior. The research was supported by the Laboratory Directed Research and Development program, with collaborations including the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory.

# Categorical Tensor-Graph Semantics for Quantum Algorithms

###### Abstract

This paper investigates foundational quantum computing protocols from the intuitive perspective of categorical tensor-graph semantics within the category FHilb. While conventional Hilbert-space formalisms often conceal the structural nature of quantum algorithms behind high-dimensional matrix operations, the topological framework directly encodes algorithmic functionalities into their graphical skeletons. We provide a comprehensive topological reinterpretation of the Bernstein–Vazirani and Simon algorithms, demonstrating how topological transformations distill their core mathematical essence and clarify the operational mechanisms of oracles. Going beyond the standard qubit model, we construct explicit representations for the qutrit-adapted topological Deutsch–Jozsa and single-shot Grover algorithms. In particular, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the single-shot Grover search. We further implement CNOT gates via complementary Frobenius structures and investigate a diagrammatic decomposition scheme for the W-state preparation protocol. By bridging tensor category theory with practical quantum algorithmic design, this work furnishes a composable, scalable diagrammatic toolkit essential for automated circuit optimization across the evolving quantum hardware ecosystem.

## 1 Introduction

Since its inception by Feynman and Deutsch in the 1980s, quantum computing has evolved from abstract models toward physical realization. Presently, platforms by Google, IBM, IonQ, and Rigetti have achieved tens to hundreds of qubits—Google claimed "quantum supremacy" in 2019, while IBM launched the 1000+ qubit Condor processor, marking the NISQ era [[14](#bib.bib14), [1](#bib.bib1)]. However, traditional Hilbert-space formal methods, though rigorous, involve high-dimensional matrix operations that obscure the intuitive structure of entanglement, superposition, and interference, and struggle with combinatorial complexity. As hardware advances rapidly, more intuitive and compositional tools are urgently needed.

Categorical quantum mechanics addresses this challenge. Under severe NISQ constraints—limited qubits, short coherence times, and high noise—minimizing circuit depth and gate count is crucial. ZX-calculus transforms complex circuit equivalences into intuitive topological operations via graphical rewriting; phase teleportation enables non-local cancellation of non-Clifford phases, significantly reducing costly T-gates [[11](#bib.bib11)]. Recent work combining reinforcement learning with ZX-calculus achieves continuous optimization at 80-qubit, 2100-gate scales, providing a new automated paradigm for large-scale compilation. Open-source libraries PyZX and Quantomatic have enabled practical deployment and commercial integration [[12](#bib.bib12)]. Graphical languages also naturally describe lattice surgery and error mitigation protocols for fault-tolerant computing [[6](#bib.bib6), [8](#bib.bib8)].

This methodology is expanding across domains. In quantum natural language processing, the DisCoCat model unifies syntax and semantics via tensor networks, leveraging entanglement for semantic composition [[2](#bib.bib2), [13](#bib.bib13)]. In quantum machine learning, diagrammatic differentiation enables automatic differentiation for parameterized circuits [[7](#bib.bib7)]. During 2024–2025, advances combining graph neural networks with reinforcement learning (e.g., PPO-based policy optimization) and dynamic grouping strategies have further enhanced scalability.

In summary, categorical quantum mechanics and diagrammatic semantics provide: (1) new mathematical perspectives linking quantum computing to topology, logic, and computer science [[9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10), [5](#bib.bib5), [15](#bib.bib15)]; (2) intuitive, compositional, and automatable tools for algorithm design; and (3) full-process support for NISQ-era compilation while opening cross-disciplinary pathways with AI and NLP. As hardware scales expand, systematic development of these theories and tools is critical for transitioning quantum computing from laboratory to practice.

The quest for an intuitive and rigorous quantum formalism is deeply rooted in the mathematical development of tensor categories [[19](#bib.bib19), [20](#bib.bib20), [21](#bib.bib21)]. In pure mathematics, the theory of tensor categories has not only achieved significant success in areas such as topological invariants but has also fundamentally proven the strict algebraic equivalence between diagrammatic reasoning and planar topological deformations. This profound mathematical foundation validates categorical graphical semantics, ensuring that topological deformations in quantum computing are not merely heuristic illustrations, but exact algebraic evaluations.

Building upon Abramsky and Coecke’s pioneering Categorical Quantum Mechanics (CQM) [[22](#bib.bib22)] and the subsequent ZX-calculus [[17](#bib.bib17)], diagrammatic semantics have established a powerful foundation for quantum protocols. Furthermore, the theoretical boundaries of this framework continue to expand, as demonstrated by Majid’s formulation of a quantum and braided ZX-calculus that generalizes these diagrammatic techniques to braided monoidal categories [Maj23]. Directly inspired by Vicary’s foundational exploration of the topological structure of quantum algorithms [[15](#bib.bib15)], our work leverages tensor-graph semantics within the category FHilb to fundamentally dissect and reinterpret complex quantum computation. Rather than treating graphical rules merely as simplification tools, we utilize rigorous topological deformations to distill the algorithmic core of the Bernstein–Vazirani and Simon algorithms, the qutrit-adapted generalized Deutsch–Jozsa and single-shot Grover algorithms, as well as complex multi-particle entanglement protocols like the W-state preparation.

This study employs categorical topological language to describe quantum algorithms and quantum mechanics, revealing the internal mechanism of quantum advantage through tensor diagrams and demonstrating operational procedures via graphical expressions.

In Section 2, we focus on the tensor diagram semantics of the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm. We introduce the algorithm’s formal definition and quantum circuit, provide its tensor diagram semantics, and prove their correctness using transformation principles. Topological transformations are then applied to derive the simplest graphical form, and a comparison with the original circuit reveals the algorithm’s mathematical essence from the tensor diagram perspective.

In Section 3, we address the Simon algorithm analogously. Tensor diagram semantics are given, verified, and simplified via topological transformations, with a comparison to the original circuit to analyze its mathematical connotation. A comparative analysis of both algorithms’ simplified semantics explains their similarities and essential differences.

In Section 4, going beyond the binary qubit paradigm, we investigate multi-valued quantum systems. We provide the qutrit-adapted generalized Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm and the generalized single-shot Grover algorithm, mapping their execution directly to topological diagrams.

In Section 5, we analyze the controlled-NOT gate and quantum entanglement from the perspective of categorical composition. We provide an alternative diagrammatic proof for the properties of complementary Frobenius structures. Furthermore, we translate the standard W-state preparation circuit into the ZX-calculus framework and perform a systematic simplification using phase gadgets, local complementation and pivot rule. We demonstrate that this topological reduction yields an expression distinct from existing standard formulations.

## 2 Topological Bernstein-Vazirani

### 2.1 Introduction

In this section, we will use the knowledge of categorical quantum mechanics mentioned in Appendix A to reinterpret the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm from a tensor diagram perspective. This formulation avoids the complex computational processes in traditional circuit diagrams, converts the connections between different qubits into topological structures in tensor diagrams, and directly attributes the algorithm’s functionality to its topological skeleton.

The Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm considers the analysis of a function with a finite number of input bits and a single output bit. Suppose we have a hidden binary string s∈{0,1}ns\in\{0,1\}^{n}, and the function f:{0,1}n→{0,1}f:\{0,1\}^{n}\rightarrow\{0,1\} satisfies f⁡(x)=x⋅sf(x)=x\cdot s. The Bernstein-Vazirani problem is to find the string ss.

In the classical case, to obtain the value of an nn -bit string ss, we need to measure nn times. However, the quantum Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm only needs to access the function ff once to obtain the values of all nn bits. Its quantum circuit is as follows and inspired by [[15](#bib.bib15)], we give the topological version of Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm.

## 3 Topological Simon

Building upon the tensor diagram semantics of the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm presented in the previous section, we now analyze another classic protocol: Simon’s algorithm..

### 3.1 Introduction

Simon’s algorithm was proposed by Daniel R. Simon in 1994. It emerged at a critical turning point in the development of quantum computing—before this, although the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm and the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm had proven the query complexity advantages of quantum computing, the problems they addressed were still regarded as highly artificial theoretical constructions. However, Simon’s algorithm can achieve a balance between “naturalness" and “structurality". It was the first to apply quantum acceleration to a structured problem with clear cryptographic relevance, building a key bridge for quantum computing to move from theoretical singularity to practical value. It requires only O⁡(n)O(n) quantum queries to determine the hidden period, while the optimal classical probabilistic algorithm requires an exponential number of queries. This exponential separation not only demonstrates the computational power of quantum parallelism and quantum entanglement, but more importantly, its problem structure directly inspired Peter Shor’s quantum algorithms for integer factorization and discrete logarithms proposed at the end of 1994.

Simon’s algorithm is also a promise problem related to a function. ## 6 Conclusion

This paper investigates foundational quantum protocols through categorical tensor-graph semantics in FHilb, demonstrating that algorithmic functionalities can be explicitly distilled into topological skeletons rather than obscured by high-dimensional matrices. By topologically reinterpreting the Bernstein-Vazirani and Simon algorithms, we elucidated the intuitive diagrammatic mechanisms of phase kickback and information retrieval. Extending beyond the standard binary qubit paradigm, we applied our diagrammatic toolkit to multi-valued quantum systems, successfully formalizing the qutrit-adapted generalized Deutsch–Jozsa. Notably, by analyzing the topological representation of the generalized Grover algorithm, we derived rigorous algebraic conditions for its deterministic success, seamlessly linking diagrammatic algorithmic design with group representation theory. Furthermore, we explored the categorical genesis of quantum entanglement by analyzing controlled-NOT gates using complementary Frobenius structures, and we investigated a diagrammatic decomposition of the W-state preparation protocol.

Specifically, our W-state reduction retained irreducible non-Clifford phase gates, diverging from standard simplified forms. This phenomenon not only highlights the more intricate topological entanglement properties inherent in the W-state compared to GHZ or Bell states, but also indicates current limitations in pure graphical axiomatic systems when handling highly complex non-Clifford resources. Consequently, resolving these residual non-Clifford elements presents a clear trajectory for future research: enriching tensor category axioms with higher-order rewrite rules to enable automated, scalable circuit optimization in modern quantum compilers.

This paper investigates foundational quantum computing protocols using categorical tensor-graph semantics within the category FHilb, providing a topological reinterpretation of quantum algorithms. The authors demonstrate how topological transformations distill algorithmic essence and clarify operational mechanisms of oracles, moving beyond conventional Hilbert-space formalisms that obscure structural nature behind high-dimensional matrix operations.

Key contributions include:
1. **Topological Bernstein-Vazirani Algorithm**: Provides tensor diagram semantics, proves correctness via transformation principles, and derives the simplest graphical form showing the algorithm's mathematical essence. The minimal form reveals that the second register is an auxiliary qubit, and measurement probability is non-zero iff y=s, demonstrating phase kickback as the core mechanism.

2. **Topological Simon Algorithm**: Similarly provides tensor diagram semantics, verified and simplified via topological transformations. The analysis reveals that despite superficial resemblance to the Bernstein-Vazirani minimal form, the underlying topological mechanisms differ fundamentally—the second object directly represents the second register itself, stemming from the unitality of the monoid.

3. **Qutrit-adapted Generalized Deutsch-Jozsa and Single-Shot Grover Algorithms**: Extends beyond binary qubit systems to multi-valued quantum systems (qutrits). For the generalized single-shot Grover algorithm with ℤ₃, the paper establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for deterministic success: if a₀=(n+1)a₁=...=(n+1)aₙ₋₁ where aᵢ counts elements with f(s)=i, the algorithm is guaranteed to return an unbalanced element. The proof connects diagrammatic algorithmic design with group representation theory.

4. **CNOT Gates and Quantum Entanglement**: Implements CNOT gates via complementary Frobenius structures, providing an alternative proof avoiding purely matrix-based calculations. Investigates a diagrammatic decomposition scheme for the W-state preparation protocol using ZX-calculus, phase gadgets, local complementation, and pivot rule. The reduction yields an expression distinct from existing standard formulations, with residual non-Clifford phase gates, indicating current limitations in pure graphical axiomatic systems.

The paper concludes that categorical tensor-graph semantics provides a composable, scalable diagrammatic toolkit essential for automated circuit optimization across evolving quantum hardware. Future work involves enriching tensor category axioms with higher-order rewrite rules to handle complex non-Clifford resources.

# Discovering a new quantum algorithm

How group theory and the non-Abelian Fourier transform open the door to new quantum computing research applications.

![](/quantum/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fresearch-website-prod-cms-uploads.s3.us.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud%2FQuantum_Algorithms_Blog_Leadspace_1_7a16d0a787.jpg&w=3840&q=75)
