From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Quantum algorithm for integer factorization

**Shor's algorithm** is a [quantum algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_algorithm "Quantum algorithm") for finding the [prime factors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_factor "Prime factor") of an integer. It was developed in 1994 by the American mathematician [Peter Shor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Shor "Peter Shor").[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-siam-2) It is one of the few known quantum algorithms with compelling potential applications and strong evidence of superpolynomial speedup compared to best known classical (non-quantum) algorithms.[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3) However, beating classical computers may require quantum computers with millions of qubits due to the overhead caused by [quantum error correction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_error_correction "Quantum error correction").[[4]](#cite_note-q2000-4)

Shor proposed multiple similar algorithms for solving the [factoring problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization "Integer factorization"), the [discrete logarithm problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_logarithm "Discrete logarithm"), and the period-finding problem. "Shor's algorithm" usually refers to the factoring algorithm, but may refer to any of the three algorithms. The discrete logarithm algorithm and the factoring algorithm are instances of the period-finding algorithm, and all three are instances of the [hidden subgroup problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidden_subgroup_problem "Hidden subgroup problem").

On a quantum computer, to factor an integer ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3), Shor's algorithm runs in [polynomial time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_time "Polynomial time"), meaning the time taken is polynomial in ![{\displaystyle \log N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/54e31347d160d1e54a70f79b23038030f33b6bf0).[[5]](#cite_note-5) It takes [quantum gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_logic_gate "Quantum logic gate") of order ![{\displaystyle O\!\left((\log N)^{2}(\log \log N)(\log \log \log N)\right)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/41344b55ef5e6494bb835b1adde9a4be4403303c) using fast multiplication,[[6]](#cite_note-Beckman-6) or even ![{\displaystyle O\!\left((\log N)^{2}(\log \log N)\right)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d16ce213864da54f3a3655b563e61555895809cd) using the asymptotically fastest multiplication algorithm currently known due to Harvey and [van der Hoeven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joris_van_der_Hoeven "Joris van der Hoeven"),[[7]](#cite_note-Integer_multiplication_in_time_<math-7) thus demonstrating that the [integer factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization "Integer factorization") problem is in [complexity class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complexity_class "Complexity class") **[BQP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BQP "BQP")**. Shor's algorithm is asymptotically faster than the most scalable classical factoring algorithm, the [general number field sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_number_field_sieve "General number field sieve"), which works in [sub-exponential time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_complexity#Sub-exponential_time "Time complexity"): ![{\displaystyle O\!\left(e^{1.9(\log N)^{1/3}(\log \log N)^{2/3}}\right)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/1956460a1cea4f2794fa0487f886e2a64cedc244).[[8]](#cite_note-8)

## Feasibility and implications

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Shor%27s_algorithm&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Feasibility and implications")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Asymmetric_encryption_scheme.png/330px-Asymmetric_encryption_scheme.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Asymmetric_encryption_scheme.png)

Diagram presenting the encryption and the decryption of a document using asymmetric cryptography. Some forms of encryption (including asymmetric cryptography) are at risk of being broken by future quantum computers.

Assuming a quantum computer with a sufficient number of [qubits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qubit "Qubit") could operate without succumbing to [quantum noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_noise "Quantum noise") and other [quantum-decoherence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_decoherence "Quantum decoherence") phenomena, then Shor's algorithm could be used to break [public-key cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public-key_cryptography "Public-key cryptography") schemes, such as

* The [RSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem) "RSA (cryptosystem)") scheme
* The finite-field [Diffie–Hellman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffie–Hellman "Diffie–Hellman") key exchange
* The [elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic-curve_Diffie–Hellman "Elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman") key exchange[[9]](#cite_note-9)

RSA can be broken if factoring large integers is computationally feasible. As far as is known, this is not possible using classical (non-quantum) computers; no classical algorithm is known that can factor integers in polynomial time. However, Shor's algorithm shows that factoring integers can be done with a polynomial complexity circuit on an ideal quantum computer. Thus, it might be feasible to defeat RSA by constructing a large enough quantum computer. This was a powerful motivator for the design and construction of quantum computers, and for the study of new quantum-computer algorithms. It has also facilitated research on new cryptosystems that are secure from quantum computers, collectively called [post-quantum cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-quantum_cryptography "Post-quantum cryptography") (PQC).

### Physical implementation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Shor%27s_algorithm&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Physical implementation")]

As of 2026, the high error rates of quantum computers and limited number of physical qubits available for [quantum error correction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_error_correction "Quantum error correction"), laboratory demonstrations of Shor's algorithm obtain correct results in only a fraction of attempts, and have only succeeded with small [semiprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiprime "Semiprime").

In 2001, Shor's algorithm was demonstrated by a group at [IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM"), who factored ![{\displaystyle 15}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ea331af19ed2ccc36bb864409b6c305e18cff30f) into ![{\displaystyle 3\times 5}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ade495bacf4e69df079d0bc51769a6cf5fad985a), using an [NMR implementation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_magnetic_resonance_quantum_computer "Nuclear magnetic resonance quantum computer") of a quantum computer with seven qubits.[[10]](#cite_note-VSBYSC01-10) After IBM's implementation, two independent groups implemented Shor's algorithm using [photonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photonics "Photonics") qubits.[[11]](#cite_note-LBYP07-11)[[12]](#cite_note-LWLBJGW07-12) In 2012, the factorization of ![{\displaystyle 15}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ea331af19ed2ccc36bb864409b6c305e18cff30f) was performed with solid-state qubits.[[13]](#cite_note-13) Later, in 2012, the factorization of ![{\displaystyle 21}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/77ebb9ccf6080ba5c9a6ea8973cb2f26c50211cf) was achieved.[[14]](#cite_note-14) In 2016, the factorization of ![{\displaystyle 15}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ea331af19ed2ccc36bb864409b6c305e18cff30f) was performed again using trapped-ion qubits.[[15]](#cite_note-15) However, none of these demonstrations fulfill the requirements of Shor’s algorithm: they compile the circuit using prior knowledge of the solution, and some have even oversimplified the algorithm in a way that makes it equivalent to coin flipping.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

## Algorithm

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Shor%27s_algorithm&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Algorithm")]

The problem that we are trying to solve is: *given an odd [composite number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_number "Composite number") ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3), find its [integer factors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization "Integer factorization")*.

To achieve this, Shor's algorithm consists of two parts:

1. A classical reduction of the factoring problem to the problem of [order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicative_order "Multiplicative order")-finding. This reduction is similar to that used for other [factoring algorithms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization "Integer factorization"), such as the [quadratic sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_sieve "Quadratic sieve").
2. A quantum algorithm to solve the order-finding problem.

### Classical reduction

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Shor%27s_algorithm&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Classical reduction")]

A complete factoring algorithm is possible if we're able to efficiently factor arbitrary ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) into just two integers ![{\displaystyle p}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/81eac1e205430d1f40810df36a0edffdc367af36) and ![{\displaystyle q}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/06809d64fa7c817ffc7e323f85997f783dbdf71d) greater than 1, since if either ![{\displaystyle p}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/81eac1e205430d1f40810df36a0edffdc367af36) or ![{\displaystyle q}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/06809d64fa7c817ffc7e323f85997f783dbdf71d) are not prime, then the factoring algorithm can in turn be run on those until only primes remain.

A basic observation is that, using [Euclid's algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm "Euclidean algorithm"), we can always compute the [GCD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_common_divisor "Greatest common divisor") between two integers efficiently. In particular, this means we can check efficiently whether ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) is even, in which case 2 is trivially a factor. Let us thus assume that ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) is odd for the remainder of this discussion. Afterwards, we can use efficient classical algorithms to check whether ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) is a [prime power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_power "Prime power").[[17]](#cite_note-17) For prime powers, efficient classical factorization algorithms exist,[[18]](#cite_note-18) hence the rest of the quantum algorithm may assume that ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) is not a prime power.

If those easy cases do not produce a nontrivial factor of ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3), the algorithm proceeds to handle the remaining case. We pick a random integer ![{\displaystyle 2\leq a<N{.}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/5259810d24c2e7c59a5a62d229c6c7f66cac08dc) A possible nontrivial divisor of ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) can be found by computing ![{\displaystyle \gcd(a,N)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/3a5fdb17f976373eb7d306835d5b8972a0331197), which can be done classically and efficiently using the [Euclidean algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_algorithm "Euclidean algorithm"). If this produces a nontrivial factor (meaning ![{\displaystyle \gcd(a,N)\neq 1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/97d86466478ba9ac38c16324a5f04c2507a34736)), the algorithm is finished, and the other nontrivial factor is ![{\displaystyle N/\gcd(a,N)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/e5b48c2c34dfc3538f6a835d409abb53a530e065). If a nontrivial factor was not identified, then this means that ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) and the choice of ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc) are [coprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coprime "Coprime"), so ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc) is contained in the [multiplicative group of integers modulo ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicative_group_of_integers_modulo_n "Multiplicative group of integers modulo n"), having a [multiplicative inverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicative_inverse "Multiplicative inverse") modulo ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3). Thus, ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc) has a [multiplicative order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicative_order "Multiplicative order") ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) modulo ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3), meaning

:   ![{\displaystyle a^{r}\equiv 1{\bmod {N}},}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/64f38cc6c3485f63beaae908b7f8a3cecae77a8d)

and ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) is the smallest positive integer satisfying this congruence.

The quantum subroutine finds ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538). It can be seen from the congruence that ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) [divides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divides "Divides") ![{\displaystyle a^{r}-1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/244196a8067782de4eb33d1cb18e0868d545603b), written ![{\displaystyle N\mid a^{r}-1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/292834aba30368e4c468989ad78ef9052be39c1e). This can be factored using [difference of squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Difference_of_squares "Difference of squares"):![{\displaystyle N\mid (a^{r/2}-1)(a^{r/2}+1).}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/aa272072a8bc1f2ccadd3e55168f38ba22a98e32)Since we have factored the expression in this way, the algorithm doesn't work for odd ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) (because ![{\displaystyle a^{r/2}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0760b9e66e6ac245838e05d1f072a39c4aa87751) must be an integer), meaning that the algorithm would have to restart with a new ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc). Hereafter we can therefore assume that ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) is even. It cannot be the case that ![{\displaystyle N\mid a^{r/2}-1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/6fec6bfe98a3799433fe33d40ecbb152e935a686), since this would imply ![{\displaystyle a^{r/2}\equiv 1{\bmod {N}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/bc93a2d1ad870d4474c3628b72c77c745bc1e669), which would contradictorily imply that ![{\displaystyle r/2}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/86106f9cb91a0b43c29b8c0f2b96af7b8ba622e2) would be the order of ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc), which was already ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538). At this point, it may or may not be the case that ![{\displaystyle N\mid a^{r/2}+1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f3e62956f0c2caf87d1452fb5cd5f39a5475130f). If ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) does not divide ![{\displaystyle a^{r/2}+1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/edb3ef8176d4715bb51de1cf474dba04291e1cba), then this means that we are able to find a nontrivial factor of ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3). We compute![{\displaystyle d=\gcd(N,a^{r/2}-1).}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/a3b184933ee32ea383f65b2af1750c3fb1b08dfa)If ![{\displaystyle d=1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/958b426c5ace91d4fb7f5a3becd7b21dba288d50), then ![{\displaystyle N\mid a^{r/2}+1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f3e62956f0c2caf87d1452fb5cd5f39a5475130f) was true, and a nontrivial factor of ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) cannot be achieved from ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc), and the algorithm must restart with a new ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc). Otherwise, we have found a nontrivial factor of ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3), with the other being ![{\displaystyle N/d}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/a85755f759b2c5299a83a580103e4d2e017ec4e9), and the algorithm is finished. For this step, it is also equivalent to compute ![{\displaystyle \gcd(N,a^{r/2}+1)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0ac54526e83e8cebebc9eb1870e596528f17bb36); it will produce a nontrivial factor if ![{\displaystyle \gcd(N,a^{r/2}-1)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/bdb72d210b4809ff466058dfc87a331d359c8e5f) is nontrivial, and will not if it's trivial (where ![{\displaystyle N\mid a^{r/2}+1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f3e62956f0c2caf87d1452fb5cd5f39a5475130f)).

The algorithm restated shortly follows: let ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) be odd, and not a prime power. We want to output two nontrivial factors of ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3).

1. Pick a random number ![{\displaystyle 1<a<N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/3fdc3525392173ed7f796720a78f1bd718e1b4bc).
2. Compute ![{\displaystyle K=\gcd(a,N)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/b1bd9b72796f87d3e07748e2fab8ac52f479d8e6), the [greatest common divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_common_divisor "Greatest common divisor") of ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc) and ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3).
3. If ![{\displaystyle K\neq 1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c639cdf767a1bc4d6d62f3b7ee2d177b5268d18b), then ![{\displaystyle K}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/2b76fce82a62ed5461908f0dc8f037de4e3686b0) is a [nontrivial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nontrivial "Nontrivial") factor of ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3), with the other factor being ![{\displaystyle N/K}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/fb8b22323ce877d3388c5ad61070e918ec513bc3), and we are done.
4. Otherwise, use the quantum subroutine to find the order ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) of ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc).
5. If ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) is odd, then go back to step 1.
6. Compute ![{\displaystyle g=\gcd(N,a^{r/2}+1)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f44e9cf96d4860252508f133fd0b1351502c596e). If ![{\displaystyle g}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d3556280e66fe2c0d0140df20935a6f057381d77) is nontrivial, the other factor is ![{\displaystyle N/g}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/3e1c596b18480216ebfc1c52bf7086bfb371958b), and we're done. Otherwise, go back to step 1.

It has been shown that this will be likely to succeed after a few runs.[[2]](#cite_note-siam-2) In practice, a single call to the quantum order-finding subroutine is enough to completely factor ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) with very high probability of success if one uses a more advanced reduction.[[19]](#cite_note-Ekerå21-19)

### Quantum order-finding subroutine

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Shor%27s_algorithm&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Quantum order-finding subroutine")]

The goal of the quantum subroutine of Shor's algorithm is, given [coprime integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coprime_integers "Coprime integers") ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3) and ![{\displaystyle 1<a<N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/3fdc3525392173ed7f796720a78f1bd718e1b4bc), to find the [order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicative_order "Multiplicative order") ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) of ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc) modulo ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3), the smallest positive integer ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) such that ![{\displaystyle a^{r}\equiv 1{\pmod {N}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/5e83a853aecb9498b8e732bc175c2f0d974d5a1d). To achieve this, Shor's algorithm uses a quantum circuit involving two registers. The second register uses ![{\displaystyle n}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/a601995d55609f2d9f5e233e36fbe9ea26011b3b) qubits, where ![{\displaystyle n}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/a601995d55609f2d9f5e233e36fbe9ea26011b3b) is the smallest integer such that ![{\displaystyle N\leq 2^{n}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/6337f0ee42d25a450ceff6e9c8d8d36bb6493b33), i.e., ![{\displaystyle n=\left\lceil {\log _{2}N}\right\rceil }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/49842e57ab1b4b2f4805e3de3a82c74e83b5bcd3). The size of the first register determines how accurate of an approximation the circuit produces. It can be shown that using ![{\displaystyle 2n}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/134afa8ff09fdddd24b06f289e92e3a045092bd1) qubits gives sufficient accuracy to find ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538). The exact quantum circuit depends on the parameters ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc) and ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3), which define the problem. The following description of the algorithm uses [bra–ket notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bra–ket_notation "Bra–ket notation") to denote quantum states, and ![{\displaystyle \otimes }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/de29098f5a34ee296a505681a0d5e875070f2aea) to denote the [tensor product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product "Tensor product").

The algorithm consists of two main steps:

1. Use [quantum phase estimation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_phase_estimation_algorithm "Quantum phase estimation algorithm") with [unitary matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_matrix "Unitary matrix") ![{\displaystyle U}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/458a728f53b9a0274f059cd695e067c430956025) representing the operation of multiplying by ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc) (modulo ![{\displaystyle N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f5e3890c981ae85503089652feb48b191b57aae3)), and input state ![{\displaystyle |0\rangle ^{\otimes 2n}\otimes |1\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/7d18805fe9a37b3d7faa723c85d2df025b43a5e4) (where the second register is ![{\displaystyle |1\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/2f53021ca18e77477ee5bd3c1523e5830189ec5c) made from ![{\displaystyle n}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/a601995d55609f2d9f5e233e36fbe9ea26011b3b) qubits). The [eigenvalues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalue "Eigenvalue") of this ![{\displaystyle U}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/458a728f53b9a0274f059cd695e067c430956025) encode information about the period, and ![{\displaystyle |1\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/2f53021ca18e77477ee5bd3c1523e5830189ec5c) can be seen to be writable as a sum of its eigenvectors. Thanks to these properties, the quantum phase estimation stage gives as output a random integer of the form ![{\displaystyle {\frac {j}{r}}2^{2n}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/508dd5c75d59d7b638a4ae23c33d62bd1f4ea65f) for random ![{\displaystyle j=0,1,...,r-1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/3ab43db46a07fee3a344fa696b6005457bb327ec).
2. Use the [continued fractions algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_continued_fraction "Simple continued fraction") to extract the period ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) from the measurement outcomes obtained in the previous stage. This is a procedure to post-process (with a classical computer) the measurement data obtained from measuring the output quantum states, and retrieve the period.

The connection with quantum phase estimation was not discussed in the original formulation of Shor's algorithm,[[2]](#cite_note-siam-2) but was later proposed by [Alexei Kitaev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexei_Kitaev "Alexei Kitaev").[[20]](#cite_note-20)

#### Quantum phase estimation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Shor%27s_algorithm&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Quantum phase estimation")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Shor%27s_algorithm.svg/500px-Shor%27s_algorithm.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shor's_algorithm.svg)

Quantum subroutine in Shor's algorithm

In general the [quantum phase estimation algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_phase_estimation_algorithm "Quantum phase estimation algorithm"), for any unitary ![{\displaystyle U}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/458a728f53b9a0274f059cd695e067c430956025) and eigenstate ![{\displaystyle |\psi \rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/cc27f1893b769a08cd6b296e115a29e61cab675e) such that ![{\displaystyle U|\psi \rangle =e^{2\pi i\theta }|\psi \rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d0e2dcd8fa5a51f8232704344f87c5028e135f00), sends input states ![{\displaystyle |0\rangle |\psi \rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/3ddd015c8542e0c70a9475df74fb25c8a8c2f33f) to output states close to ![{\displaystyle |\phi \rangle |\psi \rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/70463d8882276e28ec647b12708977b5812f89ab), where ![{\displaystyle \phi }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/72b1f30316670aee6270a28334bdf4f5072cdde4) is a superposition of integers close to ![{\displaystyle 2^{2n}\theta }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d1739eb102027810fe663e8df50309ffe52ce901). In other words, it sends each eigenstate ![{\displaystyle |\psi _{j}\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/56f7ecd53702ff0cdf117660d095fb74106cd4b7) of ![{\displaystyle U}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/458a728f53b9a0274f059cd695e067c430956025) to a state containing information close to the associated eigenvalue. For the purposes of quantum order-finding, we employ this strategy using the unitary defined by the action![{\displaystyle U|k\rangle ={\begin{cases}|ak{\pmod {N}}\rangle &0\leq k<N,\\|k\rangle &N\leq k<2^{n}.\end{cases}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/e1efd10b74f59c77f221f1c7df00b8bb07eaf9e0)The action of ![{\displaystyle U}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/458a728f53b9a0274f059cd695e067c430956025) on states ![{\displaystyle |k\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/063585a1e5a9a0b0fb63d1684d071fcf70f87d75) with ![{\displaystyle N\leq k<2^{n}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/7318dcb5122211c49f412f27b46fc703f3be8849) is not crucial to the functioning of the algorithm, but needs to be included to ensure that the overall transformation is a well-defined quantum gate. Implementing the circuit for quantum phase estimation with ![{\displaystyle U}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/458a728f53b9a0274f059cd695e067c430956025) requires being able to efficiently implement the gates ![{\displaystyle U^{2^{j}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/6acfc04ed54bbd6b83b4fb86298fea9d7e5a98d2). This can be accomplished via [modular exponentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_exponentiation "Modular exponentiation"), which is the slowest part of the algorithm.

The gate thus defined satisfies ![{\displaystyle U^{r}=I}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/e0312dcd62a75ac532b80bbcf5d6963c093bf578), which immediately implies that its eigenvalues are the ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538)-th [roots of unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_unity "Root of unity") ![{\displaystyle \omega _{r}^{k}=e^{2\pi ik/r}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f0be31bd3d110e9726d8714341cefd6b1f7923f9). Furthermore, each eigenvalue ![{\displaystyle \omega _{r}^{j}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/8635165008b0715d65ca06c8fbc9d7e24573ad8f) has an eigenvector of the form ![{\textstyle |\psi _{j}\rangle =r^{-1/2}\sum _{k=0}^{r-1}\omega _{r}^{-kj}|a^{k}\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/90f8fa0c1ea61830579f06dc30461e59f9997eb6), and these eigenvectors are such that![{\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}{\frac {1}{\sqrt {r}}}\sum _{j=0}^{r-1}|\psi _{j}\rangle &={\frac {1}{r}}\sum _{j=0}^{r-1}\sum _{k=0}^{r-1}\omega _{r}^{jk}|a^{k}\rangle \\&=|1\rangle +{\frac {1}{r}}\sum _{k=1}^{r-1}\left(\sum _{j=0}^{r-1}\omega _{r}^{jk}\right)|a^{k}\rangle =|1\rangle ,\end{aligned}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f6a48d7478f136d8659e9d5a0867f595d0af0799) where the last identity follows from the [geometric series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_series "Geometric series") formula, which implies ![{\textstyle \sum _{j=0}^{r-1}\omega _{r}^{jk}=0}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/a65c1db41ca922db368515026aae6f67f9c5b022).

Using [quantum phase estimation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_phase_estimation_algorithm "Quantum phase estimation algorithm") on an input state ![{\displaystyle |0\rangle ^{\otimes 2n}|\psi _{j}\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/94a946030e285c53846f3c45cb4cb81a85b73f5e) would then return the integer ![{\displaystyle 2^{2n}j/r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/fc15b8c68864213b7eb2bda6b12c52926646f766) with high probability. More precisely, the quantum phase estimation circuit sends ![{\displaystyle |0\rangle ^{\otimes 2n}|\psi _{j}\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/94a946030e285c53846f3c45cb4cb81a85b73f5e) to ![{\displaystyle |\phi _{j}\rangle |\psi _{j}\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ae00bb52194b9b7ed2aa03e5446f5a9e40f947d9) such that the resulting probability distribution ![{\displaystyle p_{k}\equiv |\langle k|\phi _{j}\rangle |^{2}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/1d381591ba35bb15842ac7131ce9a2c5f3115569) is peaked around ![{\displaystyle k=2^{2n}j/r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d330fe8666a63c91d96d2a5a4c55a67e8244835b), with ![{\displaystyle p_{2^{2n}j/r}\geq 4/\pi ^{2}\approx 0.4053}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/10481c6f9c5f53169d31477dadce7071988c9ea4). This probability can be made arbitrarily close to 1 using extra qubits.

Applying the above reasoning to the input ![{\displaystyle |0\rangle ^{\otimes 2n}|1\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/823b36cae1e63e4a5b94630cb9cb4f7ccfa7b80d), quantum phase estimation thus results in the evolution![{\displaystyle |0\rangle ^{\otimes 2n}|1\rangle ={\frac {1}{\sqrt {r}}}\sum _{j=0}^{r-1}|0\rangle ^{\otimes 2n}|\psi _{j}\rangle \to {\frac {1}{\sqrt {r}}}\sum _{j=0}^{r-1}|\phi _{j}\rangle |\psi _{j}\rangle .}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/64c163f1d8523243906eaa09fa40eed09cb8287b)Measuring the first register, we now have a balanced probability ![{\displaystyle 1/r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/2ab96580d23ec5eff6bb0e666531eccb7a8035d6) to find each ![{\displaystyle |\phi _{j}\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/038f455c0dc2a38568eeac72e59131d3ad41d0a8), each one giving an integer approximation to ![{\displaystyle 2^{2n}j/r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/fc15b8c68864213b7eb2bda6b12c52926646f766), which can be divided by ![{\displaystyle 2^{2n}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/85543d7c2b7e0fea744a50af20d0f58b0f0fcfb3) to get a decimal approximation for ![{\displaystyle j/r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/9eaeda188a2bab52719be360a911b1937223e0a1).

#### Continued-fraction algorithm to retrieve the period

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Shor%27s_algorithm&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Continued-fraction algorithm to retrieve the period")]

Then, we apply the [continued-fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continued_fraction "Continued fraction") algorithm to find integers ![{\displaystyle b}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f11423fbb2e967f986e36804a8ae4271734917c3) and ![{\displaystyle c}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/86a67b81c2de995bd608d5b2df50cd8cd7d92455), where ![{\displaystyle b/c}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f7e7620d85c53627979091a9869593ea23ea0c48) gives the best fraction approximation for the approximation measured from the circuit, for ![{\displaystyle b,c<N}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/82e6c210489b8dae5d2fab4236e93b60009754ea) and [coprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coprime_integers "Coprime integers") ![{\displaystyle b}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f11423fbb2e967f986e36804a8ae4271734917c3) and ![{\displaystyle c}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/86a67b81c2de995bd608d5b2df50cd8cd7d92455). The number of qubits in the first register, ![{\displaystyle 2n}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/134afa8ff09fdddd24b06f289e92e3a045092bd1), which determines the accuracy of the approximation, guarantees that![{\displaystyle {\frac {b}{c}}={\frac {j}{r}},}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/9e7feb4db7e4d737397c6112e83a55dac5014640) given the best approximation from the superposition of ![{\displaystyle |\phi _{j}\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/038f455c0dc2a38568eeac72e59131d3ad41d0a8) was measured[[2]](#cite_note-siam-2) (which can be made arbitrarily likely by using extra bits and truncating the output). However, while ![{\displaystyle b}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f11423fbb2e967f986e36804a8ae4271734917c3) and ![{\displaystyle c}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/86a67b81c2de995bd608d5b2df50cd8cd7d92455) are coprime, it may be the case that ![{\displaystyle j}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/2f461e54f5c093e92a55547b9764291390f0b5d0) and ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) are not coprime. Because of that, ![{\displaystyle b}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f11423fbb2e967f986e36804a8ae4271734917c3) and ![{\displaystyle c}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/86a67b81c2de995bd608d5b2df50cd8cd7d92455) may have lost some factors that were in ![{\displaystyle j}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/2f461e54f5c093e92a55547b9764291390f0b5d0) and ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538). This can be remedied by rerunning the quantum order-finding subroutine an arbitrary number of times, to produce a list of fraction approximations![{\displaystyle {\frac {b_{1}}{c_{1}}},{\frac {b_{2}}{c_{2}}},\ldots ,{\frac {b_{s}}{c_{s}}},}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/4657fd6c9b302fffc90c9f5647d368db504f3f8d)where ![{\displaystyle s}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/01d131dfd7673938b947072a13a9744fe997e632) is the number of times the subroutine was run. Each ![{\displaystyle c_{k}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/3d2f8052630e67b00d04e3487e1d68ed7070470b) will have different factors taken out of it because the circuit will (likely) have measured multiple different possible values of ![{\displaystyle j}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/2f461e54f5c093e92a55547b9764291390f0b5d0). To recover the actual ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) value, we can take the [least common multiple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Least_common_multiple "Least common multiple") of each ![{\displaystyle c_{k}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/3d2f8052630e67b00d04e3487e1d68ed7070470b):![{\displaystyle \operatorname {lcm} (c_{1},c_{2},\ldots ,c_{s}).}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/8a7acd24fe27632032f3cab57b1a342fd6c62dcd)The least common multiple will be the order ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) of the original integer ![{\displaystyle a}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ffd2487510aa438433a2579450ab2b3d557e5edc) with high probability. In practice, a single run of the quantum order-finding subroutine is in general enough if more advanced post-processing is used.[[21]](#cite_note-Ekerå24-21)

#### Choosing the size of the first register

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Shor%27s_algorithm&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Choosing the size of the first register")]

Phase estimation requires choosing the size of the first register to determine the accuracy of the algorithm, and for the quantum subroutine of Shor's algorithm, ![{\displaystyle 2n}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/134afa8ff09fdddd24b06f289e92e3a045092bd1) qubits is sufficient to guarantee that the optimal bitstring measured from phase estimation (meaning the ![{\displaystyle |k\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/063585a1e5a9a0b0fb63d1684d071fcf70f87d75) where ![{\textstyle k/2^{2n}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/7176690d46e61f387aa9a1f07036c41fdab6d34e) is the most accurate approximation of the phase from phase estimation) will allow the actual value of ![{\displaystyle r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0d1ecb613aa2984f0576f70f86650b7c2a132538) to be recovered.

Each ![{\displaystyle |\phi _{j}\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/038f455c0dc2a38568eeac72e59131d3ad41d0a8) before measurement in Shor's algorithm represents a superposition of integers approximating ![{\displaystyle 2^{2n}j/r}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/fc15b8c68864213b7eb2bda6b12c52926646f766). Let ![{\displaystyle |k\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/063585a1e5a9a0b0fb63d1684d071fcf70f87d75) represent the most optimal integer in ![{\displaystyle |\phi _{j}\rangle }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/038f455c0dc2a38568eeac72e59131d3ad41d0a8). args.summary:
Shor's algorithm is a quantum algorithm for finding the prime factors of an integer, developed in 1994 by American mathematician Peter Shor. It is one of the few known quantum algorithms with strong evidence of superpolynomial speedup compared to best known classical algorithms. On a quantum computer, factoring an integer N runs in polynomial time (O((log N)²(log log N)(log log log N)) quantum gates using fast multiplication), while the best classical algorithm (general number field sieve) runs in sub-exponential time.

The algorithm could break public-key cryptography schemes including RSA, finite-field Diffie-Hellman, and elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman, motivating research into post-quantum cryptography. However, practical implementation requires quantum computers with millions of qubits due to quantum error correction overhead.

The algorithm has two parts: (1) a classical reduction of factoring to order-finding, and (2) a quantum order-finding subroutine. The classical reduction picks a random integer a, computes gcd(a,N), and if trivial, uses the quantum subroutine to find the multiplicative order r of a modulo N. If r is even and N does not divide a^(r/2)+1, then gcd(N, a^(r/2)-1) yields a nontrivial factor.

The quantum subroutine uses quantum phase estimation with a unitary operator U representing multiplication by a modulo N, requiring 2n qubits in the first register (where n = ceil(log₂ N)). The eigenvalues of U encode information about the period r. A continued-fraction algorithm extracts the period from measurement outcomes.

As of 2026, laboratory demonstrations have only succeeded with small semiprimes (15, 21) using NMR, photonic, solid-state, and trapped-ion qubits, but these demonstrations compiled circuits using prior knowledge of the solution.

# Quantum's Hub: The Institute for Quantum Information and Matter (IQIM)

[Summer 2022](/post/category/Summer+2022)

Written By [Andrew Moseman](/post?author=5e8f74da9dd19d14644cbce1)

![a cartwheel in front of Beckman Auditorium](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/586ec16bb3db2b558ebfec60/d5e59adc-e02a-4d64-91c7-97399377bc3b/Piero+Chiappina.jpeg)

In quantum superposition, subatomic particles can act like waves and occupy many places at once—a little like how Caltech graduate student Piero Chiappina can be seen here performing every stage of a backflip at once. In reality, large, or macroscopic, objects like people cannot be in many places simultaneously, at least not without the help of photography. But researchers, including physicists like Chiappina, are working to scale up bizarre quantum effects such as superposition and entanglement so they can be used in quantum computers and other future technologies. Image: Lance Hayashida

### BY OMAR SHAMOUT

In 1982, Caltech’s Richard Feynman [predicted](https://medium.com/quantum1net/richard-feynman-and-the-birth-of-quantum-computing-6fe4a0f5fcc7) quantum computers would be not just possible but necessary. Classical computers could never simulate the seemingly infinite number of probabilities present in quantum systems due to the phenomenon known as superposition, which describes how particles such as electrons exist in two states at once. Such a leap would require quantum computing, which uses features of [quantum mechanics](https://scienceexchange.caltech.edu/topics/quantum-science-explained?utm_campaign=csequantum&utm_medium=web&utm_source=caltechmagazine) to perform the kinds of computation not possible before.

When John Preskill, now the Richard P. Feynman Professor of Theoretical Physics, came to Caltech in 1983, he planned to continue his work in particle physics and quantum field theory. By the mid-1990s, however, Preskill had switched his focus to a field that owes its existence to ideas posed by Feynman, Nobel laureate and Caltech professor of physics, two decades earlier: quantum information theory. It was a career change that eventually led to the creation of what is now called the Institute for Quantum Information and Matter (IQIM), Caltech’s long-standing home for cutting-edge quantum research.

“[Peter] Shor had discovered that you could efficiently factor with quantum computers,” Preskill noted in [an oral history](https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/47147) for the American Institute of Physics (AIP) conducted by science historian David Zierler, who now serves as director of the Caltech Heritage Project. “I realized with the discovery of Shor's algorithm that it really meant there was a big difference between what problems we'd be able to solve and which ones we'd never be able to solve with computing technology because it's a quantum world instead of a classical one.”

Quantum information theory is the study of information processing on the quantum level. One of its primary aims is to guide the development of quantum computers, machines capable of far surpassing even classical supercomputers on certain problems of fundamental importance.

In the late 1990s, Preskill and H. J. “Jeff” Kimble, now the William L. Valentine Professor of Physics, Emeritus, received a grant from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), which was interested in quantum computing’s potential applications in cryptography. Preskill and Kimble then hired Alexei Kitaev, now the Ronald and Maxine Linde Professor of Theoretical Physics and Mathematics, as a yearlong visitor. Kitaev’s work on fault-tolerant quantum computers was a key advance in the field and subsequently won the [2012 Breakthrough Prize in Theoretical Physics.](https://breakthroughprize.org/Laureates/L3)

*The 2013 video “Quantum Computers Animated,” produced by IQIM in partnership with PhD Comics. The video features IQIM’s John Preskill and Spiros Michalakis.*

Then, in 2000, Preskill and Kimble received a grant from the National Science Foundation, which they used to form the Institute for Quantum Information (IQI) that same year.

“NSF got a surge of funding for a program they called Information Technology Research, which included a lot of practical things but also sort of a lunatic fringe of blue-sky research. And that’s what we were part of,” Preskill told AIP. “We had an amazing group of young people in the early 2000s who came through, many of whom are leaders of research in quantum information now, like Patrick Hayden, and Guifré Vidal, and Frank Verstraete, and quite a few others.”

Vidal (postdoc ’01–’05), now a senior staff research scientist at Google, recalled those early days as a Caltech postdoc during a Heritage Project interview: “John had the vision ... to hire interesting young people for [IQI], then apply a hands-off approach. He’s not the type of person who needs to control everything and everyone.”

Dave Bacon (BS ’97), a former IQI postdoc, remembered IQI as a leading hub for quantum computing research:

“John literally started inviting everybody in the field to come visit. … It was like all of quantum computing was flowing through that place, and I was in the main place we'd have the group meetings,” he said in a Heritage Project interview. “It felt like everybody would come in and give a talk right outside my office. It was perfect.”

Liang Jiang (BS ’04), a former IQI postdoc and current professor at the University of Chicago, told Zierler during a Heritage Project interview that weekly meetings were so full of discussion and questions that Preskill had to impose a time limit: “You could only talk for one minute because some group members would get really excited with the results and would talk a lot about their research.”

By 2011, advances in quantum computing hardware, such as superconducting circuits and qubits (the quantum mechanical analogue of a classical bit) gave Preskill and Kimble the impetus to apply for more NSF funding as a means to broaden the IQI’s scope to include experimental work. They received that funding and, in 2011, changed its name to the Institute for Quantum Information and Matter, for which Preskill serves as the Allen V. C. Davis and Lenabelle Davis Leadership Chair of the Institute for Quantum Science and Technology.

Spiros Michalakis, staff researcher and manager of outreach at [IQIM](https://iqim.caltech.edu), described this name change in a recent Heritage Project interview as a “visionary move,” one that is still paying off: “We attach ‘M’—matter—and it really mattered because … we started to have conversations with how you can implement certain things and how you can convert some of the theories into experiments. … I didn’t know many physicists or many people who were part of physics or even mathematical physics … who were not, basically, in one way or another, associated with IQIM. … If you look at the roster, even now, for the second iteration of IQIM, the second cycle we have, there’s a pretty cool medley of people.”

As a sign of quantum computing’s progression at Caltech and beyond, [the Institute partnered with Amazon](https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/caltech-and-amazon-partner-to-create-new-hub-of-quantum-computing) to build the AWS Center for Quantum Computing, which opened on campus last year. The goal of the collaboration is to create quantum computers and related technologies that have the potential to revolutionize data security, machine learning, medicine development, sustainability practices, and more.

“It is wonderful to see many of the graduate students and postdocs from the early days of IQIM come back to campus as senior research scientists at the [AWS Center for Quantum Computing](https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/caltech-and-amazon-partner-to-create-new-hub-of-quantum-computing),” Michalakis says. “IQIM brought together theorists and experimentalists with a vision toward a transformative future for all. Amazingly, we are reaping the benefits of that vision already, as the era of quantum information science and engineering unfolds before our eyes at an unprecedented pace. What an exciting time to be alive.”

This article from Caltech Magazine (Summer 2022) chronicles the history and evolution of the Institute for Quantum Information and Matter (IQIM) at Caltech, a leading center for quantum research. 

The story begins with Richard Feynman's 1982 prediction that quantum computers would be necessary for simulating quantum systems. When John Preskill arrived at Caltech in 1983, he initially worked on particle physics, but shifted to quantum information theory in the mid-1990s after Peter Shor's discovery of quantum factoring algorithms. In the late 1990s, Preskill and H.J. "Jeff" Kimble received a DARPA grant, and they hired Alexei Kitaev, whose work on fault-tolerant quantum computers later won the 2012 Breakthrough Prize.

In 2000, Preskill and Kimble used an NSF grant to form the Institute for Quantum Information (IQI). The early 2000s saw a remarkable group of young researchers pass through, including Patrick Hayden, Guifré Vidal (now at Google), and Frank Verstraete. Weekly meetings were so intense that Preskill imposed one-minute speaking limits. In 2011, as quantum computing hardware advanced, the institute expanded to include experimental work and changed its name to IQIM (adding "Matter" to the name). 

More recently, Caltech partnered with Amazon to build the AWS Center for Quantum Computing on campus, aiming to create quantum computers that could revolutionize data security, machine learning, medicine, and sustainability. The article highlights how many early IQIM researchers have returned as senior scientists at the AWS Center.

[![Caltech](/static/core/img/caltech-new-logo.png)](https://www.caltech.edu)
