From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Research institute in Waterloo, Canada

Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics

| Established | 1999 |
| Type | Research institute |
| Location | * [Waterloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterloo,_Ontario "Waterloo, Ontario"), [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"), Canada |
| Director | [Marcela Carena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcela_Carena "Marcela Carena") |
| Website | [www.perimeterinstitute.ca](http://www.perimeterinstitute.ca) |

**Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics** (**PI**, **Perimeter**, **PITP**) is an independent research centre in foundational [theoretical physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theoretical_physics "Theoretical physics") located in [Waterloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterloo,_Ontario "Waterloo, Ontario"), [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"), Canada. It was founded in 1999.[[1]](#cite_note-1) The institute's founding and major benefactor is Canadian entrepreneur and philanthropist [Mike Lazaridis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Lazaridis "Mike Lazaridis").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

The original building, designed by Saucier + Perrotte,[[3]](#cite_note-3) opened in 2004[[4]](#cite_note-4) and was awarded a [Governor General's Medal for Architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_General's_Medal_for_Architecture "Governor General's Medal for Architecture") in 2006.[[5]](#cite_note-5) The Stephen Hawking Centre, designed by [Teeple Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teeple_Architects "Teeple Architects"), was opened in 2011[[6]](#cite_note-6) and was LEED Silver certified in 2015.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

In addition to research, Perimeter also provides scientific training and educational outreach activities to the general public. This is done in part through Perimeter's Educational Outreach team.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/The_Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics_%287481548126%29.jpg/250px-The_Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics_%287481548126%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics_(7481548126).jpg)

Inside the Perimeter Institute

In 1999, [Howard Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Burton "Howard Burton")—who had a PhD in theoretical physics from the [University of Waterloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Waterloo "University of Waterloo")—emailed [Mike Lazaridis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Lazaridis "Mike Lazaridis") along with 20 CEOs in an attempt to leave his [Wall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street "Wall Street") job.[[9]](#cite_note-:0-9): 118 Lazaridis then pitched the idea of the Perimeter Institute to Burton as he wanted to use his [BlackBerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BlackBerry "BlackBerry") wealth for a philanthropic endeavour.[[9]](#cite_note-:0-9): 118 Lazaridis' initial donation of $100 million was announced on October 23, 2000, believed to be the biggest private donation in Canadian history to that point.[[10]](#cite_note-10) [Jim Balsille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Balsillie "Jim Balsillie") and [Doug Fregin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Fregin "Douglas Fregin") each donated $10 million.[[9]](#cite_note-:0-9): 119 The city of Waterloo offered four sites of land for free; Lazaridis chose the former site of the [Waterloo Memorial Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterloo_Memorial_Arena "Waterloo Memorial Arena") (near Uptown Waterloo).[[9]](#cite_note-:0-9): 120

Research operations began in 2001, in a temporary site in a nearby post office.[[9]](#cite_note-:0-9): 120 Burton became the institute's founding director.[[9]](#cite_note-:0-9): 116 The permanent building's construction finished in 2004.[[9]](#cite_note-:0-9): 120 The Ontario budget, announced in March 2006, included a commitment to provide $50 million in funding to PI from the [Ministry of Research and Innovation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Research_and_Innovation_(Ontario) "Minister of Research and Innovation (Ontario)").

In May 2008, Dr. [Neil Turok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Turok "Neil Turok"), a cosmologist, was appointed as Perimeter Institute's second director replacing Burton.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Lazaridis donated a subsequent $50 million on June 4, 2008.[[12]](#cite_note-12) In November 2008, it was announced that physicist [Stephen Hawking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Hawking "Stephen Hawking") would take the position of Distinguished Visiting Research Chair, a visiting position, at the institute.[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Designed by [Teeple Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teeple_Architects "Teeple Architects"), a new 5,000 m2 (55,000 sq ft) expansion, the [Stephen Hawking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Hawking "Stephen Hawking") Centre at Perimeter Institute, was completed in September 2011.[[15]](#cite_note-15) The centre's grand opening was in September 2011 and included a video greeting from Hawking, who rarely traveled due to disability.[[16]](#cite_note-16) This was the first-ever Gold Seal-managed project in Ontario, it attained [LEED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadership_in_Energy_and_Environmental_Design#LEED_Canada "Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design") Silver certification in 2015.[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)

On February 28, 2019, [Robert Myers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Myers_(physicist) "Robert Myers (physicist)") was appointed as the third director of the Perimeter Institute. On Nov 4, 2024, [Marcela Carena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcela_Carena "Marcela Carena") was announced as the fourth director.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

## Design

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Design")]

The Institute was designed by Montréal-based architectural firm [Saucier + Perrotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saucier_+_Perrotte "Saucier + Perrotte").[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20) A concrete stairwell in the building's atrium was designed by Blackwell Engineers.[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20) The Institute's front aluminum wall is black with small windows to represent a [blackboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackboard "Blackboard").[[9]](#cite_note-:0-9): 117 There are wooden fireplaces and blackboards throughout the building.[[9]](#cite_note-:0-9): 117 Writing for *[The Globe and Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Globe_and_Mail "The Globe and Mail")*, architecture critic Lisa Rochon praised the Institute's "seamless connections" between the building's interior and exterior and said the building is about "the flow of light and the directions we can take".[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20) Rochon described the building as [modernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_architecture "Modern architecture"), and cited [Tadao Ando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadao_Ando "Tadao Ando") as an influence.[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20)

## Research

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Research")]

Perimeter's research encompasses nine fields:[[21]](#cite_note-21)

* [Cosmology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmology "Cosmology")
* [Mathematical physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_physics "Mathematical physics")
* [Particle physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_physics "Particle physics")
* [Quantum fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory "Quantum field theory") and [strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_theory "String theory")
* [Quantum foundations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_foundations "Quantum foundations")
* [Quantum gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_gravity "Quantum gravity")
* [Quantum information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_information_science "Quantum information science")
* [Quantum matter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condensed_matter_physics "Condensed matter physics")
* [Strong gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_gravity "Strong gravity")

## Programs

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Programs")]

### Perimeter Institute Recorded Seminar Archive (PIRSA)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Perimeter Institute Recorded Seminar Archive (PIRSA)")]

An extensive, up-to-date archive of the institute's varied research activities is readily available to the public via the internet. The Perimeter Institute Recorded Seminar Archive (PIRSA),[[22]](#cite_note-22) is a permanent, free, searchable, and citable archive of recorded seminars, conferences, workshops and outreach events. Seminars with video and timed presentation materials can be accessed on-demand in Windows and Flash formats together with MP3 audio files and PDFs of the supporting materials. The PIRSA project is enlarged by the creation of SciVideos (See below).

### SciVideos

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: SciVideos")]

After more than 13,000 talks uploaded to PIRSA, Perimeter Institute created in 2020 a new public video archive called **SciTalks**,[[23]](#cite_note-23) which was later renamed to **SciVideos**,[[24]](#cite_note-24) with the support of the [Simons Foundations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simons_Foundation "Simons Foundation"). It is a [meta-repository](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metadata_repository "Metadata repository") search tool of scientific talks beyond what is produced at PI, including institutions such as [CERN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CERN "CERN"), [Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simons_Institute_for_the_Theory_of_Computing "Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing"), [ICTP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Centre_for_Theoretical_Physics "International Centre for Theoretical Physics") and [ICTP-SAIFR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICTP-SAIFR?action=edit&redlink=1 "ICTP-SAIFR (page does not exist)").[[25]](#cite_note-25) As a [meta-repository](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metadata_repository "Metadata repository"), SciVideos only stores metadata and links related to the videos, which are stored in other databases. [[26]](#cite_note-26)

## Educational outreach

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Educational outreach")]

Perimeter's educational outreach team's activities include a monthly public lecture series, a two-week summer camp for the world's top science students, a series of in-class resources, week-long professional development workshops for science teachers, cultural activities with local and international artists, an online archive of educational resources, an extensive network of science teachers to share content across Canada, and many other special events and science festivals contributing to [physics outreach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics_outreach "Physics outreach").[[27]](#cite_note-27)[[28]](#cite_note-28) Perimeter Institute operates an international outreach program.

The annual EinsteinPlus[[29]](#cite_note-29) summer school for high school physics teachers is held for one week each summer. The International Summer School for Young Physicists (ISSYP) is a physics camp for high school students.[[30]](#cite_note-30)[[31]](#cite_note-perimeterinstitute.ca-31) It brings approximately 20 Canadian students and 20 International students aged 16–18 to Perimeter for two weeks each year.[[32]](#cite_note-32)

### Public lectures series

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Public lectures series")]

Perimeter Institute has welcomed a number of very prominent scientists to deliver lectures on a wide variety of subjects.[[33]](#cite_note-33) Lecturers have included: [Freeman Dyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeman_Dyson "Freeman Dyson"), [Gerard ‘t Hooft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_‘t_Hooft "Gerard ‘t Hooft"), [Jay Ingram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Ingram "Jay Ingram"), [Seth Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seth_Lloyd "Seth Lloyd"), [Jay Melosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Melosh "Jay Melosh"), [Sir Roger Penrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Roger_Penrose "Sir Roger Penrose"), [Michael Peskin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Peskin "Michael Peskin"), [Leonard Susskind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Susskind "Leonard Susskind"), [Frank Wilczek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Wilczek "Frank Wilczek") and [Anton Zeilinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Zeilinger "Anton Zeilinger").[[34]](#cite_note-34)

### BrainSTEM: Your Future is Now

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: BrainSTEM: Your Future is Now")]

This festival connected technological innovations to the scientific breakthroughs that make them possible. The festival, held September 30 to October 6, 2013, featured science-centre styled exhibits, special presentations, public lectures, Science in the Club events and insider-tours of the Perimeter Institute. Webcast Public Lectures featured James Grime, [Ray Laflamme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Laflamme "Raymond Laflamme") and [Lucy Hawking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_Hawking "Lucy Hawking").[[35]](#cite_note-35)

### Quantum to Cosmos: Ideas for the Future festival

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Quantum to Cosmos: Ideas for the Future festival")]

Held in October, 2009, the Quantum to Cosmos: Ideas for the Future festival (Q2C Festival) was a [science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science "Science") outreach event held in [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"). The festival included events and activities spanning: lectures, panel discussions, pub talks, cultural activities, a PI documentary premiere (The Quantum Tamers: Revealing Our Weird and Wired Future), [sci-fi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sci-fi "Sci-fi") film festival, an art exhibit and the hugely popular Physica Phantastica exhibit centre, a 460-square-metre (5,000 sq ft) space filled with demonstrations, hands-on activities, experiments and an immersive 3D tour of the [universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universe "Universe") narrated by [Stephen Hawking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Hawking "Stephen Hawking").[[36]](#cite_note-36)

The Q2C Festival attracted some 40,000 attendees (including over 6,000 in the secondary school program that brought students from [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario") and [New York State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State "New York State") and nearly one million viewers –  and counting –  through online streaming, video-on-demand services and special television broadcasts. Special editions of [TVO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TVOntario "TVOntario")’s “[The Agenda with Steve Paikin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Agenda "The Agenda")", filmed live in PI's Atrium in [Waterloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterloo,_Ontario "Waterloo, Ontario") attracted hundreds of thousands of viewers from across Canada with just five broadcasts.[[37]](#cite_note-37)

## Training

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Training")]

### Joint masters-level program

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Joint masters-level program")]

In partnership with the [University of Waterloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Waterloo "University of Waterloo"), PI conducts Perimeter Scholars International (PSI),[[38]](#cite_note-38) a master's level course in theoretical physics.[[39]](#cite_note-39) The 10-month course was inaugurated in August 2009, and admits around 30 scholars per year. Students admitted (on average 3% of all applicants[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]) receive full scholarships and living expenses. The master's degree itself is issued by the [University of Waterloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Waterloo "University of Waterloo").[[40]](#cite_note-40)[[41]](#cite_note-41)[[42]](#cite_note-42)

### Doctoral studies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Doctoral studies")]

Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics also hosts PhD students wishing to pursue full-time graduate studies under the supervision of a PI faculty member. PhD students receive their doctoral degrees from a university partner, such as the University of Waterloo.

### Courses

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Courses")]

Perimeter Institute offers a number of planned courses each year, including cross-listed programs with universities and mini-courses given by PI faculty, associate faculty and visiting researchers. The courses are made available to all students enrolled in surrounding universities. The popular courses are attended by students from [University of Waterloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Waterloo "University of Waterloo"), [University of Western Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Western_Ontario "University of Western Ontario"), [McMaster University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMaster_University "McMaster University"), [University of Guelph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Guelph "University of Guelph"), [University of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto "University of Toronto"), [York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_University "York University"), and other centres.

args.summary:
The Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics (PI, PITP) is an independent research centre in foundational theoretical physics located in Waterloo, Ontario, Canada. Founded in 1999 by Mike Lazaridis (founder of BlackBerry) with an initial $100 million donation, the institute opened its permanent building in 2004. The Stephen Hawking Centre expansion opened in 2011. As of November 2024, the institute's fourth director is Marcela Carena.

The institute's research spans nine fields: cosmology, mathematical physics, particle physics, quantum fields and strings, quantum foundations, quantum gravity, quantum information, quantum matter, and strong gravity.

Educational outreach programs include a public lecture series featuring prominent scientists, the International Summer School for Young Physicists (ISSYP) for high school students, the EinsteinPlus summer school for physics teachers, and the BrainSTEM and Quantum to Cosmos festivals. The institute also maintains the Perimeter Institute Recorded Seminar Archive (PIRSA) and the SciVideos meta-repository.

Training programs include the Perimeter Scholars International (PSI) master's program in partnership with the University of Waterloo, doctoral studies, and various courses open to surrounding university students.

# Mathematical physics

## Breadcrumb

![Many equations layered on top of each other on a dark background](/sites/default/files/styles/banner_full_1000/public/2020-11/RESERS_Mathematical-Physics_AdobeStock_215441621.jpg)

Theoretical physics is, broadly speaking, the application of mathematics and mathematical thinking to understand the basic aspects of the universe. It follows that Perimeter is very interested in the development of novel mathematical ideas and approaches, especially when these might ultimately offer new insights into fundamental questions in physics. In recent years, Perimeter has pursued a clear strategy to raise the level of mathematical culture and expertise, more generally, within the Institute and the field and, equally, to foster mutually beneficial interactions between pure mathematics and physics.

Mathematical physics was founded as an official research area at Perimeter in 2014, with the arrival of [Kevin Costello](/people/kevin-costello) as a senior faculty member. Three associate faculty members, [Alexander Braverman](/people/alexander-braverman), [Ben Webster](/people/ben-webster), were recruited shortly afterwards, and more recently [Theo Johnson-Freyd](/people/ben-webster). Hence, the Institute’s initial focus has been on mathematics related to string theory and to quantum field theory. Costello’s interests span from the mathematical definition of perturbative quantum field theory, to the formalization of known and novel dualities in string theory, to integrability. Braverman and Webster are world experts in geometric representation theory and its relationship to supersymmetric quantum field theory and dualities. The group also comprises 10 postdoctoral researchers and six PhD students. Further, many researchers (e.g., [Davide Gaiotto](/people/davide-gaiotto)) in other areas at Perimeter have a deep interest in, and have made important contributions to, mathematical physics.

Perimeter’s mix of physicists and mathematicians with compatible interests fuels a unique research and learning environment, where physical intuition is not treated as a mysterious oracle but is incorporated into and guides mathematical work, and where novel mathematical results are mapped directly to a new physical understanding of problems in quantum field theory, string theory, and condensed matter physics. Our objective is to catalyze the growth of a truly ‘bilingual’ community, both at Perimeter and beyond, through our research and through the organization of timely workshops and schools.

Recent highlights of mathematical physics at Perimeter include progress on physics-related mathematical dualities, such as the geometric Langlandsprogram and symplectic duality; on the classification of topological phases of matter with homotopy and higher category theory; on exactly computable subsectors of holographic dualities; and on a new understanding of integrable theories.

# Quantum Information Research at Perimeter Institute

Quantum information explores and exploits uniquely quantum laws, such as the uncertainty principle.

![Abstract digital looking background with beams of light heading to one point](/sites/default/files/styles/banner_full_1000/public/2020-11/WHAT_Quantum-information_AdobeStock_97967086.jpg)

Among other things, Perimeter researchers are working on quantum error correction (the techniques needed to safeguard and verify information amid the errors inherent to quantum computation), study quantum complexity (which attempts to classify computational problems by how difficult they are for a quantum computer to solve), and pursue the application of quantum information techniques and insights to other areas of physics, including quantum foundations and condensed matter.

Quantum mechanics allow atoms to be in a **quantum superposition**. Superposition is a little like being in two places at one time. However, if you look at a quantum superposition, the particle has to decide where to be, and you can only ever see it in one of those two places.

Quantum information is the effort to both understand and use the properties of the quantum world.

The memory of a regular computer consists of a sequence of bits representing some number (which in turn might represent a picture or words or anything else). The computer does computations by changing that number according to its program. If we can instead build a computer out of single atoms or other microscopic objects, the memory of the computer could instead be in a quantum superposition. The information stored in such a computer would be quantum information, composed of qubits (short for "quantum bit") instead of bits. A **quantum computer** could perform some computations much faster than any plausible classical computer.

![a down arrow on a dot labelled zero and an up arrow on a dot labelled one](/sites/default/files/2020-11/Spin_Up_Down_large2.jpg "WHAT_quantum-information-spin")

The properties of qubits are sometimes very different from the properties of classical bits. Qubits cannot be copied to create multiple replicas. Another property of qubits is entangled states. They are special kinds of quantum states that allow two qubits to be more highly correlated than is possible for classical bits. These special properties allow other surprising applications of quantum mechanics. For instance, **quantum cryptography** allows more secure secret codes by taking advantage of the resistance of qubits to copying.

![Arrows on three sets of three layered dots (i.e., quantum superposition) showing: up, up, down (011); down, down, up (100); and up, down, up (101).](/sites/default/files/2020-11/Three_Qubits_large2.jpg "WHAT_quantum-information-qbits")

One major focus of quantum information researchers at Perimeter is to understand the properties of quantum information. Sometimes this takes the form of figuring out what new technologies quantum information can enable (such as new quantum cryptography protocols). Sometimes, we instead find limits on the power of quantum information (for instance, by discovering that certain computational problems are likely to be too hard for even a quantum computer to solve).

Sometimes we try to pinpoint the ways in which quantum systems are different from classical systems (by studying the distinction between quantum systems that can be easily simulated on a classical computer and those that cannot). And sometimes, we simply try to understand the strange behavior of quantum states with no particular application in mind (for instance, by studying the structure of complicated entangled states).

Actually building a quantum computer is a daunting task because of the challenges involved in manipulating individual atoms with high precision. Some of our associate faculty at the Institute for Quantum Computing (IQC) are engaged in **experiments** aimed at constructing quantum computers. At Perimeter, we do a good deal of theoretical work that can help in this long-term task. We study quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computation to allow experimenters to more easily construct large quantum computers, without requiring that the individual components of the quantum computer be perfect. We also think about improved ways to measure the properties of quantum systems, particularly those which are to be used to build a quantum computer.

The deeper insight we are trying to develop into the properties of quantum states pays off in other areas of physics as well, since so many systems of interest to physicists are inherently quantum-mechanical. A number of Perimeter researchers have a shared interest in quantum information and condensed matter or quantum foundations, and have also pursued applications of quantum information ideas to particle physics, astronomy, string theory, and quantum gravity.

# RIKEN Center for Quantum Computing (RQC)

* [Japanese Page](/research/labs/rqc/index.html)



![Yasunobu Nakamura (D.Eng.)](/medialibrary/riken/research/labs/rqc/img_center_pi.jpg) Director: Yasunobu Nakamura (Ph.D.)

The RIKEN Center for Quantum Computing (RQC) is an internationally unique research organization that develops and owns actual quantum computers based on different approaches, such as the superconducting quantum computer, including the first domestic quantum computer “A”, and the world's first general-purpose optical quantum computing platform.

The RQC develops and improves the performance of actual quantum computers based on various approaches such as superconductivity, optics, semiconductors, and cold atoms. While integrating cutting-edge physical science, information science, computer science, optics, and electronics technologies, the RQC expands the range of computational possibilities to solve social issues and promotes research to establish next-generation quantum computer technologies.

Sep. 27, 2024 **Press Release**  **Computing / Math**

# Powerful quantum error correction with a beautiful geometry

* [Japanese Page](/press/2024/20240905_1/index.html)

**In work published in Science Advances, Hayato Goto from the RIKEN Center for Quantum Computing in Japan has proposed a new quantum error correction approach using what he calls “many-hypercube codes.” This approach, which turns out to have an elegant geometry, could help realize extremely efficient error corrections and contribute to highly parallel methods that will allow fault-tolerant quantum computing, the next stage in the evolution of quantum computers.**

According to Goto, “Thanks to recent experimental progress, there is now great hope that we will be able to build fault-tolerant quantum computers, meaning quantum computers that can correct errors and surpass the power of conventional computers on certain tasks. To achieve this, however, it is important to develop efficient quantum error correction.”

Scientists have proposed many different methods of error correction over the last several decades. The conventional approach to quantum error correction is typically based on encoding a single logical qubit—the qubit being the equivalent of a bit on a classical computer—onto many entangled physical ones, and then using a decoder to retrieve the logical qubit from the physical ones. However, scalability is a problem with this approach, since the number of physical qubits required goes up enormously, and this results in huge resource overheads. To overcome this problem, high-rate quantum codes, such as quantum low-density parity-check codes, have been considered. However, with this approach the logical gates, which make calculations possible, have to be set up quite sequentially rather than fully parallel, making them less efficient time-wise.

As a means to remedy this, Goto proposed using an approach that he calls “many-hypercube codes." Specifically, it is a method with a complex name—high-rate concatenated quantum codes—and what is innovative is that the logical qubits can be visualized mathematically as forming what is known as a “hypercube”—a type of shape, including squares and cubes as well as higher-order shapes such as the tesseract. The beautiful mathematical and geometric structure of the code is remarkable, as most high-rate quantum codes have complicated structures.

Goto emphasizes that in order for the new codes to result in higher performance, he needed to develop a novel dedicated decoder that could interpret the result from the physical qubits. This innovative technique is based on level-by-level minimum distance decoding, which allows for high performance. Unlike other similar methods, it also allows for logical gates to be put in parallel rather than in a series, which makes the system analogous to parallel processing in classical computers, leading Goto to call it “high-performance fault tolerant computing” as an analogy to “high-performance computing” which is used for massively parallel computing.

The work paid off. The codes achieve an encoding rate—a number that indicates the ratio between logical and physical qubits—of up to 30% which Goto says appears to be the world's highest among the codes used for fault-tolerant quantum computing. And even with this high rate, the performance is comparable to conventional low-rate codes.

Goto says, “in practice, this code could be implementing with physical qubit systems such as laser-trapped neutral-atom qubits.”

Rate this article

## Reference

Goto H (2024) **High-performance fault-tolerant quantum computing with many-hypercube codes.** Sci Adv. doi: [10.1126/sciadv.adp6388](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adp6388)

The method uses high-rate concatenated quantum codes where logical qubits form mathematical hypercubes (including higher-dimensional shapes like tesseracts). This approach achieves an encoding rate of up to 30%, reportedly the world's highest among codes used for fault-tolerant quantum computing, while maintaining performance comparable to conventional low-rate codes. A key innovation is a dedicated decoder using level-by-level minimum distance decoding, which allows logical gates to operate in parallel rather than sequentially, enabling "high-performance fault tolerant computing." The approach could potentially be implemented with laser-trapped neutral-atom qubits.

RIKEN Hakubi Team Leader: Bartosz Regula (Ph.D.)

## Research Summary

![Bartosz Regula](/medialibrary/riken/research/labs/hakubi/r_math_qtm_inf/bartosz_regula.jpg)

Our group studies the mathematical underpinnings of quantum information theory, with a particular focus on the investigation of the mathematical structure of quantum resources — physical phenomena that underlie practical advantages of quantum technologies in areas such as communication and computation. We aim to develop technical frameworks that help address the fundamental questions of how to quantify, manipulate, and take advantage of physical resources in quantum information and communication tasks. Our approach is to establish a solid and rigorous mathematical foundation which can be directly used to study a variety of physical settings, allowing for broad applications and generalisations.

* Theory of informatics-related

# Summary of Prof. Yasunobu Nakamura's Talk on Microwave Quantum Optics in Superconducting Circuits

**Speaker:** Prof. Yasunobu Nakamura, Director at RIKEN Center for Quantum Computing (Japan) and Professor at University of Tokyo  
**Event:** QIQT Summer School (July 12, 2021)  
**Topic:** Microwave quantum optics in superconducting circuits, focusing on cavity QED and waveguide QED

## Key Content

### 1. RIKEN Center for Quantum Computing
- Founded April 2021, with ~14 teams working on quantum computing (both experimental and theoretical)
- Research covers superconducting quantum computing, optical quantum computing, semiconductor spin qubits, cold atoms, electrons on helium, quantum computing theory, algorithms, and quantum software

### 2. Superconducting Qubits & Circuit QED
- Qubits are realized using Josephson junctions (tunnel junctions between superconducting electrodes) which act as nonlinear inductors, creating non-equidistant energy levels essential for qubit operation
- "Artificial atoms" are created using transmon qubits embedded in 3D microwave cavities
- The system is described by the Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian

### 3. Waveguide QED Key Concepts
- In 1D waveguide systems, an atom (qubit) coupled to a waveguide can achieve perfect reflection of incident microwaves due to destructive interference between incident and re-emitted light
- In 2010 experiment: demonstrated ~94% reflection (later improved to >99.9% with better coherent qubits)

### 4. Microwave Single Photon Detector (First Experiment)
- Used a lambda-type three-level system in a driven superconducting circuit
- Achieved impedance matching condition where two transition rates are symmetric
- Demonstrated single photon detection with ~66% efficiency
- Absorptive-type detection where the photon is absorbed and destroyed

### 5. Non-Demolition Single Photon Detector
- Used a qubit embedded in a 3D cavity (off-resonant, dispersive regime)
- Conditional pi-phase gate: depending on qubit state, reflected photon acquires opposite phase
- Achieved ~84% quantum efficiency with ~1.5% dark count rate
- Demonstrated non-demolition detection: photon number state preserved after detection (84% fidelity)
- Acts as a photon number parity detector (even/odd photon number detection)

### 6. Microwave Cluster State Generation
- Generated single photons deterministically in ~140 nanoseconds
- Created 1D cluster states by repeatedly emitting entangled photon trains
- Reconstructed density matrix for up to 35 modes using matrix product operator representation
- Fidelity of 62% for 5-mode cluster state
- Characterized localizable entanglement up to 6 consecutive modes

### 7. Quantum Network Proposal
- Proposed a 1D quantum network with multiple quantum nodes connected along a waveguide
- Each node uses two qubits coupled to a waveguide with a cancellation resonator
- Enables deterministic emission, absorption, and transmission of photons
- Node can emit photons directionally (100% into right-going mode)
- Can absorb incoming photons perfectly with proper time-dependent coupling control

## Q&A Highlights
- Discussed effects of vacuum fluctuations on energy levels (Lamb shift)
- Explained how three-level systems are effectively modeled from multi-level systems
- Addressed polarization limitations in coplanar waveguide structures
- Discussed PT-symmetric Hamiltonians as potential future direction

The **Institute for Quantum Computing** (**IQC**) is an affiliate scientific research institute of the [University of Waterloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Waterloo "University of Waterloo") located in [Waterloo, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterloo,_Ontario "Waterloo, Ontario") with a multidisciplinary approach to the field of [quantum information processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_information_processing "Quantum information processing"). IQC was founded in 2002[[1]](#cite_note-1) primarily through a donation made by [Mike Lazaridis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Lazaridis "Mike Lazaridis") and his wife Ophelia whose substantial donations have continued over the years.[[2]](#cite_note-2) The institute is now located in the [Mike & Ophelia Lazaridis Quantum-Nano Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_&_Ophelia_Lazaridis_Quantum-Nano_Centre "Mike & Ophelia Lazaridis Quantum-Nano Centre") and the Research Advancement Centre at the University of Waterloo.

Its executive director is physics professor Norbert Lütkenhaus and hosts researchers based in 7 departments across 3 faculties at the University of Waterloo. In addition to theoretical and experimental research on [quantum computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computer "Quantum computer"), IQC also hosts academic conferences and workshops, short courses for undergraduate and high school students, and scientific outreach events including open houses and tours for the public.

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Institute_for_Quantum_Computing&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Institute for Quantum Computing was officially created in 2002, sparked by [Research In Motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_In_Motion "Research In Motion") co-founder [Mike Lazaridis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Lazaridis "Mike Lazaridis") and then-president of the University of Waterloo, [David Johnston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Johnston_(governor_general) "David Johnston (governor general)"), for research into quantum information. Since inception, Lazaridis has provided more than $100 million in private funding for IQC. The institute is a collaboration between academia, the private sector, and the federal and provincial governments. [Raymond Laflamme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Laflamme "Raymond Laflamme") was the founding executive director.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

At its establishment, the institute was composed of only a handful of researchers from the Departments of Computer Science and Physics. Ten years later, there are more than 200 researchers across six departments within the Faculties of Science, Mathematics, and Engineering at the University of Waterloo.

In 2008, IQC moved into the Research Advancement Centre 1 (RAC I) in the University of Waterloo's Research & Technology Park. In 2010, research operations expanded into the adjacent building, Research Advancement Centre 2 (RAC II).

In 2012, IQC expanded into the Mike & Ophelia Lazaridis Quantum-Nano Centre. The 285,000-square-foot facility is shared with the [Waterloo Institute for Nanotechnology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterloo_Institute_for_Nanotechnology "Waterloo Institute for Nanotechnology"), and is built to stringent standards (controls for vibration, humidity, temperature, and electromagnetic radiation) for quantum and nanotechnology experiments. The building was designed by Toronto-based firm [Kuwabara Payne McKenna Blumberg Architects (KPMB)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KPMB_Architects "KPMB Architects").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

## Research

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Institute_for_Quantum_Computing&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Research")]

Research at IQC focuses on three main applications of quantum information science and technology using the physical sciences, mathematics and engineering from both theoretical and experimental perspectives.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Areas of research currently studied at IQC include:

* [quantum computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_computer "Quantum computer")
* [quantum communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_channel "Quantum channel")
* [quantum sensing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_sensor "Quantum sensor")
* [quantum materials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_materials "Quantum materials")
* [quantum engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_engineering "Quantum engineering")

In collaboration with the University of Waterloo, IQC offers research positions and advanced courses in the foundations, applications, and implementation of quantum information processing for graduate students. In addition, IQC also offers an interdisciplinary graduate program in Quantum Information which leads to MMath, MSc, MASc, and PhD degrees.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

## Facilities

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Institute_for_Quantum_Computing&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Facilities")]

IQC currently has offices and laboratories in both Research Advancement Centre I and II, located in the University of Waterloo's [David Johnston Research & Technology Park](http://www.rtpark.uwaterloo.ca/) [Archived](https://web.archive.org/web/20090227152537/http://rtpark.uwaterloo.ca/) February 27, 2009, at the [Wayback Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayback_Machine "Wayback Machine").

On 9 June 2008, Mike and Ophelia Lazaridis, together with Ontario Premier [Dalton McGuinty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalton_McGuinty "Dalton McGuinty"), University of Waterloo President [David Johnston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lloyd_Johnston "David Lloyd Johnston"), and other guests officially broke ground on the project which will consist of three areas: one to house IQC, one for the [Waterloo Institute for Nanotechnology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterloo_Institute_for_Nanotechnology "Waterloo Institute for Nanotechnology"), and a [clean fabrication and metrology suite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleanroom "Cleanroom") to be shared between the two institutes.[[7]](#cite_note-7) It will house offices, laboratory space, and areas for collaboration among researchers. The QNC opened September 21, 2012.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

args.summary: The webpage highlights the University of Waterloo as a premier institution for quantum research and education. Key facilities include the newly-opened Mike & Ophelia Lazaridis Quantum-Nano Centre (QNC), a state-of-the-art collaborative facility. Research spans multiple departments: the Department of Combinatorics and Optimization (researchers Andrew Childs, Debbie Leung, Michele Mosca, Ashwin Nayak) focuses on quantum cryptography, fault-tolerant computation, quantum walks, and key distribution; the Cheriton School of Computer Science (Richard Cleve, John Watrous) works on quantum algorithms, cryptographic protocols, and complexity theory; and the Department of Applied Mathematics (Joseph Emerson, Achim Kempf, Robert Koenig) explores quantum information science, foundations of quantum theory, and quantum cosmology. The Institute for Quantum Computing (IQC) connects researchers to harness quantum laws for transforming information technology. UWaterloo also offers a unique interdisciplinary graduate program in Quantum Information at both masters and PhD levels, jointly run by the Faculties of Mathematics, Science, and Engineering.

args.summary:
The Institute for Quantum Computing (IQC) is a world-leading research centre in quantum information science and technology at the University of Waterloo, located in Waterloo, Ontario. Founded in 2002 as part of a vision by Mike Lazaridis and his wife Ophelia, IQC was one of the earliest global centres of quantum information research. It employs 51-200 people with 171 associated members, and specializes in quantum computing, quantum communication, quantum materials, quantum sensors, and quantum devices. The institute received a $1.5M grant from the Canadian Space Agency in 2018.

Key recent developments include:
- A new nanoscale diamond structure that better collects and controls light, producing a 'nanojet' of light, published in Science Advances by Dr. Michal Bajcsy's group, with potential for quantum sensors and biomedical imaging.
- A new material that captures light with unprecedented precision for next-generation photodetectors, led by Sasan V. Grayli.
- QuantumCore, Inc., a startup spun out of IQC research founded by Dr. Christopher Wilson and Eugene Profis, raised $10.7M and listed publicly to develop amplifiers for superconducting quantum chips.
- Five IQC faculty received $1.8M in NSERC Alliance Quantum grants for quantum sensing and computing research.
- The 2026 USEQIP program welcomed 30 students from Canada, the U.S., and internationally.
- Submissions opened for the second annual Machine Learning to Advance Quantum Technologies (ML4QT) Symposium.
- The 2026 ETSI/IQC Quantum Safe Cryptography Conference was held at Carleton University with representatives from 25+ countries.

IQC is part of Waterloo's Quantum Valley ecosystem, with collaborations including Perimeter Institute and other partners. Similar organizations include Quantum Center ETH Zurich, Perimeter Institute, MIT Center for Quantum Engineering, PsiQuantum, Xanadu, and QuEra Computing.

args.summary: The Fields Institute hosted a Thematic Program on "Mathematics in Quantum Information" in July-August 2009. The program was organized into three streams: Operator Structure Stream, Quantum Marginal Stream, and Mathematics in Experiment Stream. The organizing committee was chaired by David Kribs (Guelph), with Raymond Laflamme (IQC, Waterloo), Kevin Resch (IQC, Waterloo), and Mary Beth Ruskai (Tufts). The program featured several workshops: a Workshop on Operator Structures in Quantum Information (July 6-10, 2009), a Workshop on Quantum Marginals and Density Matrices (July 27-31, 2009), and a Workshop on Mathematics in Experimental Quantum Information Processing (August 10-14, 2009, held at IQC Waterloo). Additionally, a Distinguished Lecture Series was given by Matthew B. Hastings (Microsoft Research Station Q) on August 17, 18, and 20, covering quantum channels, computational complexity of ground states, and time evolution of quantum systems. The program also included the 9th Canadian Quantum Information Summer School (August 17-21, 2009) and the 6th Canadian Quantum Information Student Conference (August 22-23, 2009). Affiliated activities included TQC 2009 (May 11-13, 2009) and the CQIQC III conference (August 24-28, 2009). Additional support was provided by the Institute for Transdisciplinary Research in Quantum Computing, with pending NSF funding for junior US visitors.

# Graduate Studies - Quantum Information at Waterloo

The University of Waterloo, in collaboration with the Institute for Quantum Computing (IQC), offers graduate students unique opportunities to learn about and engage in world-leading research in quantum information through a wide range of advanced research projects and advanced courses on the foundations, applications and implementation of quantum information processing.

In particular, we offer a new interdisciplinary graduate program in Quantum Information that leads to MMath, MSc, MASc, and PhD degrees. The program is offered in collaboration with:

* [The Faculty of Mathematics](http://uwaterloo.ca/math/)![Students working in a research lab](https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/sites/ca.institute-for-quantum-computing/files/styles/sidebar-220px-wide/public/uploads/images/img-9040-copy.jpg.jpg?itok=0h5i1qwR)
  + [Department of Applied Mathematics](http://uwaterloo.ca/applied-mathematics/)
  + [Department of Pure Mathematics](https://uwaterloo.ca/pure-mathematics/)
  + [Department of Combinatorics and Optimization](http://uwaterloo.ca/combinatorics-and-optimization/)
  + [David R. Cheriton School of Computer Science](https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/)
* [The Faculty of Science](https://uwaterloo.ca/science/)
  + [Department of Chemistry](https://uwaterloo.ca/chemistry/)
  + [Department of Physics and Astronomy](https://uwaterloo.ca/physics-astronomy/)
* [The Faculty of Engineering](https://uwaterloo.ca/engineering/)
  + [Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering](https://uwaterloo.ca/electrical-computer-engineering/).

![ Frank Wilhelm's Theory Group](https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/sites/ca.institute-for-quantum-computing/files/styles/sidebar-220px-wide/public/uploads/images/IQC%2025.jpg?itok=qK3BGq8_)Students are required to complete the requirements of both their home unit and the specific requirements of the Quantum Information (QI) program to achieve the special QI designation. For example, MMath in Computer Science (Quantum Information), PhD in Chemistry (Quantum Information), MASc in Electrical and Computer Engineering (Quantum Information).

MMath, MSc, and MASc students will receive a strong and broad foundation in quantum information science, coupled with knowledge and expertise from their home program. This will prepare them for the workforce or further graduate studies and research leading towards a PhD.

PhD students will be prepared for careers as scholars and researchers, with advanced expertise in quantum information science, along with the focus of their home program. The new program is designed to provide knowledge of quantum information, including theory and implementations, their home program discipline, and also developed advanced expertise in their particular research area within quantum information.

At present IQC has a critical mass of expertise in several major research areas within quantum information, including (but not limited to):

* [Quantum error correction & fault tolerance](https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/research/areas-research/quantum-error-correction-and-fault-tolerance)
* [Quantum complexity](https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/research/areas-research/quantum-complexity)
* [Quantum algorithms](https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/research/areas-research/quantum-algorithms)
* [Quantum information theory](https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/research/areas-research/quantum-information-theory)
* [Spin-based quantum information processing](https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/research/areas-research/spin-based-quantum-information-processing)

* [Nanoelectronics-based quantum information processing](https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/research/areas-research/nanoelectronics-based-quantum-information-processing)
* [Optical quantum information processing](https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/research/areas-research/optical-quantum-information-processing)
* [Quantum cryptography](https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/research/areas-research/quantum-cryptography)

![](https://quantuminstitute.yale.edu/sites/default/files/styles/threshold-480/public/iqc_waterloo_-_nov_2015.jpg?itok=E6yCg1PL)

# National centre of excellence in quantum opens at UNSW

The Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence in Quantum Computation and Communication Technology at UNSW Sydney has been officially launched.

Published on the 15 Feb 2019 by Lucy Carroll

![Director of CQC2T and Scientia Professor Michelle Simmons with Jason Falinski MP at the launch of the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence in Quantum Computation and Communication Technology.](https://newsroom.unsw.edu.au/sites/default/files/styles/full_width__2x/public/thumbnails/image/20190215_cqc2topening_media_screen-28_2.jpg)

Director of CQC2T and Scientia Professor Michelle Simmons with Jason Falinski MP at the launch of the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence in Quantum Computation and Communication Technology.

#### Media contact

**Lucy Carroll**  
UNSW External Communications  
9385 8732, 0402 005 319  
[l.carroll@unsw.edu.au](mailto:l.carroll@unsw.edu.au)

The Australian Research Council (ARC) Centre of Excellence in Quantum Computation and Communication Technology (CQC2T) at UNSW Sydney was officially launched today by Mr Jason Falinski MP receiving $33.7 million in federal funding to continue its development of the world’s first quantum computer.

The CQC2T is an international collaboration between seven Australian universities and more than 25 partners to form one of the largest combined efforts in quantum computation and communication research in the world.

The centre, led by 2018 Australian of the Year Professor Michelle Simmons, is a global leader in quantum computing research developing quantum processes in silicon and optical platforms that will be linked over secure communication networks.

“We are very fortunate to have a team of exceptional researchers in Australia delivering world leading quantum information research” says Professor Michelle Simmons, Director of the CQC2T.

"At the very forefront of what humans have achieved to date, our research achievements and strong global collaborations, have put us in pole position to drive an industry that will shape the information economy of the 21st century."

Funded by the Australian Research Council since 2000, the centre now holds 200 researchers and has nodes at the University of Melbourne, Australian National University, RMIT University, University of Technology, Sydney, University of Queensland and Griffith University.

In addition to announcing major breakthroughs in 3D architectures for a large-scale silicon quantum computer, the centre has announced the development of the next generation of photonic microchips that will be the key to developing large-scale photonic quantum computer.

Researchers at the centre are now proposing to implement quantum processors able to run error corrected algorithms and transfer information across networks with absolute security. The technology developed will provide a strategic advantage in a world where information and information security are of paramount importance.

At today’s launch, Professor Simmons emphasised the centre’s research achievements and strong global collaborations.

The ongoing success of CQC2T has led to the development of two Australian companies, QuintessenceLabs for secure communication systems and Silicon Quantum Computing for silicon-based quantum computing.

“The commercial success and collaboration across other quantum centres nationally have made Australia the quantum capital of the world,” said Professor Simmons.

At the opening, Mr Falinski said the funding would allow the centre to build on its strong successes.

“Australia has firmly established itself as a global leader in this 21st century technology – $33.7 million in funding will enable the Centre to continue to build on its world-leading research to develop complex quantum processors that correct errors and transfer information across vast networks with absolute security,” Mr Falinski said.

![20190215_cqc2topening_media_screen-24.jpg](https://newsroom.unsw.edu.au/sites/default/files/styles/full_width/public/thumbnails/image/20190215_cqc2topening_media_screen-24_1.jpg?itok=yKTyKEQz "20190215_cqc2topening_media_screen-24.jpg")

Director of the CQC2T and Scientia Professor Michelle Simmons, Jason Falinski MP and the Chief Executive Officer of the Australian Research Council, Professor Sue Thomas at the launch of the ARC Centre of Excellence in Quantum Computation and Communication Technology.

UNSW President and Vice-Chancellor Professor Ian Jacobs said the CQC2T researchers were working at the forefront of quantum information technology and innovation, which would lead to significant impacts across the global economy.

“Quantum computing not only has the potential to completely revolutionise the way many of us will work but could create jobs and even new industries we haven’t even imagined yet,” Professor Jacobs said.

“We applaud the ARC’s recognition of CQC2T as a fine example of Australia’s truly world-leading research.”

Professor Sue Thomas, Chief Executive Officer of the ARC, said the CQC2T has had an unparalleled record of success.

“At the ARC, it’s our great privilege to be able to support (this) work and we look forward to the great successes to follow,” Professor Thomas said.

For more information about the scheme, visit the [ARC website](http://www.arc.gov.au/).

args.summary: The Australian Research Council (ARC) Centre of Excellence in Quantum Computation and Communication Technology (CQC2T) at UNSW Sydney was officially launched on February 15, 2019, receiving $33.7 million in federal funding to continue developing the world's first quantum computer. Led by 2018 Australian of the Year Professor Michelle Simmons, the centre is an international collaboration between seven Australian universities and more than 25 partners. It holds 200 researchers across nodes at UNSW, University of Melbourne, Australian National University, RMIT, University of Technology Sydney, University of Queensland, and Griffith University. The centre has announced major breakthroughs in 3D architectures for silicon quantum computers and the next generation of photonic microchips. Its ongoing success has led to two Australian companies: QuintessenceLabs (secure communication) and Silicon Quantum Computing (silicon-based quantum computing). The funding was presented by MP Jason Falinski, with remarks from UNSW President Professor Ian Jacobs and ARC CEO Professor Sue Thomas.

# CQC2T: Centre for Quantum Computation & Communication Technology

[The ARC Centre of Excellence for Quantum Computation and Communication Technology](https://www.cqc2t.org/) (CQC²T) is focused on delivering world-leading quantum research to develop full-scale quantum systems – encompassing ultra-fast quantum computation, secure quantum communication and distributed quantum information processing.

UTS QIS joined CQC²T in 2017 as a collaborating partner led by Chief Investigator Professor Michael Bremner.  Prof Bremner’s research at CQC²T is focussed on methodologies and capabilities of quantum software and information technologies, with a significant focus on the development of new applications for these technologies.

For more information on the partnership: **[The Quantum Algorithms and Complexity Program](https://www.cqc2t.org/quantum-algorithms-and-complexity-program/)**

The webpage is about the ARC Centre of Excellence for Quantum Computation and Communication Technology (CQC²T) and its partnership with UTS QIS, led by Chief Investigator Professor Michael Bremner. The main content is a transcript of a panel discussion chaired by Hyman Devitt on the quantum applications stack and its impact on the private sector.

Panel participants include:
- **Martin Roeller (Microsoft Research)**: Focuses on quantum algorithms, chemistry, material science, and machine learning applications. Microsoft is pursuing topological quantum computing with intrinsically protected qubits.
- **Matt Johnson (QC Ware CEO)**: Quantum software company focused on quantum machine learning, finance, and search for enterprise problems.
- **Michael Brett (Q Branch CEO)**: Data analytics company using machine learning, viewing quantum computing as a long-term strategic differentiator.
- **Gabriela (Volkswagen Data Lab)**: Applied quantum computing for traffic flow optimization using D-Wave systems, routing optimization for hundreds of cars in seconds.
- **Michael Bremner (UTS/CQC²T)**: Theoretical aspects of quantum computing, quantum algorithms, and benchmarking.

Key discussion points: the distinction between near-term noisy quantum devices and fully error-corrected universal quantum computers; the need for approximately 100 logical qubits for quantum chemistry applications like nitrogen fixation; Volkswagen's successful traffic optimization pilot using D-Wave's 1000-2000 qubit system; the importance of classical emulators for enterprise quantum development; and Microsoft's topological quantum computing approach using Majorana zero modes as a potential path to scalable quantum computing with reduced error correction requirements.

URL: https://thequantuminsider.com/2025/11/14/google-ai-outlines-five-stage-roadmap-to-make-quantum-computing-useful

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Google's Quantum AI team has proposed a five-stage framework to guide the development of useful quantum computing applications, as detailed in a paper published on arXiv and a companion blog post by Ryan Babbush, Director of Research, Quantum Algorithms and Applications. The framework shifts the focus from hardware milestones (like qubit counts) to application maturity and real-world utility.

The five stages are:
- **Stage I – Discovery:** New quantum algorithms in abstract mathematical settings. The researchers note a concerning decline in foundational algorithm research due to risk-averse incentives in funding.
- **Stage II – Hard Instances:** Identifying concrete problem instances where quantum computers outperform classical ones. This stage is often overlooked but critical for bridging theory to practice.
- **Stage III – Theory-to-Application Gap:** Demonstrating quantum advantage on real-world tasks. This is identified as the most significant bottleneck. Google recommends an "algorithm-first" approach (starting with known quantum primitives like simulation) rather than a "problem-first" approach.
- **Stage IV – Engineering the Advantage:** Optimizing, compiling, and estimating resources (qubits, gates) for implementation. This is described as tedious but essential, with tools like Qualtran, Q#, QREF, and Bartiq emerging to help.
- **Stage V – Deployment:** Application in real production environments. No confirmed real-world quantum advantage exists yet, but early efforts like certified random number generation hint at the path forward.

The researchers call for renewed investment in foundational research, cross-disciplinary collaboration, open-source tools, and a shift toward measuring progress by problems solved rather than qubit counts. Google suggests AI (including large language models like Gemini) could help bridge knowledge gaps by scanning for real-world problems matching known quantum speedups. The team is also building a "Compendium of Super-Quadratic Quantum Advantage" and backing the Google Quantum AI XPRIZE to encourage progress.
</summary>

Microsoft and UC Santa Barbara researchers unveiled an eight-qubit topological quantum processor, the first of its kind, on Wednesday. The chip, developed by Microsoft Station Q led by UCSB physics professor Chetan Nayak, represents a breakthrough in quantum computing by creating a "topological superconductor" — a new state of matter that hosts Majorana zero modes (MZMs). These quasiparticles, which are their own antiparticles and can retain memory of their positions over time, enable more stable and fault-tolerant quantum computing by distributing quantum information across a physical system rather than individual particles. The researchers realized MZMs by placing an indium arsenide semiconductor nanowire close to an aluminum superconductor. The eight-qubit processor serves as a proof-of-concept, accompanied by a paper in Nature and a preprint roadmap for scaling up the technology. The topological approach promises more robust error correction built at the hardware level, reducing the need for additional qubits for error correction. Key collaborators include Chris Palmstrom (materials), Susanne Stemmer (fabrication), and the work builds on Nobel Prize-winning ideas of the late Herb Kroemer.

## What is Quantum Computing?

This IBM Think article (published June 2025, updated April 2026) provides a comprehensive overview of quantum computing, authored by Josh Schneider and Ian Smalley.

### Definition
Quantum computing is an emergent field that harnesses quantum mechanics to solve problems beyond the capability of even the most powerful classical computers. Large-scale quantum computers could tackle certain complex problems in minutes or hours that would take conventional machines millennia to complete.

### Four Key Principles of Quantum Mechanics
The article outlines four essential principles:
1. **Superposition** – Qubits can exist as a combination of all possible configurations simultaneously, creating complex multidimensional computational spaces.
2. **Entanglement** – Qubits can correlate their states with other qubits, allowing information about one to be immediately determined by measuring another.
3. **Interference** – Quantum waves can amplify or cancel out outcomes, serving as the "engine" of quantum computing.
4. **Decoherence** – The collapse of a quantum state into a nonquantum state, which must be avoided or minimized.

### How Quantum Computers Work
Quantum computers use qubits (quantum bits) instead of classical bits. Qubits can represent 0, 1, or a superposition of both simultaneously. Common types include superconducting qubits, trapped ion qubits, quantum dots, and photons. Key hardware components include quantum processors, superconductors (requiring temperatures near absolute zero), control electronics, and quantum software (notably IBM's Qiskit SDK).

### Classical vs. Quantum Computing
- **Classical**: Uses bits (0 or 1), processes information sequentially, provides singular answers.
- **Quantum**: Uses qubits (0, 1, or superposition), processes data with quantum logic, provides ranges of possible answers. Quantum and classical computers work together in combined workflows.

### Quantum Utility vs. Quantum Advantage
- **Quantum Utility**: Quantum computations providing reliable solutions beyond brute-force classical simulation (first demonstrated by IBM in 2023).
- **Quantum Advantage**: When quantum provides a better, faster, or cheaper solution than all known classical methods. IBM expects to realize this by late 2026.

### Practical Applications
Quantum computing is expected to be useful for modeling physical systems (chemistry, pharmaceuticals, material science) and identifying patterns in data (machine learning, finance, biology).

### Key Challenges
1. Scaling quantum processors (IBM aims for 200 logical qubits by 2029, 2,000 by 2033)
2. Scaling quantum hardware (reducing footprint, cost, energy)
3. Quantum error correction (IBM announced a landmark code 10x more efficient in 2024)
4. Quantum algorithm discovery
5. Quantum software and middleware
6. Quantum-centric supercomputing

### Industry Outlook
Quantum computing is estimated to become a USD 1.3 trillion industry by 2035 (McKinsey). Leading institutions include IBM, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Rigetti, and IonQ.

--- SOURCE 19: Not Everyone Is Convinced by Microsoft's Topological Qubits ---
URL: https://spectrum.ieee.org/topological-qubit

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Summary: Not Everyone Is Convinced by Microsoft's Topological Qubits

This IEEE Spectrum article (published 19 Mar 2025, by Dina Genkina) reports on the contentious state of topological quantum computing, focusing on efforts by **Microsoft** and **Nokia Bell Labs**.

### What is a Topological Qubit?
Unlike conventional qubits that encode information via fragile local properties (e.g., electron spin), topological qubits use a global, topological property of electrons—akin to a "knot" that is resistant to environmental noise. These states are theoretically more robust but extremely difficult to create and prove experimentally.

### Microsoft's "Majorana 1" Chip
- Microsoft announced its first topological quantum chip, the **Majorana 1**, in February 2025.
- The approach uses a semiconductor nanowire layered with a superconductor at millikelvin temperatures to create **Majorana zero modes** (the "knots").
- **Controversy**: Microsoft previously claimed this milestone in 2018 but later retracted the paper after skepticism. Their 2023 and 2025 claims remain contentious.
  - **Chetan Nayak** (Microsoft lead): "We are very confident that our devices host Majorana zero modes."
  - **Henry Legg** (U. of St. Andrews): "There is no evidence of even the basic physics of Majoranas in these devices."
  - **Bertrand Halperin** (Harvard): "Further experiments and better data are necessary."
- Microsoft's chip has **8 lithographically fabricated qubits**, but they are not yet functional. Error-free state duration is ~5 microseconds (vs. 400 ms for IBM's superconducting qubits).
- The team demonstrated one necessary measurement operation; preliminary results for another were shown at a private Station Q meeting.

### Nokia Bell Labs' Approach
- Led by **Robert Willett**, the team uses a **gallium arsenide** sandwich structure at millikelvin temperatures under a strong magnetic field to create a 2D topological state.
- Claims to have demonstrated key ingredients in 2023 (Physical Review X).
- **Status**: Not yet able to perform operations with the device. Error-free states can be maintained for **days**, but they cannot be controlled yet. Results on operations are expected in Q2 2025.
- **Michael Eggleston** (Nokia): "We're very confident that we have a topological state."

### Outlook
Topological quantum computing is at an earlier stage than other approaches but holds theoretical promise. Eggleston compares topological qubits to the **transistor**—something small, robust, and scalable—versus other qubit types being like "vacuum tubes" from the 1940s. The practical milestone will be demonstrating a controllable, noise-resistant qubit, regardless of whether the underlying topology is definitively proven.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"I would say all quantum computing is early stages. But topological quantum computing is further behind. It could catch up; it's taking a somewhat different path." — Bertrand Halperin, Harvard, "We are very confident that our devices host Majorana zero modes." — Chetan Nayak, Microsoft, "There is no evidence of even the basic physics of Majoranas in these devices, let alone that you could build a qubit out of them." — Henry Legg, U. of St. Andrews, "I look at these other qubit types... they're really challenging to scale up. To me, topological qubits really offer the potential that the transistor did. Something small, something robust, something that's scalable." — Michael Eggleston, Nokia
</key_excerpts>

# Applied Quantum Computing Symposium 2025 Summary

The Applied Quantum Computing Symposium 2025, hosted by the Institut quantique de l'Université de Sherbrooke, took place on November 13, 2025. The event focused on the central question: "How can we make quantum computing useful?" addressing both hardware challenges (quantum error correction) and software/applications development.

## Opening Remarks
- **Organizers**: The quantum algo lab team at Université de Sherbrooke, led by manager and scientific director Stephanos Cortis (physics professor and Pascal chair in AI/quantum AI).
- **Michelle Pier** (new director of the Sherbrook quantum innovation zone) highlighted the importance of talent and the recently established francophone bachelor's degree in quantum computing.

1. **Sherhack 2026** – March 2026 in Sherbrook (3rd edition)
2. **Canadian Workshop on Quantum Algorithms** – April 2026 in Montreal (organized by quantum algorithmic alliance)
3. **Algolab Summer School 2026** – June 7-19, 2026 (2nd edition, theme: "Towards Full Tolerant Quantum Computing")
4. **TQC (Quantum Computation and Quantum Algorithms)** – August 31 - September 4, 2026 in Sherbrook (2nd biggest quantum computing conference)

## Keynote Presentation: Functional Programming and Causal Structure in Quantum Computation
**Presenter**: Christensen (Assistant Professor, University of Montreal, Mila, IDO)

### Key Points:
- **Four main challenges** for quantum computing: building experimental systems with enough qubits, efficient error correction, reliable quantum communication networks, and developing killer applications.
- **Quantum functional programming**: Introduces modularity to quantum computation, allowing functions of functions (higher-order computation) similar to classical programming.
- **No-go theorems**: Universal inverse of unitary gates and quantum "if statements" are impossible in general, but workarounds exist using multiple copies or additional information about physical implementations.
- **Hamiltonian simulation**: Developed algorithms that transform Hamiltonians by any linear or differentiable function without knowing the Hamiltonian's internal structure, enabling the simulation of one physical system by another.
- **Time reversal**: An algorithm that simulates negative time dynamics (requires no auxiliary qubits) and is being tested experimentally at Oxford and through spectroscopy labs.
- **Quantum causality**: Higher-order quantum transformations are fundamentally linked to quantum causal models, which can help understand causal structure in quantum algorithms and machine learning.

## Second Presentation: Variational Quantum State Preparation
**Presenter**: Jacob Biamonte (Professor at ETS Montreal, MEIE chair, director of institute on quantum science and technologies)

### Key Points:
- Most quantum algorithms deployed today follow a variational principle.
- The "stability lemma" shows that expected values of Hamiltonians can be measured to approximate ground state preparation.
- **Parent Hamiltonians**: Instead of minimizing a given operator, the approach is to construct operators whose ground state is the desired quantum state.
- **Clifford circuits**: When using Clifford circuits, the cardinality of the operator is fixed, allowing for a large class of stabilizer Hamiltonians.
- A variational outer loop approach was attempted to break IBM's state preparation record on their own hardware, with interesting challenges identified.

--- SOURCE 11: Topological Quantum Computing: The Devil is Not in the Details | KITP ---
URL: https://www.kitp.ucsb.edu/news/topological-quantum-computing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the KITP Newsletter (Spring 2006) describes the KITP program "Topological Phases and Quantum Computation" (Feb. 21 to May 19, 2006), which brought together approximately 80 participants from four research streams: condensed matter theorists (experts on fractional quantum Hall effect and topological phases), condensed matter experimentalists (studying fractional quantum Hall states in gallium arsenide), quantum computation theorists, and proponents of topological quantum computing. The program was organized by Chetan Nayak (Microsoft's topological quantum computing project), Sander Bais (University of Amsterdam), and John Preskill (Caltech). 

The article explains the key concepts behind topological quantum computing. Unlike conventional approaches that use qubits based on individual particles (like electron spin), topological quantum computing uses anyons—collective excitations that exist only in two-dimensional space with "fractional statistics" between bosonic and fermionic. The term "anyon" was coined in 1982 by Frank Wilczek at KITP. 

The key advantage of the topological approach is inherent error correction. Since information is stored in the topology (shape) of the system rather than local details, small perturbations don't cause errors. Computation is performed through "braiding"—moving one excitation around another—and the exact path doesn't matter, only the topological relationship. This gives an error rate of essentially zero.

Key historical developments include: Peter Shor's 1994 discovery of quantum factoring algorithms; Alexei Kitaev's 1997 landmark paper on non-abelian anyons and built-in error correction; and work by Freedman, Wang, and Larsen showing non-abelian anyons have equal computational power to standard qubits. The most promising experimental system is the 5/2 fractional quantum Hall state (discovered in 1987), with a specific computation scheme proposed in 2004 by Nayak, Freedman, and Das Sarma. The 12/5 state may be even better but more delicate. The article notes that serious experimental efforts were underway to realize topological quantum computing devices in gallium arsenide, with groups in friendly competition.
</summary>
