Bob Coecke, Chief Scientist at Quantinuum, is interviewed by Yuval Boger. Bob and Yuval discuss his new book ”Quantum in Pictures”, ZX Calculus, Quantum natural language processing, spiders, the transition from academia, and much more.

### Transcripts

**Yuval Boger:** Hello, Bob. And thank you for joining me today.

**Bob Coecke:** It’s pleasure.

**Yuval:** So who are you and what do you do?

**Bob:** Okay, so I’m Bob. That’s one thing. Currently, I’m Chief Scientist at Quantinuum. Before that, I was Chief Scientist at Cambridge Quantum before the merger with Honeywell Quantum Systems. And before that, I was a faculty at Oxford University, where I’ve been for some 20 years, mostly as a full professor, and I built a big group there in computer science, so 50 people. And by training, a physicist. But I’ve been pretty much all over the place, to be honest. I am. And since recently, I’m also a distinguished visiting Research Chair at the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics in Canada.

**Yuval:** Well, it’s an honor to have you, and I think that amongst your other accomplishments, you’re also a book author, and you have a book that’s coming out. Maybe you can tell me a little bit about that, please?

**Bob:** Yes, there’s two books actually. I Had a book called Picturing Quantum Processes, which I think came out in 2017. I wrote with Aleks Kissinger. And there was a book full of diagrams showing that you can actually translate all of quantum theory in diagrammatic languages. But it was a university-level book. It was something we wrote for the course that Aleks and I were giving at Computer Science Oxford University. I mean, I think any younger graduate could take it, but we were pretty much teaching it at a post-grad level at the time.

Now there’s a new book out with Stephano Gogioso called Quantum in Pictures. And there, we’ve taken away any mathematical barrier so that this should be a broadly accessible book. We had, for example, teenagers in mind, maybe younger. Who knows? And the amateur doesn’t have a math background but is very interested in physics or the professional, because there’re STEM in there that’s actually cutting-edge new too.

**Yuval:** The book seems to introduce ZX-calculus, I think, through images. Are you targeting it for a particular age group? And once they finish the book, do you expect them to then move into tensors and more sophisticated math? Or …

**Bob:** The interesting thing is that there is nothing more sophisticated than you’ll find in that book for teenagers because this entire field, and that’s how I started and came into it, was through category theory. Category theory’s sort of considered the most sophisticated maths in the world. Most abstract, for sure. So I mean, I started this in 2003, reformulating quantum theory in a new way, an entirely new way, which I mean, I can elaborate on that later. But it turned out that you could equivalently do this kind of abstract math by just drawing pictures.

This was a very new result from the late ’90s that you could do this. And this traces back to work Penrose did in the ’60s and the ’70s where he started to draw tensor notation as pictures. So it’s highly nontrivial stuff. And the last couple of years, this particular math, even though we use it as an educational vehicle, also is being used widespreadly now in quantum industry to tackle problems of complexities that you simply can’t handle otherwise. So it’s bold, in a way, cutting-edge quantum text, and it makes quantum stuff accessible to a much broader audience.

**Yuval:** I didn’t mean to suggest that it was simplistic. I understand that it …

**Bob:** Let me say something to you. The international community, quantum computing community, they were very suspicious because it looked simplistic. They said, “This is never going to be useful for anything.” And the quantum computing companies, when they had to start dealing with complex problems, they kind of realized that this was the perfect language to do so.

For example, a company like PsiQuantum, which is the biggest quantum photonics company, it’s spoken language now. This is the language they speak there. And the cherry on the cake was a few weeks ago when Peter Shor, the person who came up with the factoring algorithm and all that, published a paper on ZX-calculus saying how good it was and all that. So it’s taken the community a while because people just couldn’t believe that something looking that simple could ever be useful for something important.

**Yuval:** And in the book you introduce quantum gates as spiders. Is the spiders terminology used in academic research as well or do they start calling it something else?

**Bob:** I mean, we start to use this term already in the previous book, which is a little bit more academically, so to say. Mostly people now use them in academics everywhere where they’re dealing with these types. So that’s a word which is state more or less. Now there’s a good reason for that because the official previous technical term, which you would find in my early papers… I’m trying not to get it wrong because it’s not easy. Dagger special commutative Frobenius algebra. And actually, Frobenius algebra is even. You said dagger special commutative Frobenius monoid, something like that. So I mean, it’s kind of a mouthful. It’s not very convenient. And so people just went to spiders.

**Yuval:** And through this diagram it seems that it’s easier to simplify quantum circuits and to optimize them so you can get fewer gates and lower depth of the circuit. Is that correct?

**Bob:** Yes. So basically what happens there is quantum circuits are typically made up of single-qubit gates or two-qubit gates. And then what ZX-calculus does, it breaks your two-qubit gates up into smaller things, which is typically a CNOT or something like that, your two-qubit gates, which is much more easy to reason with than the gate as a whole. So you break something that’s quite complex into two pieces, and these two pieces turn out to be very simple, and then you can show that also the phase gates and all that, sort of come naturally with these pieces. So you end up with a little graph calculus.

And yeah, it makes circuit simplification much easier. For example, in quantum optics, in photonics has photonic quantum computer, the error correction becomes much easier. That’s also what Shor was advertising. We now should use these things for error correction too. They have been used by Google for surface codes and things like that. Lots of practical things which now come up in quantum computing. And myself, these diagrams led to the field quantum natural language processing. It would never have come about without the diagrams. There’s no way anybody would now even be doing this on a quantum computer without the diagrams.

**Yuval:** The diagrams refer to gate-based quantum computers. I’m wondering, is there an analogy for the analog computers, the analog Hamiltonian simulation type?

**Bob:** Okay. So recently, people sort of figured out how to exponentiate and integrate and differentiate Hamiltonians in ZX-calculus. It’s a very new thing. This is from 2022. So things are moving in that direction for sure, and they’ve been used for quantum machine learning. Okay. You mentioned gate-based quantum computing. So there is another paradigm which most photonics companies are doing, which is measurement-based quantum computing. And the interesting historical thing is that in 2007, Ross Duncan, who’s the head of software at Quantinuum, and myself, we came up with ZX-calculus by actually looking at measurement-based quantum computing, not gate-based quantum computing. And the measurement-based were all the photonics people use, and it’s not a surprise. They were the first to completely starting to adopt this in quantum industry as their language because it was kind of made for them, but then it turned out to be good for gate-based too and some other things.

**Yuval:** You mentioned quantum natural language processing and natural language processing is very much in the news these days with ChatGPT and all these train models. How is quantum NLP different and what type of better results might you be able to expect one day with quantum NLP?

**Bob:** So historically, this direction started for me… I mean, I had no background whatsoever in linguistics, natural language processing, but I was developing this stuff you find in our books, which is technically called categorical quantum mechanics. It’s a heavy name, so we call it now quantum picturalism or quantum pictures. But initially, it was categorical quantum mechanics.

I was developing this, and I gave a talk about this in 2005 at McGill University and in the audience was Jim Lambek, who is somebody who wrote a paper in 1956, The Mathematics of Sentence Structure, which is very similar and created a lot of the computational linguistics field. And he saw me talking about quantum teleportation in pictures, like, “You finally did the new book,” and all that. He saw presenting quantum teleportation, and he said, “Hey, Bob. This is grammar.” I said, “No, Jim. This is quantum teleportation. This is physics.” “No, no, Bob. This is grammar.”

And he was right because through the right glasses, which are these glasses of category theory, which I was wearing at the time, grammatical structure and description of structure in language is exactly the same as the sort of math you used to describe quantum teleportation in pictures. It’s the same thing. Exactly the same thing. I mean, a bit later, Steve Clark, who’s now the head of AI at Quantinuum, who was a colleague then in University of Oxford of me, he explained the problem people had at the time in language theory. We had theories for grammar. We had theories for meaning like, now, ChatGPT and all these GPTs using which are vector bearings, but they didn’t know how to combine them. They didn’t know, for example, when you know the meaning of the words and grammatical structure, can we produce something representing the meaning of an old sentence, an entire sentence?

It’s a very natural thing. It’s something we humans can do very easily. We do it naturally, but there was no theory there. And then we basically following Jim Lambek’s observation; we just used the diagrammatic quantum formalism to build a new theory of language. At the time, we weren’t thinking at all about quantum computers. We had no quantum computers in mind whatsoever. But yeah, then later, when the quantum computers came, I mean, it was a natural thing to do. And because of this extra structure, we could actually do something that nobody expected. Train a quantum computer to understand some sentences and to understand some words and then do something like question and answering.

I mean, it was a complete shock for me that this was even possible in any way. But yeah, we did it. We did in 2020. And what we are hoping to do is to bring back a little bit more structure in AI or machine learning or whatever you call it, because, at the moment, it’s just this black-box thing. Nobody knows what’s happening actually. I mean, it looks all very impressive in the way it can simulate how a person would speak. So it’s very, very impressive. But we don’t understand how it goes. I mean, there are also issues whether you could imagine whether such a thing could actually ever be creative in some way. I mean, a lot of the machine learning field, AI field is now going into the direction of VI. We probably need to bring in some more structure again because we can’t just go brute force all the way. And that’s kind of what we are bringing in.

**Yuval:** And if you look at the quantum NLP today with today’s computers, what is quantum NLP able to achieve in terms of complexity or results?

**Bob:** So, I mean, the latest published experiments were done by IBM because there’s like two or three teams at IBM now doing our form of QNLP. And what they did is what they call mid-scale machine learning. So it’s not large scale yet, but it’s mid-scale yet, and the results are really good, like we get nice convergences. Of course, the scale is not big enough to do what we actually hope to, that we can really be so much better at than what current machine learning does. And that’s really deep understanding of a text or something. Genuine, deep understanding of a text. Long-range correlations, they’re really bad at the moment, the language models. They’re good at short… And also, they don’t update. They’re very static, like ChatGPT doesn’t know what happened in the last two years or something like that, or last year and a half. I can’t remember exactly the date. And our systems would naturally update all the time. So they would be different. So we are expecting a lot of advantages, but for that scale, we need a lot bigger machines.

Something I didn’t say is, so we had these nice theory, but we were struggling on classical machines because it’s quantum models. So just like chemistry, just like materials, they weren’t seen on the quantum computer. So that was a problem we had at that time. So it’s an interesting area where you expect the same advantages as quantum chemistry and quantum materials, but we are not talking about quantum substance. We are talking about language. And We are doing more general cognitive stuff too, and then going to more general AI and things like that. So it’s not just that we restrict ourselves to language.

**Yuval:** As a chief scientist at Quantinuum, what else are you working on, if you can tell us?

**Bob:** What I am working on, I mean, I just published a book. So the main thing I’ve been working on the last year, and year and a half, which may sound a bit weird, is really on new theories of languages beyond the one we came up with in 2008 and 2009. And we got a new language form. Listen, we put out a blog post, I think, one or two weeks ago. It was a medium blog, and it was something called Looking for University of Language. So by actually working with these quantum computers, we actually had to turn language, which is normally written on the line, into a quantum circuit. So we turn something one-dimension into something two-dimension. And then, by doing this properly and getting all the mathematics right, we discovered that in doing so, differences between languages, like how your words would be differently ordered in one language as in another language and your punctuation would be completely different, that all these differences vanished when we went to the circuits.

So we kind of found something underneath language, which seems to be much more universal than whatever we speak. And also stylistic differences vanish. And so that’s something we are working on a lot now because it’s a completely different thing. And also, today at my office downstairs, Eduardo Miranda arrived. So Eduardo Miranda is somebody who’s been playing around with quantum computers to do music. I mean, I’ve been doing this before with him too. We created something called quanthoven, which was a way to generate music with quantum computer of a certain genre. Again, small scale, but we did it. We actually produced new music with a quantum computer. And then a very funny thing happened. This became number one on some classical charts. So anyway, this is what we’re going to work a little bit on this week too with Eduardo, doing some more quantum music. Yeah, I mean, I’m doing lots of stuff actually. Too much. It keeps me awake.

**Yuval:** And I’ve had Eduardo on this podcast as well, so I enjoy it. Absolutely. You made the transition from a professor to industry. It must be different. Is that a path that you would recommend for others?

**Bob:** That’s an interesting question. And then the thing is, you should have asked me this question before I did it, record my answer, and then ask it now and record my answer. And they would be very different. I can tell you that. So I was a very long time in academia and I’ve got a feeling now that I’ve actually regained academic freedom, which may sound contradictory to what most people would tell you, but actually I have a lot more freedom now. Just to say, this book which came out now, I’ve been trying to finish with Stefano for many years at university, and I just couldn’t find the time or support. And now it’s published by Quantinuum with a lot of support. We got a lot of support for the publication of this book.

So interestingly, initially, I mean, I mentioned that there was some sort of skepticism in the community about whether this stuff would be ever useful. So the reason we initially started to write this was to set up an experiment in which we take, on the one hand, Oxford University students taking a regular quantum course, and on the other end, teenagers take learning from this book, and then give them the same exam and see who out-performs who. So that was the experiment we had in mind, but we just couldn’t find any support in academia. Hardly any support to do it. And now it’s all supported by actually mainly the quantum industry, not just Quantinuum, but also IBM is helping with it.

So the industry is much more keen for things like this book, which is all about inclusivity, and then you would actually find in academia, which is very interesting. And also, the sort of stuff I’m doing now with QNLP, would’ve been impossible in academia because the nature of the jobs and the nature of people’s careers is very different. I mean, I could write a book about it. I could write a book about it, but I mean, a lot of people actually are full of my example and gave up faculty positions, and quite a number who are now working in my team.

**Yuval:** When you look at the advancements in the quantum industry, obviously Quantinuum has a lot of resources, but the industry, best of all, has more minds and more money and more directions that are working on. What would you like to see other companies in the industry doing that they’re not doing right now?

**Bob:** I mean, what I’ve noticed is that we have a good chunk of the industry; they’re actually collaborating a lot more than you sometimes find in academia, where universities are competing against each other for rankings, people are competing against each other for getting the paper the first time out, and things like that. So I mean, something that surprised me is really this collaborative edge, and that’s something that needs to continue. And some companies aren’t as collaborative as other ones.

Let’s put it like that. And some companies are very, very honest in what they’re doing and very, very straight. And these are typically the big ones. The big ones who are not necessarily funded by venture capital. So sometimes those funded by vendor capital, by no means all, they kind of give the whole field a bad name by saying things they shouldn’t be saying. And that’s maybe a little bit too much of that. But on the other hand, if you, for example, look at the video of Tony Uttley at Q2B, you get the most honest and direct representation of what actually is going on at the moment. For example, in Quantinuum, what we can do, what we can’t do, what we expect. And a lot of people are like that.

**Yuval:** Very good. So I want to end with a hypothetical question. So if you could have dinner with one of the quantum greats, dead or alive, who would that person be?

**Bob:** Oh, well, that would be, I guess, Schrodinger.

**Yuval:** And why?

**Bob:** So one of the things, which this book also puts forward in all these diagrammatic formalism, is a new worldview really, which departs from what is almost 2,500-year-old worldview going back to Aristotle and Parmenides and all these people, where you think about the thing of how it is made up. So if you understand the physics thing, you go to smaller particles inside. If you want to understand human, you start doing autonomy. You understand maths, you break it down into its elements and set theory. So the kind of maths which we have in our book, it actually puts composition of systems on the first place. You’ve got things, and they also understand things by what happens if you bring them together. Like you bring two people together, what is the relationship which emerges and all that?

And this sort of more relational mathematics, I mean, Schrodinger actually put this forward in somewhere in ’35 by saying actually, the most important thing in quantum is not measurement, but is tensor product. And to some extent, all that I’ve done is basically taking that idea seriously and translating all of quantum mechanics in tensor language only, composition language only. So I mean, Schrodinger’s done a lot of bad things in his life, very bad things. It’s maybe not the most… But he was an hypothetical question, assuming that Schrodinger didn’t do bad things in his life, let’s put it… It was just about the scientific idea. Yeah.

**Yuval:** Absolutely. And maybe if he saw your book, it would not be Schrodinger’s cat, but Schrodinger’s spider.

**Bob:** Yeah.

**Yuval:** So we covered a lot of topics today, from quantum natural language processing to unified model of languages and spiders and ZX-calculus. Is there anything else that you’d like to share with the community before we end our discussion today?

**Bob:** No, no, it’s all fine. Just go and buy the book. It’s available since today. Since today, which is probably a different day from when you actually will hear this, but just a few hours to go, it just came on the market. So it’s now available for everybody pretty much in every country instantly.

**Yuval:** Excellent. I certainly enjoyed reading it, and I hope my listeners will as well. Bob, thank you so much for joining me today.

**Bob:** Thank you. Bye.

*Yuval Boger is an executive working at the intersection of quantum technology and business. Known as the “Superposition Guy” as well as the original “Qubit Guy,” he can be reached on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/yuvalboger/) or at [this email](mailto:superpositionguy@gmail.com?subject=from_QCR).*

# Bob Coecke

![Personal photo - Bob Coecke](/files/8452//1896799_10153038154662169_2656086483075285052_n.jpg)

**Professor Bob Coecke**

Associate Member

Emeritus Fellow, [Wolfson College](http://www.wolfson.ox.ac.uk)

**E:** bob.coecke@gmail.com

**T:** +44 7881 333990

## Themes:

* [Quantum](/research/fls)
* [Security](/research/security)
* [Data, Knowledge and Action](/research/dk)

## Completed Projects:

* [more…](#CompletedProjects)

## See Also:

* [Archive of old webpages](http://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/bob.coecke/archive.html)

## Interests

I was Professor of Quantum Foundations, Logics and Structures 2011-2021, Lecturer of Quantum Computer Science 2007-2011, EPSRC Advenced Research Fellow 2004-2009, Postdoc 2001-2003, and created and headed the [Quantum Group](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/activities/quantum/), here at the Department of Computer Science.  After that, I was Chief Scientist at [Quantinuum](https://www.quantinuum.com/about).  Atm I am writing two books, and developing quantum music.  I am also a [Distinguished Visiting Research Chair](https://perimeterinstitute.ca/people?view_by=field_research_position) at the [Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics](https://perimeterinstitute.ca).

I am still active at Oxford University, where I mainly teach, supervise and mentor, here at the Department of Computer Science, at the Mathematical Institute, and at the Department of Physics.

At [Wolfson College](Wolfson%20College, where I am Emeritus Fellow), where I am Emeritus Fellow, I lead the [Quantum Foundations Research Cluster](https://www.wolfson.ox.ac.uk/quantum-foundations-research-cluster).

Below is a brief bio.

You can contact me by email at **bob [.] coecke [@] gmail [.] com**

My courses:

* I am teaching [Classical and Quantum Compositional Distributional Meaning](https://courses.maths.ox.ac.uk/course/view.php?id=833) in Hilary
* I am co-teaching [Introduction to Quantum Information](https://courses.maths.ox.ac.uk/course/view.php?id=162) in Hilary with [Artur Ekert](https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/people/artur.ekert) where I cover [ZX-calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZX-calculus) - [lecture notes](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/bob.coecke/ZX-lectures_JPG.pdf)
* I co-created [Quantum Processes and Computation](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/teaching/courses/2022-2023/quantum/) with [Aleks Kissinger](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/aleks.kissinger/) and covers our book [Picturing Quantum Processes](https://www.cambridge.org/gb/academic/subjects/physics/quantum-physics-quantum-information-and-quantum-computation/picturing-quantum-processes-first-course-quantum-theory-and-diagrammatic-reasoning)

## Biography

I am currently focussing on writing two books, one on a novel relational/compositional worldview, and one on quantum music. I am [Distinguished Visiting Research Chair](https://perimeterinstitute.ca/people?view_by=field_research_position) at the [Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics](https://perimeterinstitute.ca), [Emeritus Fellow at Wolfson College Oxford](https://www.wolfson.ox.ac.uk), and Visiting Fellow at the Computer Science Department and the Mathematical Institute of Oxford University.  I am in FQxI's Scientific Advisory Council, a father of Quantum Physics and Logic (QPL) and Applied Category Theory (ACT) conference series, and the diamond-open-access journal [Compositionality](https://compositionality.episciences.org/), and Cambridge University Press' Applied Category Theory book series.

I received the [2024 test-of-time award by IEEE-LiCS](https://lics.siglog.org/lics24/tot.php).  I pioneered [Categorical Quantum Mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Categorical_quantum_mechanics) (now in AMS's MSC2020 classification, and received the above mentioned award for it), [ZX-calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZX-calculus), [DisCoCat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DisCoCat) natural language meaning, mathematical foundations for resource theories, [Quantum Natural Language Processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_natural_language_processing), and [DisCoCirc](https://medium.com/quantinuum/our-quest-for-finding-the-universality-of-language-d0f7a40b76e6) natural language meaning. I was the first person to have Quantum Foundations as part of his academic title.

I co-authored [Picturing Quantum Processes](https://www.cambridge.org/gb/academic/subjects/physics/quantum-physics-quantum-information-and-quantum-computation/picturing-quantum-processes-first-course-quantum-theory-and-diagrammatic-reasoning), with [Aleks Kissinger](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/aleks.kissinger/), a book providing a fully diagrammatic treatment of quantum theory and its applications. I co-authored [Quantum in Pictures](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W9HrTMQ0VoE), with [Stefano Gogioso](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/stefano.gogioso/), which does the same, but now accessible to people with no maths background.  We did an amazing experiment, covered in [The Guardian and The Observer](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2023/dec/16/physicist-bob-coecke-its-easier-to-convince-kids-than-adults-about-quantum-mechanics), by [Quantinuum](https://www.quantinuum.com/blog/quantum-in-pictures), and [here](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/news/2280-full.html).

I was Professor of Quantum Foundations, Logics and Structures at the Department of Computer Science at Oxford University, where I was 20 years, 2001-2020, and co-founded and led a multi-disciplinary [Quantum Group](https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/activities/quantum/) that grew to 50 members and I supervised 80 PhD students.  After that, I was [Chief Scientist at Quantinuum](https://www.quantinuum.com/qai/bobcoecke), for some 7 years, which included being the head of Quantinuum's [Oxford-based Quantum NLP & Compositional Intelligence sub-team](https://www.quantinuum.com/qai/qci).

I am still supervising, at Oxford and elsewhere, and also still teach at Oxford's Mathematical Institute. I co-authored some 250 research papers. I obtained approx. 40 grants, including from NFWO, EPSRC, Leverhulme, EU, ONR, AFOSR, FQXi, JTF.  I am a founding father of the QPL (Quantum Physics and Logic) and ACT (Applied Category Theory) communities, of the diamond-open-access journal Compositionality, and Cambridge University Press' Applied Category Theory book series.

I may have been the 1st person to talk about Quantum Music, in the 90's.  I am a founding shareholder of Moth Quantum, having co-composed the 1st ever piece of music generated by a quantum computer, under the pseudsonym Quanthoven.  You can read about it here.

**Bob Coecke** (born 23 July 1968) is a Belgian [theoretical physicist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theoretical_physics "Theoretical physics") and [logician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic "Logic"). He was Professor of Quantum foundations, Logics, and Structures at [Oxford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University "Oxford University") until 2020. He was Chief Scientist at quantum computing company [Quantinuum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantinuum "Quantinuum"), until 2025 and founded a startup called [Relational Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relational_Intelligence?action=edit&redlink=1 "Relational Intelligence (page does not exist)") in 2026.[[4]](#cite_note-4) He is also Distinguished Visiting Research Chair at the [Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics "Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics"), and Emeritus Fellow at [Wolfson College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfson_College,_Oxford "Wolfson College, Oxford").

He pioneered [categorical quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Categorical_quantum_mechanics "Categorical quantum mechanics") (entry 18M40 in Mathematics Subject Classification 2020), Quantum Picturalism,[[5]](#cite_note-5) [ZX-calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZX-calculus "ZX-calculus"), [DisCoCat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DisCoCat "DisCoCat") model for natural language,[[6]](#cite_note-6), [quantum natural language processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_natural_language_processing "Quantum natural language processing") (QNLP) and quantum education through the book Quantum in Pictures. He is a founder of the Quantum Physics and Logic community and the Applied Category Theory communities and conference series, and of the journal *Compositionality*.

Coecke is also a composer and musician, who has been called a pioneer of [industrial music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_music "Industrial music"),[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) and is also one of the pioneers of employing quantum computers in music.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

## Education and career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Bob_Coecke&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Education and career")]

Coecke obtained his doctorate in sciences at the [Vrije Universiteit Brussel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vrije_Universiteit_Brussel "Vrije Universiteit Brussel") in 1996,[[3]](#cite_note-mathgene-3) and performed postdoctoral work in the Theoretical Physics Group of [Imperial College, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_College,_London "Imperial College, London") in the Category Theory Group of the Mathematics and Statistics Department at [McGill University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McGill_University "McGill University") in Montreal, in the [Department of Pure Mathematics and Mathematical Statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Pure_Mathematics_and_Mathematical_Statistics "Department of Pure Mathematics and Mathematical Statistics") of [Cambridge University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_University "Cambridge University"), and in the [Department of Computer Science, University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Computer_Science,_University_of_Oxford "Department of Computer Science, University of Oxford").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

He was an [EPSRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EPSRC "EPSRC") Advanced Research Fellow at the [Department of Computer Science, University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Computer_Science,_University_of_Oxford "Department of Computer Science, University of Oxford"), where he became Lecturer in Quantum Computer Science in 2007, and jointly with [Samson Abramsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samson_Abramsky "Samson Abramsky") built and headed the Quantum Group.[[10]](#cite_note-oxf-10) In July 2011, he was nominated professor of Quantum Foundations, Logics and Structures at Oxford University, with retroactive effect as of October 2010. He was a Governing Body Fellow of [Wolfson College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfson_College,_Oxford "Wolfson College, Oxford") since 2007, where he now is an Emeritus Fellow.[[10]](#cite_note-oxf-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12)

In January 2019, Coecke became Senior Scientific Advisor of [Cambridge Quantum Computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Quantum_Computing "Cambridge Quantum Computing"), and in January 2021 he resigned from his Professorship at Oxford, to become Chief Scientist of [Cambridge Quantum Computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Quantum_Computing "Cambridge Quantum Computing"). After the merger of Cambridge Quantum Computing with Honeywell Quantum Systems, he stayed on as Chief Scientist of the joint entity [Quantinuum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantinuum "Quantinuum") until 2025.[[13]](#cite_note-quant-13)

In January 2023 he also became Distinguished Visiting Research Chair at the [Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perimeter_Institute_for_Theoretical_Physics "Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics").[[14]](#cite_note-PI-14)

## Work

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Bob_Coecke&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Work")]

Coecke's research focuses on the foundations of physics, more particularly [category theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_theory "Category theory"), [logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic "Logic"), and diagrammatic reasoning, with application to [quantum informatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_informatics "Quantum informatics"), [quantum gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_gravity "Quantum gravity"), and [NLP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_language_processing "Natural language processing").[[15]](#cite_note-15)[*[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*] He has pioneered [categorical quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Categorical_quantum_mechanics "Categorical quantum mechanics") together with [Samson Abramsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samson_Abramsky "Samson Abramsky"), and spearheaded the development of a diagrammatic quantum formalism based on [Penrose graphical notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose_graphical_notation "Penrose graphical notation"), on which he wrote a textbook entitled Picturing Quantum Processes with Aleks Kissinger. With Ross Duncan he pioneered [ZX-calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZX-calculus "ZX-calculus"). He pioneered the DisCoCat model for natural language, with Stephen Clark and [Mehrnoosh Sadrzadeh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehrnoosh_Sadrzadeh "Mehrnoosh Sadrzadeh"). He also pioneered quantum natural language processing (QNLP), with Will Zeng, and colleagues at [Cambridge Quantum Computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Quantum_Computing "Cambridge Quantum Computing").[[16]](#cite_note-16)

## Music

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Bob_Coecke&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Music")]

Coecke is also a musician, performing and recording since the eighties. He retrospectively has been named a pioneer of [industrial music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_music "Industrial music").[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18) His band, Black Tish, "used cutting edge sampling techniques for the time, a host of synth and sound loops and metal-style guitars to create a heavy rock/electronica fusion unlike anything heard before",[[19]](#cite_note-19) and "bridge the gap between the pure experimental nature of bands like [Throbbing Gristle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Throbbing_Gristle "Throbbing Gristle") and [Einstürzende Neubauten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstürzende_Neubauten "Einstürzende Neubauten") and the (comparatively) more radio accessible [Ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_(band) "Ministry (band)") or [Nine Inch Nails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Inch_Nails "Nine Inch Nails")".[[20]](#cite_note-20)

Coecke is also one of the pioneers of employing quantum computers in music.[[21]](#cite_note-21)

args.summary:
Bob Coecke (born 23 July 1968) is a Belgian theoretical physicist and logician. He was Professor of Quantum Foundations, Logics, and Structures at Oxford University until 2020. He served as Chief Scientist at quantum computing company Quantinuum until 2025 and founded a startup called Relational Intelligence in 2026. He is also Distinguished Visiting Research Chair at the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics and Emeritus Fellow at Wolfson College, Oxford.

Coecke pioneered categorical quantum mechanics, Quantum Picturalism, the ZX-calculus, the DisCoCat model for natural language, and quantum natural language processing (QNLP). He is a founder of the Quantum Physics and Logic community and the Applied Category Theory communities and conference series.

He obtained his doctorate from Vrije Universiteit Brussel in 1996, with postdoctoral work at Imperial College London, McGill University, Cambridge University, and Oxford University. He became Lecturer in Quantum Computer Science at Oxford in 2007 and was nominated Professor of Quantum Foundations, Logics and Structures in 2011. He joined Cambridge Quantum Computing as Senior Scientific Advisor in 2019, became Chief Scientist in 2021, and continued in that role at Quantinuum after the merger with Honeywell Quantum Systems until 2025.

Coecke is also a composer and musician, considered a pioneer of industrial music through his band Black Tish, and is among the pioneers of employing quantum computers in music. His selected publications include textbooks \"Picturing Quantum Processes\" (2017) and \"Quantum in Pictures\" (2022), as well as numerous influential articles on categorical quantum mechanics, quantum NLP, and diagrammatic reasoning.

(UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna

**Bob Coecke**

Chief Scientist

Quantinuum

Bob Coecke is Chief Scientist at Quantinuum, head Quantinuum's Oxford-based Quantum NLP & Compositional Intelligence sub-team, Distinguished Visiting Research Chair at the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, Emeritus Fellow at Wolfson College Oxford, and Visiting Fellow at the Computer Science Department and the Mathematical Institute of Oxford University. Previously he was Professor of Quantum Foundations, Logics and Structures at the Department of Computer Science at Oxford University, where he was 20 years, and co-founded and led a multi-disciplinary Quantum Group that grew to 50 members and he supervised close to 70 PhD students.  He is still supervising, at Oxford and elsewhere, and also still teaching at Oxford's Mathematical Institute. He pioneered Categorical Quantum Mechanics (now in AMS's MSC2020 classification), ZX-calculus, DisCoCat natural language meaning, mathematical foundations for resource theories, Quantum Natural Language Processing, and DisCoCirc natural language meaning.   I co-authored Picturing Quantum Processes, with Aleks Kissinger, a book providing a fully diagrammatic treatment of quantum theory and its applications. I co-authored Quantum in Pictures, with Stefano Gogioso, which does the same, but now accessible to people with no maths background.  I co-authored some 200 research papers. I obtained approx. 35 grants, including from NFWO, EPSRC, Leverhulme, EU, ONR, AFOSR, FQXi, JTF.  I still hold grants with the latter two.  I am a founding father of the QPL (Quantum Physics and Logic) and ACT (Applied Category Theory) communities, a steering board member of QPL, ACT and QISS (Quantum Information Structure of Spacetime), and in the Scientific Advisory Council of FQxI.  I founded the diamond-open-access journal Compositionality, and Cambridge University Press' Applied Category Theory book series. I was the first person to have Quantum Foundations as part of his academic title. My work has been headlined by various media outlets, including Forbes, New Scientist, PhysicsWorld, ComputerWeekly, IFL Science.

**Title/Abstract:**

*From quantum picturalism to quantum NLP and quantum AI*

In 2020 our Oxford-based Quantinuum team performed Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP) on IBM quantum hardware [1, 2].  Key to having been able to achieve what is conceived as a heavily data-driven task, is the observation that quantum theory and natural language are governed by much of the same compositional structure -- a.k.a. tensor structure.   Hence our language model is in a sense quantum-native, and we provide an analogy with simulation of quantum systems in terms of algorithmic speed-up [forthcoming].  Meanwhile we have made all our software available open-source, and with support [github.com/CQCL/lambeq].     The compositional match between natural language and quantum extends to other domains than language, and argue that a new generation of AI can emerge when fully pushing this analogy, while exploiting the completeness of categorical quantum mechanics / ZX-calculus [3, 4, 5] for novel reasoning purposes that go hand-in-hand with modern machine learning.

[1]     B. Coecke, G. De Felice, K. Meichanetzidis and A. Toumi (2020) Foundations for Near-Term Quantum Natural Language Processing.  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.03755>  
[2]     R. Lorenz, A. Pearson, K. Meichanetzidis, D. Kartsaklis and B. Coecke (2020) QNLP in Practice: Running Compositional Models of Meaning on a Quantum Computer.  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12846>  
[3]     B. Coecke and A. Kissinger (2017) Picturing Quantum Processes. A first course on quantum theory and diagrammatic reasoning.  Cambridge University Press.  
[4]     B. Coecke, D. Horsman, A. Kissinger and Q. Wang (2021) Kindergarten quantum mechanics graduates (...or how I learned to stop gluing LEGO together and love the ZX-calculus).  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.10984>  
[5]     B. Coecke and S. Gogioso (2022) Quantum in Pictures.  Quantinuum, 2023.

# Applied Quantum Computing Symposium 2025 Summary

The Applied Quantum Computing Symposium 2025, hosted by the Institut quantique de l'Université de Sherbrooke, took place on November 13, 2025. The event focused on the central question: "How can we make quantum computing useful?" addressing both hardware challenges (quantum error correction) and software/applications development.

## Opening Remarks
- **Organizers**: The quantum algo lab team at Université de Sherbrooke, led by manager and scientific director Stephanos Cortis (physics professor and Pascal chair in AI/quantum AI).
- **Michelle Pier** (new director of the Sherbrook quantum innovation zone) highlighted the importance of talent and the recently established francophone bachelor's degree in quantum computing.

## Upcoming Events Announced:
1. **Sherhack 2026** – March 2026 in Sherbrook (3rd edition)
2. **Canadian Workshop on Quantum Algorithms** – April 2026 in Montreal (organized by quantum algorithmic alliance)
3. **Algolab Summer School 2026** – June 7-19, 2026 (2nd edition, theme: "Towards Full Tolerant Quantum Computing")
4. **TQC (Quantum Computation and Quantum Algorithms)** – August 31 - September 4, 2026 in Sherbrook (2nd biggest quantum computing conference)

## Keynote Presentation: Functional Programming and Causal Structure in Quantum Computation
**Presenter**: Christensen (Assistant Professor, University of Montreal, Mila, IDO)

### Key Points:
- **Four main challenges** for quantum computing: building experimental systems with enough qubits, efficient error correction, reliable quantum communication networks, and developing killer applications.
- **Quantum functional programming**: Introduces modularity to quantum computation, allowing functions of functions (higher-order computation) similar to classical programming.
- **No-go theorems**: Universal inverse of unitary gates and quantum "if statements" are impossible in general, but workarounds exist using multiple copies or additional information about physical implementations.
- **Hamiltonian simulation**: Developed algorithms that transform Hamiltonians by any linear or differentiable function without knowing the Hamiltonian's internal structure, enabling the simulation of one physical system by another.
- **Time reversal**: An algorithm that simulates negative time dynamics (requires no auxiliary qubits) and is being tested experimentally at Oxford and through spectroscopy labs.
- **Quantum causality**: Higher-order quantum transformations are fundamentally linked to quantum causal models, which can help understand causal structure in quantum algorithms and machine learning.

## Second Presentation: Variational Quantum State Preparation
**Presenter**: Jacob Biamonte (Professor at ETS Montreal, MEIE chair, director of institute on quantum science and technologies)

### Key Points:
- Most quantum algorithms deployed today follow a variational principle.
- The "stability lemma" shows that expected values of Hamiltonians can be measured to approximate ground state preparation.
- **Parent Hamiltonians**: Instead of minimizing a given operator, the approach is to construct operators whose ground state is the desired quantum state.
- **Clifford circuits**: When using Clifford circuits, the cardinality of the operator is fixed, allowing for a large class of stabilizer Hamiltonians.
- A variational outer loop approach was attempted to break IBM's state preparation record on their own hardware, with interesting challenges identified.

This article from the KITP Newsletter (Spring 2006) describes the KITP program "Topological Phases and Quantum Computation" (Feb. 21 to May 19, 2006), which brought together approximately 80 participants from four research streams: condensed matter theorists (experts on fractional quantum Hall effect and topological phases), condensed matter experimentalists (studying fractional quantum Hall states in gallium arsenide), quantum computation theorists, and proponents of topological quantum computing. The program was organized by Chetan Nayak (Microsoft's topological quantum computing project), Sander Bais (University of Amsterdam), and John Preskill (Caltech). 

The article explains the key concepts behind topological quantum computing. Unlike conventional approaches that use qubits based on individual particles (like electron spin), topological quantum computing uses anyons—collective excitations that exist only in two-dimensional space with "fractional statistics" between bosonic and fermionic. The term "anyon" was coined in 1982 by Frank Wilczek at KITP. 

The key advantage of the topological approach is inherent error correction. Since information is stored in the topology (shape) of the system rather than local details, small perturbations don't cause errors. Computation is performed through "braiding"—moving one excitation around another—and the exact path doesn't matter, only the topological relationship. This gives an error rate of essentially zero.

Key historical developments include: Peter Shor's 1994 discovery of quantum factoring algorithms; Alexei Kitaev's 1997 landmark paper on non-abelian anyons and built-in error correction; and work by Freedman, Wang, and Larsen showing non-abelian anyons have equal computational power to standard qubits. The most promising experimental system is the 5/2 fractional quantum Hall state (discovered in 1987), with a specific computation scheme proposed in 2004 by Nayak, Freedman, and Das Sarma. The 12/5 state may be even better but more delicate. The article notes that serious experimental efforts were underway to realize topological quantum computing devices in gallium arsenide, with groups in friendly competition.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: topological quantum computation in nLab ---
URL: https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+quantum+computation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Topological Quantum Computation

## Main Topic
The nLab page on **topological quantum computation** (TQC) describes a paradigm for quantum computing that uses topological quantum field theory (TQFT) to achieve inherent protection against decoherence and noise, in contrast to conventional approaches that rely on post-hoc quantum error correction.

## Core Idea

### The Problem
Common quantum computing architectures (superconducting qubits, trapped ions, spin resonance) suffer from an intrinsic tension: quantum gates require interaction between subsystems, but coherence requires avoiding interaction. This problem plagues contemporary NISQ devices and has contributed to the "Quantum Winter."

### The Bold Solution
Topological quantum computing aims to implement quantum gates that operate **without interaction** by exploiting the quantum adiabatic theorem. The approach requires a quantum system (e.g., a crystalline quantum material) with three key properties:

1. **Ground state degeneracy**: Multiple distinct ground states even at absolute zero (the Hilbert space of ground states has dimension > 1)
2. **Energy gap**: All excitations require energy above a threshold Δ, so quanta with energy < Δ have no interaction
3. **Control parameters**: Continuously tunable parameters (strain, voltage) that maintain the above properties

### How It Works
Under adiabatic conditions, slowly varying external parameters transforms ground states into each other via Berry phases (holonomic quantum gates). These are protected from noise quanta but may still be sensitive to noise in the parameter paths themselves.

**Topological invariance** requires additional properties:
- **Parameter topology**: The parameter space has non-contractible loops (non-trivial fundamental group)
- **Local parameter independence**: Continuously deformable parameter paths yield the same transformation (flat Berry connection)

Materials with all these properties are **topologically ordered**, and the resulting processes are **topological quantum gates**, protected against both external noise and parameter path noise.

## Via Anyon Braiding

The most developed approach (originally proposed by Kitaev 2003 and Freedman et al. 2003) envisions:
- A 2D quantum material (like graphene)
- With defect points whose positions constitute the control parameters
- The configuration space of points yields braid group representations acting on ground states
- These defects are referred to as **defect anyons**

### Experimental Status
- **Abelian anyons** have been observed in fractional quantum Hall systems, though controlled movement seems out of reach
- **Non-Abelian anyons** (needed for universal quantum computation) remain theoretically expected but experimentally challenging
- Claims of Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in the 2010s "seem not to hold water"
- More recent work focuses on **quantum simulation of anyons** on ordinary quantum hardware

### Mathematical Framework
Defect anyons are expected to be described by Chern-Simons theory/Reshetikhin-Turaev theory, classified by modular tensor categories. Quantum gates are encoded by braid group elements and executed through braid representations on the space of quantum states.

### Topological Quantum Compilation
Braid-based quantum gates differ significantly from standard quantum gates. For example, a single CNOT gate requires a lengthy braid. This makes **compilation** of quantum algorithms to machine-level gates a major challenge, with formal verification likely a practical necessity.

## Key References
Foundational works include Kitaev (2003), Freedman, Kitaev, Larsen & Wang (2003), and Nayak et al. (2008). Monographs by Wang (2010), Pachos (2012), and Simon (2023) provide comprehensive treatments.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The idea of topological quantum computation is to implement quantum computation on quantum systems whose dynamics is described by topological quantum field theory (TQFT), so that the defining invariance of TQFTs under local perturbations implements protection of the quantum coherence by fundamental physical principles, instead of after the fact by quantum error correction.,Find quantum gates operating without interaction!,The chief advantage of anyonic [topological quantum] computation would be physical error correction... In contrast, the presumptive qubit-model of quantum computation, which repairs errors combinatorically, requires a fantastically low initial error rate...,The central idea of TQC is to encode qubits into states of topological phases of matter. Qubits encoded in such states are expected to be topologically protected, or robust, against the prying eyes of the environment, which are believed to be the bane of conventional quantum computation.,What is missing is the breakthrough... bypassing quantum error correction by using far-more-stable qubits, in an approach called topological quantum computing.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Shor's algorithm - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shor%27s_algorithm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Shor's algorithm is a quantum algorithm for finding the prime factors of an integer, developed in 1994 by American mathematician Peter Shor. It is one of the few known quantum algorithms with strong evidence of superpolynomial speedup compared to best known classical algorithms. On a quantum computer, factoring an integer N runs in polynomial time (O((log N)²(log log N)(log log log N)) quantum gates using fast multiplication), while the best classical algorithm (general number field sieve) runs in sub-exponential time.

The algorithm could break public-key cryptography schemes including RSA, finite-field Diffie-Hellman, and elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman, motivating research into post-quantum cryptography. However, practical implementation requires quantum computers with millions of qubits due to quantum error correction overhead.

The algorithm has two parts: (1) a classical reduction of factoring to order-finding, and (2) a quantum order-finding subroutine. The classical reduction picks a random integer a, computes gcd(a,N), and if trivial, uses the quantum subroutine to find the multiplicative order r of a modulo N. If r is even and N does not divide a^(r/2)+1, then gcd(N, a^(r/2)-1) yields a nontrivial factor.

The quantum subroutine uses quantum phase estimation with a unitary operator U representing multiplication by a modulo N, requiring 2n qubits in the first register (where n = ceil(log₂ N)). The eigenvalues of U encode information about the period r. A continued-fraction algorithm extracts the period from measurement outcomes.

As of 2026, laboratory demonstrations have only succeeded with small semiprimes (15, 21) using NMR, photonic, solid-state, and trapped-ion qubits, but these demonstrations compiled circuits using prior knowledge of the solution.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Shor's algorithm is a quantum algorithm for finding the prime factors of an integer, On a quantum computer, to factor an integer N, Shor's algorithm runs in polynomial time, meaning the time taken is polynomial in log N, The algorithm has been demonstrated with small semiprimes but none of these demonstrations fulfill the requirements of Shor's algorithm: they compile the circuit using prior knowledge of the solution, and some have even oversimplified the algorithm in a way that makes it equivalent to coin flipping

When John Preskill arrived at Caltech in 1983, he initially worked on particle physics, but shifted to quantum information theory in the mid-1990s after Peter Shor's discovery of quantum factoring algorithms. The early 2000s saw a remarkable group of young researchers pass through, including Patrick Hayden, Guifré Vidal (now at Google), and Frank Verstraete. Weekly meetings were so intense that Preskill imposed one-minute speaking limits. In 2011, as quantum computing hardware advanced, the institute expanded to include experimental work and changed its name to IQIM (adding "Matter" to the name). 

More recently, Caltech partnered with Amazon to build the AWS Center for Quantum Computing on campus, aiming to create quantum computers that could revolutionize data security, machine learning, medicine, and sustainability. The article highlights how many early IQIM researchers have returned as senior scientists at the AWS Center.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Caltech Heritage Project interview with Alexei Kitaev, the Ronald and Maxine Linde Professor of Theoretical Physics and Mathematics at Caltech, conducted by David Zierler across four sessions in January and February 2022. The interview covers Kitaev's research in quantum information, topological quantum computing, the SYK model, and his views on the state of quantum computation.

**Key topics covered:**

**Current Research:** Kitaev is working on the SYK model (a many-body quantum system analogous to black holes) and the classification of topological phases of matter. He works part-time at Google Quantum AI in Santa Barbara on superconducting qubits.

**On Quantum Computing Progress:** Kitaev states that true quantum computers do not yet exist because they lack error correction. Current state-of-the-art is about 50 qubits without error correction. He compares the current situation to Charles Babbage's attempts to build a classical computer in the 19th century, suggesting current quantum computers may be "big, very inefficient machines" and that a new technology might emerge within ten years.

**On Quantum Error Correction:** Kitaev explains the need for quantum error correction, describing Shor's nine-qubit code and the surface code. He describes how quantum information must be protected from both bit-flip and phase errors, and how the environment "watching" quantum information destroys it.

**On Topological Quantum Computation:** Kitaev explains his invention of topological quantum computation, which uses anyons and Majorana fermions. Anyons are quasi-particles in two-dimensional systems with non-Abelian properties. Moving particles around each other (braiding) changes hidden internal degrees of freedom that are immune to errors, enabling protected quantum computation.

**On Applications of Quantum Computers:** Key applications include breaking RSA encryption, simulating quantum mechanical systems (molecules, materials, high-Tc superconductors), and possibly simulating field theories. Kitaev does not believe quantum computers will replace classical computers for most tasks or be used in personal devices.

**On Black Holes and Quantum Information:** Kitaev discusses the Hayden-Preskill paper about recovering information from black holes using entanglement and Hawking radiation. He notes that observational advances like the Event Horizon Telescope and LIGO are not directly relevant to these theoretical questions.

**Personal Background:** Kitaev was born in Voronezh, Russia. His father was an applied physicist at Voronezh University working on acousto-optics. As a child, Kitaev played with oscilloscopes in his father's lab. He was inspired by Manin's book on mathematical logic and Feynman's paper on quantum simulation.

**On the State of Theory:** Kitaev notes that the foundations of quantum computing theory were established in the 1990s and are unlikely to change. He credits Caltech (IQIM/IQI) as the leading institution for training quantum information physicists.

This paper presents a categorical framework that extends the quantum circuit model by realizing a dagger-compact category (called QC) that can model finite-dimensional quantum systems with arbitrary, possibly unequal dimensions. The framework can handle generic tensor network states, including matrix product states. The authors define QC as a category where objects are finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces with dimensional typing, and morphisms are bounded linear maps. Key features include: a dagger functor (Hermitian adjoint), compact structures (cups and caps corresponding to Bell states and Bell effects), symmetric dots (copy dots • and plus dots ⊕), and generalized quantum gates (Z, X, ADD, NADD, NEG, discrete Fourier transform H). The framework subsumes the standard quantum circuit model while providing a rigorous mathematical foundation based on category theory. The paper demonstrates applications including circuit simplification, GHZ state preparation, superdense coding, quantum teleportation, and teleportation through a gate. Key results include the spider law for merging dots, the bialgebra and Hopf laws, and the ability to convert between diagrams and physically implementable quantum operations through complete sets of morphisms.

--- SOURCE 19: Categorical quantum mechanics - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Categorical_quantum_mechanics

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Categorical quantum mechanics is the study of quantum foundations and quantum information using monoidal category theory, pioneered in 2004 by Samson Abramsky and Bob Coecke. The mathematical setup is captured by a dagger symmetric monoidal category, where composition of morphisms models sequential composition of processes and the tensor product models parallel composition. Key structural features include: dagger compact categories (which distinguish input/output and allow description of entangled states, measurements, and protocols like quantum teleportation), completely positive maps for mixed states and quantum channels, no-cloning/no-deleting theorems reflected in wire structure, special commutative dagger Frobenius algebras for classical information, and complementary Frobenius algebras embodying complementarity (used in the ZX-calculus).

A notable feature is the use of string diagrams (tracing back to Penrose graphical notation, 1970s) which faithfully capture the compositional structure. The ZX-calculus has emerged as a diagrammatic counterpart to linear algebraic reasoning about quantum gates, with some versions proven complete.

Branches of activity include: axiomatization and new models (deriving quantum phenomena from weak abstract constraints), completeness and representation results (linking the abstract categorical setting to traditional Hilbert space quantum mechanics), categorical quantum mechanics as logic (a type-theoretic form of quantum logic supporting formal deductive reasoning), as a foundation for quantum mechanics (enabling study of which features single out quantum theory), and the DisCoCat framework (applying categorical quantum mechanics to natural language processing, leading to quantum natural language processing).
</summary>

Bob Coecke, Chief Scientist at Quantinuum and former Oxford University professor, presented a talk at the Royal Institution (posted January 7, 2025) introducing a new diagrammatic approach to understanding quantum mechanics that replaces complex mathematics with intuitive pictures. 

Coecke argues that the standard quantum formalism (von Neumann's Hilbert space approach) was denounced by von Neumann himself just three years after publication. He contrasts this with Schrödinger's insight that the most important aspect of quantum mechanics is what happens when two systems interact (entanglement/relationships), rather than von Neumann's focus on measurement.

Key to the approach is using "wires and boxes" (spiders) - a diagrammatic language inspired by Roger Penrose's 1950s notebook sketches. The rules are simple: same-colored spiders fuse together; different-colored spiders with two wires between them cancel out. This language is used to simplify quantum computing circuits (a state-of-the-art technique used in industry).

The most striking result: Coecke and Stefano ran an experiment with UK high school students aged 15-17. These students were given an 8-week online course (with black screens, no face-to-face interaction) using the diagrammatic method. At the end, they were given an Oxford University postgraduate exam - and 50% of the high school students achieved distinction, outperforming the typical Oxford postgraduate cohort. The course also motivated students to pursue STEM careers.

The approach has since been adopted internationally, with Greece receiving ministerial approval to teach quantum mechanics in high schools using this method, and courses being taught in Ghana.

--- SOURCE 30: Research – Quantum Information Theory | ETH Zurich ---
URL: https://qit.ethz.ch/research.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the research page of the Quantum Information Theory (QIT) group at ETH Zurich. The group's research is rooted in the insight that information and the laws of physics are closely intertwined. This relationship has two dimensions: (1) information processing is ultimately a physical process, so quantum mechanics determines what information-processing possibilities exist; (2) many physical phenomena (e.g., non-local correlations in quantum physics and the second law of thermodynamics) can be understood more deeply from an information perspective. The research has implications for both technology and fundamental science.

**Implications for technology:** The group aims to implement important information processing primitives (e.g., in cryptography) by harnessing elementary natural phenomena, such as non-local correlations from entangled quantum states. Applications include efficient and practical generation of randomness, a central resource in computer science.

**Fundamental implications:** The group seeks deeper insight into physical laws (particularly quantum physics and thermodynamics) by studying them from an information-theoretic viewpoint, using tools like entropy and randomness.

The page lists sub-pages for further reading: Quantum Information Theory, Quantum Cryptography, Quantum Computing, Quantum Thermodynamics, Time and Quantum Clocks, and Quantum Foundations.
</summary>

The initiative capitalizes on the "second wave" of quantum mechanics, where quantum information science (QIS) harnesses properties like superposition and entanglement for computing, sensors, and fundamental physics research. Q-FARM builds on Stanford and SLAC's existing expertise in quantum materials, quantum sensors, and the interface between QIS and fundamental physics, including work by Nobel laureate Robert Laughlin and physicist Leonard Susskind. Located in Silicon Valley near companies like Google investing in quantum computing, Q-FARM's priorities include creating postdoctoral and graduate fellowships, organizing research seminars, developing educational programs for undergraduates and graduates, and attracting government funding—including potential centers from the $1.275 billion National Quantum Initiative passed by the U.S. Senate in 2018.

On October 26, 2021, a research team led by Pan Jianwei, Lu Chaoyang, and Liu Naile from the University of Science and Technology of China (USTC), in collaboration with the Shanghai Institute of Microsystems and the National Parallel Computer Engineering Technology Research Center, successfully developed "Jiuzhang 2.0," a quantum computing prototype operating with 113 photons and 144 modes. The system features phase-programmable functionality and solves the Gaussian boson sampling task — used to demonstrate "quantum computational advantage" — at a speed 10^24 times faster than the fastest supercomputers using the best classical algorithms. The work was published in Physical Review Letters as an Editors' Suggestion and praised by quantum physicist Barry Sanders of the University of Calgary as a "dramatic tour de force" and "an impressive advance over the state-of-the-art."

Key innovations in Jiuzhang 2.0 include: (1) stimulated dual-mode quantum squeezed light sources, inspired by laser technology, which significantly improved photon yield, quality, and collection efficiency; (2) 3D integration and compact optical design expanding the multi-photon quantum interference circuit to 144 dimensions; (3) dynamic phase adjustment enabling reconfigurable Gaussian boson sampling matrices, demonstrating programmability. The output state space dimension reached 10^43. This work builds on the original Jiuzhang (2020), which used 76 photons and 100 modes and achieved a speed advantage of 10^14 times over supercomputers. The team notes that quantum advantage research is an ongoing competition between classical algorithms and quantum hardware, with long-term quantum parallelism expected to eventually surpass classical capabilities.

**核心问题：** 量子资源蒸馏是量子计算中的核心问题，旨在将受噪声影响的低质量量子资源转化为高质量资源。魔态（magic state）蒸馏是容错量子计算的关键瓶颈，其资源消耗直接影响未来大规模量子计算机的实现成本。此前，一次性有限资源场景中的蒸馏开销至少随目标精度按对数规律增长。

**主要创新：**
1. 引入"量子催化"机制——一个辅助量子系统参与变换后保持自身不变，可被重复使用。
2. 证明任意多shot量子蒸馏协议可被转化为一次性催化蒸馏协议，实现一次性常数级资源开销，突破对数下界。

4. 提出基于催化的时空资源转换（catalytic spacetime conversion）机制，实现量子空间资源与时间资源之间的可调节交换。

**额外成果：** 研究团队还将催化理论推广至量子信道（quantum channels）变换问题，证明"信道互信息"能完全决定量子信道之间的催化可转换性，解决了此前国际同行提出的一个公开猜想。

**发表信息：** 研究成果以"One-shot distillation with constant overhead using catalysts"为题，于2026年5月4日发表于《自然·通讯》（*Nature Communications*）。刘子文和方堃为共同通讯作者。

**意义：** 该工作理论上突破了量子资源蒸馏中的长期限制，为未来容错量子计算架构设计提供了新路线。由于方案主要依赖经典控制与系统重排等相对简单的操作，有望在可重构原子阵列等量子硬件平台上进行实验验证。

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The University of Tokyo and IBM Research have developed a Krylov Quantum Diagonalization (KQD) algorithm to extend quantum computers' capabilities for simulating condensed matter systems. Published in Nature Communications in June 2025, the research was led by UTokyo Associate Professor Nobuyuki Yoshioka and IBM Principal Research Scientist Antonio Mezzacapo, along with collaborators. The algorithm demonstrates exponential convergence toward estimating ground state energy for complex systems, such as organic molecules composed of hundreds of interacting particles. The work aims to calculate ground states of complex systems more efficiently than purely classical methods, with potential applications across chemistry and high-energy physics.

The post generated significant discussion, including a skeptical comment from Alan Shields arguing that without stable, scalable, error-corrected logical qubits, algorithmic breakthroughs remain theoretical and rely on classical post-processing. In contrast, Mehdi Jenab praised the achievement, noting successful convergence on systems as large as 56 qubits and highlighting how subspace methods bridge near-term heuristics and future fault-tolerant algorithms.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: How UTokyo & IBM developed new quantum simulation algorithm | IBM Quantum Computing Blog ---
URL: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/utokyo-kqd-algorithm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IBM Research blog post (published December 4, 2025) describes how researchers from the University of Tokyo and IBM developed a new quantum simulation algorithm called Krylov quantum diagonalization (KQD). The algorithm, described in a June 2025 paper in Nature Communications, is a technique for finding the ground state (lowest-energy state) of physical systems—a calculation that is often extremely challenging for classical supercomputers when dealing with many-body quantum systems like complex molecules.

KQD works by using quantum computers to solve linear algebra problems, specifically matrix diagonalization. The researchers leveraged Aleksey Krylov's 1931 technique of constructing subspaces that capture important features of a matrix. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive review paper on the ZX-calculus, authored by John van de Wetering (Radboud Universiteit Nijmegen and Oxford University, December 2020). The ZX-calculus is a graphical language for reasoning about quantum computation that has seen increasing use in quantum circuit optimization, surface codes, lattice surgery, measurement-based quantum computation, and quantum foundations.

The paper is divided into two main parts. Sections 2-5 provide a gentle introduction to ZX-diagrams and the ZX-calculus, suitable for those familiar with quantum computing basics. Sections 6-10 cover advanced topics more independently.

Key topics covered include:
- **ZX-diagrams**: Graphical representations of linear maps between qubits, using "spiders" (Z-spiders as white dots, X-spiders as grey dots) with phases, connected by wires. The diagrams are universal (can represent any linear map between qubits), sound, and complete.
- **Rewrite rules**: Spider fusion (same-color spiders connected by wires fuse with phases added), identity removal, copy rules, π-commutation, bialgebra and Hopf rules, Hadamard color-changing rules.
- **Clifford computation**: The paper discusses graph states, graph-like diagrams, local complementation, pivoting, and provides a graphical proof of the Gottesman-Knill theorem (Clifford computation can be classically efficiently simulated).
- **ZH-calculus**: An extension using H-boxes for convenient reasoning about Toffoli gates and other multi-linear Boolean logic gates.
- **Completeness results**: The paper reviews the history of completeness proofs (2017-2018 from Oxford and Nancy groups), showing that certain rule sets for the ZX-calculus are complete, meaning any equality between linear maps can be proven diagrammatically.
- **Extensions**: Mixed states, decoherence, discarding, classical control via doubling, and higher-dimensional qudits.
- **Categorical foundations**: The origins of ZX-calculus in categorical quantum mechanics, including Frobenius algebras, bialgebras, and monoids.

The paper includes extensive appendices with cheatsheets of generators, rewrite rules, and circuit identities. It also references software tools: Quantomatic (first rewriting software), PyZX (modern Python library for circuit conversion and simplification), and Tikzit (for typesetting diagrams).
</summary>

# Summary: Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (qLDPC) Codes

This article provides an in-depth technical analysis of Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (qLDPC) codes, an emerging class of quantum error-correcting codes that promise to dramatically reduce the overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Written by Marin Ivezic, it is an updated and expanded version of a 2023 article, reflecting the field's rapid progress through early 2026.

## What Are qLDPC Codes?

qLDPC codes are stabilizer codes (typically CSS codes) where each stabilizer generator involves a bounded number of qubits and each qubit touches only a bounded number of stabilizers. This sparse structure enables more efficient error syndrome extraction and potentially higher error correction performance than traditional approaches like the surface code. Key features include high encoding rates (many logical qubits per physical qubits), low overhead, and potentially high error thresholds.

## Key Code Families

**Bivariate Bicycle (BB) Codes:** Introduced by Bravyi, Cross, Gambetta, Maslov, Rall, and Yoder (2023/2024, Nature 2024). These are CSS codes constructed from two cyclic polynomials over a bivariate group algebra. IBM's "gross" code encodes 12 logical qubits into 144 data qubits and 144 syndrome ancillas (288 total physical qubits), achieving a net physical encoding rate of ~4.2%. These form the foundation of IBM's fault-tolerant roadmap.

**Generalized Bicycle (GB) Codes:** Extend the BB construction to broader abelian groups, enabling higher distances (e.g., d=24) at comparable block sizes. These are the exact family used in Iceberg Quantum's Pinnacle Architecture for breaking RSA-2048.

## Key Theoretical Breakthroughs

The article traces the evolution from Kitaev's toric code (1997) through Tillich & Zémor's hypergraph product codes (2009/2014), which achieved constant rate with distance scaling as Θ(√n). Major milestones include:
- **2020 (Hastings, Haah, O'Donnell)** : Quantum LDPC codes with linear distance
- **2021 (Breuckmann & Eberhardt)** : Asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes
- **2021 (Panteleev & Kalachev)** : Efficient constructions with linear distance and constant rate
- **2022 (Dinur, Hsieh, Lin, Vidick)** : Quantum Tanner codes achieving constant rate, constant relative distance, and efficient decoding

## Industry Adoption

### IBM
IBM underwent a major strategic pivot from surface codes to qLDPC codes. Key developments:
- **Loon processor (Nov 2025)** : Experimental chip with multi-layer routing and extra-long-range c-couplers for degree-6 qubit connectivity
- **Real-time decoding latencies below 480 nanoseconds**
- **"Tour de Gross" architecture (June 2025)** : First complete end-to-end fault-tolerant architecture built on qLDPC codes, targeting Starling (2029) with ~200 logical qubits executing 100 million gates

### Iceberg Quantum
An Australian startup founded in 2024, specializing in qLDPC code design.
